FOWL FEEDING.
A Varied Diet is Absolutely Essential
in the Winter.

it isNof little use for the early spring markets, since ducklings of this variety grow slowly. Orleans has apparently transferred its affec- tion for a rent-provider to the hen. Thus writes Mr. Consul-General Carew-Hunt on the sub- ject: "The high cost of living in the South of late, which, roughly speaking, makes i one spend five, coins here to obtain what two coins will buy in the United Kingdom, has made families with limited incomes look round to see how they can reduce their nousehold expenses. The old way of several couples joining together and taking a house between them and thus con- ducting a- sort of joint-stock housekeeping establishment does not work well in this semi- tropical climate, as the damp heat leads to fric- tion amongst the occupants. The keeping of poultry in sufficient numbers to reduce the butcher's bill is found to be a step in the rig4t direction, and nearly every back-yard in the town is turned into a poultry farm. The music of turkeys, geese, ducks and 'fowls is heard night and day. This new family industry has been a blow to the cold storage plants. They have had to get rid of their stale eggs at any price, as the family trade is closed to them now -that everyone has more eggs than they know The Aylesbury is the breed which should 'be de- pended upon, for it is an extraordinarily rapid grower. Thousands of ducklings of this variety are marketed every spring, each weighing from 411 b. to 51b., when only eight weeks old. This is quite a fortnight sooner than the liouen: The importance of this can hardly be exag- gerated, particularly where prices are at their highest point or when they are on the decline, for a week sometimes makes as much as a shilling or eighteenpence difference in the value. Those who are anxious to cater for this trade should pin their faith to the Aylesbury. In making arrangements for this trade it is neces- sary to pay particular attention to the stock birds, since much depends upon the stamina and their quality. In order to procure eggs during the winter young birds must be relied upon, for ducks coming on to their second season are Usually later in commencing to lay. This in itself means that the germs contained in fertile eggs are not so strong, since the par- ents have not reached maturity.

This lac% of vitality, however, can be over- come to a great extent by mating the young ducks with the two-year-old drakes. To ensure fertility it is advisable to mate only three ducks with each male during the earlier part of the season, though later on as spring advances the number may be slightly increased. .

div.head: DUCKS WHICH PAY.
div.p: DUCKS WHICH PAY.

The exact amount of meat to give per bird can only be definitely stated when the condi-' lions are known as to the amount of liberty the birds enjoy, and whether they have access to, land where insect and grub life may be ob- tained. The season must also be considered, since during an open season, such as we have had up to the present time, natural food is more abundant—at least, more readily secured than when the ground Is covered with snow or in the grip of a hard frost. Always essential, the necessity for change in the dietary is intensified as the natural re- sources of the poultry range become seasonably limited? The shortcomings of the feeder may be more or less remediecP during the open months by the greater ability of fowls to exer- cise some instinctive discrimination regarding vegetable and insect food; but in the coming season foraging is a comparatively profitless undertaking—apart from the benefits of activity. Unless the large producer provides the neces- sary variety and character, the small egg-pro- ducer is relatively better off in winter on account of the sufficiency for his purpose of the available broken food from his own table.

The farmer gives his pigs much kitchen and other refuse that might be more profitably fed to his fowls, and, although the value would be practically lost if fed indiscriminately to a large stock, such egg-forming material might very well be reserved for the layers. If only on account of their varied character, such house scraps of meat and vegetables are better than purchased substitutes for the summer range of natural food; and, by way Of seasonable variety in corn-feeding, the climatic changes will prob- ably soon justify the sparing use of maize and barley.

div.head: HEN THAT PAYS THE RENT.
div.p: THE HEN THAT PAYS THE RENT.

We have all-heard of the Irishman's pig as "the gentleman that pays the rent " ; New what to do with. This increased interest in all kinds of the feathered tribe has led to the starl- ing of numerous poultry shows in the prin- cipal cities. All of these have proved financial successes. Valuable prizes are given by them to the exhibitors, who are thus encouraged to ..extend their business as much as possible and rai)e the quality of their pets."
DUCKS WHICH PAY.

THE EXAMINER, SATUR JAY, OCTOBER 18, 1913.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.

With the arrival of dark mornings and even- ings, says a "Farm and Home" writer, it be- comes more difficult to obtain clean milk, how- ever clean the cows are kept. I know, this trouble of old. The 'men arrive in ,_the early *morning, light their lanterns, and get to work, first., Owing to the lower temperature, and pos- sibly to rain as well, closing the doors and windOws of the, cowshed. The stools are placed ,on the stall beside he cows, in spite of the inanure, which cannot be seen in the dark; no udders are washed, for a similar reason; and, ' unless an employer is determined on having his way, and makes a point of visiting the men, they milk just as they are—sometimes just as they got out of bed. Dairy farmers are progressive men, and will not tolerate dirt; but the milkers have not yet learnt what it means, and the care they exer- cise during the light mornings of summer is. ignored when winter arrives, and they Work at higher pressure. I have frequently and lately seen suggestions which relate to the straining of the milk for the renvval of dirt. Neither Sieves nor strainers are equal to cotton wool, which can now be obtained-adapted to the pur- pose of straining. One -of the most important changes to be effected in the cowhouse is by the intwduction of electric light, so that the men can milk under conditions equal to those of suminer—first hav- ing removed the dung. from the stall, washed the udders' of the cows, together with their glands, and subsequently donned their overalls. The question of clean milk is So important that it ought to be a universal matter of conscience, -which-indeed it is already on so/many farms.

div.head: BEATING IN HAY.
div.p: BEATING IN HAY.

Hay heats in the rick at all times if the con- ditions are good, but over-heating is promoted by stacking hay which is too moist; then, if there is too much air, there 1s trouble, zuld, as We have seen, sometimes ignition. I have' known maily eases in which rick § have been opened to get at the middle when hay has shown signs of excessive heat; but that is the very worst thing to do. By the exclusion of, air, and the consequent exclusion of oxygen,' the heat is contriolled. Normal heating not only accounts for the colour of the,hay, which gets too brown in the centre of a rick if the temperature rises too high, but for its flavour and aroma, both of which are almost absent when .there has been insufficient heat developed in the process of fermentation. Although over-heated and exces- sively brown hay is often consumed on the farm, it must not be forgotten that its value is •diminished, for, a portion of the carbohydrates ,which form its chief nutriment has been destroyed.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
NEW SWEET PEAS.

The outstanding novelty- of We season is a variety raised by Mr. Robert Holmes, who has already put on the market several well-known varieties. It is to be named ,after the late Mr. Robert Sydenham. It is a grand., deep self- coloured orange. It will not be in Commerce, however, until the autumn of 1914, and there IS sure to be a big demand for it. Florence Wright Spencer is mentioned as. a white variety, which will go well. Margaret Atlee, a cream-pink, is mentioned as likely to be the best of our cream-pinks.

div.head: DYING PLANT FOLIAGE.
div.p: DYING PLANT FOLIAGE.

The decaying foliage of plants in the her- baceous border often tempts the owner to cut down the plants soon after flowering, on the score of untidiness, forgetful of the fact that the material 4 which the green-colouring matter is composed, and especially the starch, recede from the leaves to the stems, and eventually to the crowns, where they remain for futtn4 use. This fact was demonstrated by Sachs, and since his discovery gardeners generally do not cut down the foliage until it is completely decayed. The question is now asked if it is not unwise to cut down Raspberry canes, as soon as the crop is gathered, for the same reason as other plants. If the materials . stored in the stems of herbaceous plants is necessary for their well- being, why should not the same rule apply' to all plants, fruiting as well as flowering. •

div.head: FREE-FLOW ERING PENSTEMON.
div.p: A FREE-FLOW ERING PENSTEMON.

Though of comparatively recent introduction, Penstemon Southgate Gem is rapidly increasing in popular favour, says t The Garden." A hybrid .between Hartwegii (Newbury Gem) and one of the large-flow-ered sorts, Southgate Gem inherits the fred-flowering..qualities of Hart- wegii, and has considerably • larger bright red flowers. .For the past two months four %large beds (containing about two hundred and fifty plants in each) 'in front of the lialm House at Kew have been admired' by thousands of visi- tors, and a succession of flowers seems assured for some time to come, judging by the number of uhopened buds. /

div.head: INCREASING PLANTS.
div.p: INCREASING PLANTS.

It is advisable, even if there is already a good stock of Pansies, to take cuttings in the autumn, and as the weather conditions have been so fav- ourable there should bb plenty of material. Those who have choice sorts should propagate freely by cuttings, as flowers are much superior on a new root each year. If glass space is scarce earlier rooted plants may be moved into their flowering quarters, and the space devoted to later cuttings. Give the cuttings a good watering at the time of planting, and keep moist all through, but not soddened with wet.

div.head: GET tNT Illi BULBS NOW.
div.p: GET tNT Illi BULBS NOW.

Those who int,end flowering bulbs should now lose no time in getting them in, whatever method pf growing be decided upon. They may be flowered in:soil, in fibre, and over water 'in glasses., as most people know-. The earlier they are planted the earlier they will flower, and this is a consideration when there are perhaps no other plants in bloom. If a large quantity of bulbs are purchased it is a good plan to plant at intervals, .thus ensuring a continuance of bloom. The Bofno,n Hyacinth is a very early bulb, and same plant as early as August.. Large bulbs of the Boman kind should 'be obtained, as they throw up as many as four and five spikes of flowers, whereas the small bulbs may perhaps only show one spike. Whether Hyacinths are grown 'in soil, fibre, or water they are in a way expensive bulbs,, and care is needed just as much after flowering as before. After they have been flowered in pots they always come in useful for planting in the garden the following season, and will give good- sized blooms. Showy flowers are more accept- able in the winter and spring than at any other period' of the year. Among the first ••arrivals are the Aconites, • with the Golden Buttercup- like blooms, set in a green frill ;'the Snowdrops. of the purest whiteness; the Sciflas and the Chionodoxas, with sprays of the richest- blue and white.

Then ,come Crocuses, in blue, purple, white md yellow, the latter appes.iring first. Along with these come the golden Daffodils and some of the early Narcissus. These of themselves will make a beautiful display, when economy has to be considered. These are followed by the I-Iyacinlhs,, bearing stately spikes, exhibit- ing all the richest shades of colour; and the gorgeous Tulips in every Shade and tint except- ing blue. Next in order come others of the Narcissus tribe, the Mhy-flowering Tulips, and the pure white scented Narcissus, to carry on the sequence until the more tender summer bedding. plants can be put out.

div.head: OUR RIGHT TO PURER AIR.
div.p: OUR RIGHT TO PURER AIR.
Representatiue Demands for the Abatement of

div.head: Smoke.
div.p: Smoke.
LEAGUE FORMED RI WARRIRIGTORI
The articles that have appeared in "The Examiner" of late upon the smoke problem have focussed public opinion on a question that has needed attention for years.

On Tuesday night a conference was held at the Academy, and, after speeches had been made by representative men, and numerous promises of support had been read, it was decided to form. a branch of the Smoke Abatement League for Warrington.

A .meeting, called at the Academy on Tues- day night by a circular signed by Canon Mor- iey Stevenson, Alderman Bennett, Mr: Charles E. Parker, and Mr. J. E. Ransome, to consider the advisability of forming a Vigilance Com- mittee or branch 'of the Smoke Abatement League for Warrington, was well attended, and many letters sympathising with the movement and offering co-operation were sent by those who were unable to be present. Alderman BENNErr, who presided at the out- set, read the letters of apology from those who were unable through prior engagements and other causes' to attend. '

prevent the output of noxious vapours. - It seemed strange•to hilt' that so many who lived on the fringe of the town were so deeply interested in this subject, but it was the old story that we, could not see ourselves as others see us. They saw it from that ditaflCe which lent enchantment to the view, and they could see at holiday times, and particularly during the late, coal strike, what a different atmos- phere hung over Warrington when the chim- neys were still. They noticed especially dur- ing the coal strike the clearness of the atmos- phere , and beautiful sunsets. (ApplauSe.) . There was not the slightest doubt as to _ the truth of what Dr. Manson saidlthat smoke was injurious to health ; no unbiased medical man could have two opinions about that. He knew of two cases in point. A child, suffering 7in town from pneumonia and complications which often arose in' town, was removed in almost a moribundchoaididitbioeenntolytihneg ountry. Although practicallythe child on its death bed for six weeks, it recovered by means of three weeks of country air. The treatment was just the same, and the child was not taken from a poor home. A map who had suffered for five months in the centre, of the town with chest complaint, made noprogress ;. in three weeks at Fearnhead he gained 191 b. II was not a question of, treatment, but of pure air. Ap- plause.) SOME SUGGESTIONS.

_ . , Mr. BANSOMW thought that if manufaVurers lived in the smoke instead of ,outside the town, thy would soon waken up to the unhealthy condition of the atmosphere in which the bulk of the population had to live. At a Went con- ference it was stated that tthere was a smoke question even in the 13th century, when it was provided that offenders should be condemhed to the gallows-,(laughter)—though there was no record of such a judgment having been car- ried out. (Laughter.) The London boroughs had taken action,, and the nuisance had ceased to exist on the factory side of_the question. It was said that Vesuvius was a child at turning out. black vapour, compared with the London' houses. He thought they might tackle ,the fac- tories locally, and thus go a considerable dis- tance towards improving the town.

--Kir:. B. S. TOWNROE said that something should be done in the interests of the health of the children who had to live in town. Of the firm that had taken a leading part in experi- menting in the reduction of smoke, the •Chair- man of Directors had lived close to the works, and Capt. Crosfield had lived not far away. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. H. SHERBURN said education on the subject was badly needed. Even in the Coun- cil Chamber one member echoed, the old cry that he liked to see smoke pouring out of the chimneys, because it meant good trade in the town. That statement was dictated by gross ignorance or something worse. Smoke from works, conld be reduced without injuring .trade, just as smoke from houses could 93e reduced by the careful putting on of coal which would ensure The gas being burnt instead of thrown away.

MI'S. PEMBERTON said the works smoke made a great deal of the filth with -which women had to contend in their homes. After they had tackled this, she thought they might pay at- tention to the stoking of house fires. Land- lords -should be made to use grates that would burn the smoke More than at present. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: AN INFLUENTIAL MOVEMENT.
div.p: AN INFLUENTIAL MOVEMENT.

Alderman BENNETT said that, as many of them , knew, be had been fighting this question in the council for nearly twenty years 1 with very little support, and he had sonietimeS. felt that he was "a voice crying in the wilderness." (naughter.) He had, however, "cast his bread Upon the waters," and he was finding it "after many days." (Hear, hear.) Thanks largely to. the magnificent backing which he had received. froM "The Examiner," public opinion was be- ginning to crystallise upon the question, and the interesting letters which it had been his privilege to read, and the representative at-- tendance at the meeting, were indicative of a widespread feeling which was only waiting for an opportunity of suitable eXpresSion. lithe Council and the Health Committee • could be made to feel that smoke abatement was .not a mere fad, but a practical business proposition, and that the public Were p,waking to the enormity of the evil, and were keeping a close eye upon them, he did not doubt that they would begin to seriously grapple ,with the pro- blem. He had frequently discussed the mat- ter with Mr. Parker, Canon SteKenson, and others, and they were all of opinion that, in order to focus opinion on the subject, it was desirable to form some definite 10-Cal organisa- tion. He need scarcely say that none of them wanted to hamper ofir local industries, but they thought it very necessary th-at the responsible committee should apply a gentle, but persist- ent pressure to the offenders, in order to make ,them realise their duty to the town and neigh- bourhood, and their responsibilities under the Public Health Act; and he, was perfectly con- fident that, if they could only get them to instal the proper appliances and to exercise reasonable care, they would be able to reduce the nuisance.to a ruinimum,and that trade would benefit, instead of suffering, by the 'change. (Hear, hear.) It was highly gratifying to know that they were supported by three of their most Prominent local manufacturers—Mr. -Parker and Mr. Fiansome, who were present at the meeting, and Captain ,Crosfield, whose .letter .they had heard, and whose firm was famous all over England for its "smokeless chimneys." .(Hear, hoar.) Others would eventually rally to their cause;, and he did not doubt that they ivould be able to launch that night an influ- ential and far-reaching movement. In order to open the matter for discussion lie—would formally move: "That a Warrington and Dis- trict Branch of the Smoke Abatement League be and is hereby established." (Applause.)

div.head: WHY WE SUFFER.
div.p: WHY WE SUFFER.

Mr. PARKER, in seconding, stated, that what was needed in Warrington was an effort to make the Town Council realise the need there was for taking action. It was the duty of the Council to carry out tile provisions of the Public Health Act, and it was Clear they could do se without injuring any interest. As a matter of fact„ he was one of those who had had to study closely the saving in costs that could be effected in the mattei. of steam power pro- duction by the proper treatment of fuel. No effective action had been taken by the War- rington authorities, and this had caused the Offenders to think no action would be taken. This accounted for the state of things under Which we suffered. (Hear, hear.)'

DOCTORS DISAGREE WITH THE MAYOR. Dr. NIANsoN, supporting, said the men in his projession would sooner try to keep the people healthy than to have to give them a bottle of medicine. He noticed that the Mayor (Dr. Joseph) agreed with the Chairman of the I:Tealth Committee (Alderman James Evans) that smoke had not been proved to be injurious to health. The Mayor went further, and said it was pos- sibly beneOcial—(laughter)—and they both quoted, figures referring to a town where the Smoke Abatement League had been in active work. The death-rate of Manchester was .1.5 above that of Warrington—from all causes. The Chairman of the Health Committee was right when he said the action of snioke had reference 6hiefly to the respiratory system, but he -did not quote the figures bearing upon that side of the question. Dr. Niven, of Manchester, had conclusively proved that smoke and fogs, which were largely due /to carbon particles, in the atmosphere, had an ill-effect, and that after fogs deaths did increase from these - causes. Dr. Fife, of Glasgow, had proved the same fact. He (the *speaker) thought that the idea that smoke was not injurious to health could be put out of court as being too childish to be con- sidered.

Dr. BENNETT emphasised what "The Examiner" said on Saturday with regard to the position of the Chairman of ifie. Health Committee. The Chairman ccunpared War- rington with Manchester, but 'he forgot the density of population, theotarrow streets, the alien population and the large- area of Manches- ter, which must be considered against the fact that Warrington had country ,all round. (Hear, hear.) If the Manchester death-rate was any- where near that of Warrington, Warrington ought to be ashamed of itself. (HAar, hear.) MancheSter had offensive waterways, back-to- back houses, and a considerable rainfall—Provi- dential, perhaps, because it cleansed the atmos- phere of the impurities of its smoke more rapidly. Some of the Heafih Committee seemed to protedt themselves by saying that smoke was not only smoke but vapour. Gasses did escape that were, perhaps, detrimental to health, but that was no reason why we should let the smoke go on undisturbed. "Let us get something remedied," said the Doctor, amid applause. div.head: MINISTER'S COMPARISONS.
div.p: A MINISTER'S COMPARISONS.

The Rev. T. T. JAMES thought they were tak- ing a reasonable and desirable step. He thought they might exaggerate the idea Of the dirt which came from domestic smoke, because on Sundays, when the works were practically stopped, all the house fires were going; that was the only day on Which ,many people cooked a dinner. Yet there was a remarkable differ- ence in the atmosphere on Sundays cornpared with working days. He did not think they needed further legislation; if they got a reason- able administration of the , powers already possessed the necessary improvement would be effected, it appeared to him to be madness, and throwing away money to spend so much on educating children, while they allowed them to live in conditions that reduced their health below the standard.when they could take proper advantage of the instruction. For a town the size of Warrington he thought we produced a tremendous amount of dirt. Sheffield was di iy but he was afraid _Warrington was worse. (Applause.) Mr. W. WILKINSON, Pinewood-avenue, Pad- gate-lane, supported as a, working inan. There was a lack of interest in the question among the working classes, which he very much regretted. Dr: MANSON mentioned the firing of house chimneys, which was a great nuisance ; they might get the police to act. The resolution was carried unanimously.

div.head: ELECTIONS.
div.p: ELECTIONS.

Alderman BENNETT proposed Nlr. Parker as president of the branch. No one, he said, had worked harder to promote 'better conditions in Warrington. Every good movement had Mr. Parker's support, and the community wore deeply indebted to him.' - (Applause.) Mr. Parker, at all events, could not be cbnsidered a faddist on this question,•as he was a practical man, engaged in the management of works. (hear, hear.) • Mr. BANSOME seconded, and it was unani- mously carried.

Mr. PARKER was then asked to take the chair, and in doing so said he had been deeply inter- ested in the question. Sheffield, which had been mentioned, had greatly increased its sun- shine, but they had a capital inspector; Mr. Nichol Son, who had done admirable work. On the motion of Dr. BENNETT, seconded by the Bev. T. I'. JAMES, the following provisional committee was appoint,ed to draw • up a, con- stitution and nominate the officials :—The Chaii•man, Alderman Bennett, Dr. Mansoh, Mrs. Pemberton, Mr. BanAome and Mr. Townroe. They were empowered to consider the advis- ability of making the smoke nuisance one of the questions at the approaching elections.

div.head: BOY SINGER IN PUBLIC-HOUSE.
div.p: BOY SINGER IN PUBLIC-HOUSE.
A Latchford Man's istake.

William lace, licensee of the. Man at the Wheel Hotel, Church-street, Runcorn, was sum- moned On Monday for allowing a child under the age of fourteen years to be on his premises during opening hours, Mr. W. E. Hough, who prosecuted on behalf of the police, said on September 27 Sergeant Worthington and Constable , Robinson visited the premises at 9.40 in the evening. They found between forty and fifty young fellows singing in the bar parlour, and they also saw a boy singing. ~The sergeant called the defendant's attention' to tho boy, and he immediately replied that the boy was turned fourteen but not six- teen. After the boy, had finished singing he and his father and the licensee went into the kitchen. The sergearit then asked the boy his age, and he said fourteen on February 2 last.

Mr. F. A. Lake, who defended, said by tile sub-section of the Children Act, under which the prosecution was taken, the onus lay on the prosecution to show whether the publican did not exercise due diligence in preventing a child being admitted to his house. His client's wife asked the boy's father whether his lad was four- teen years of age, and he replied that he was over fourteen.

The case was dismissed on payment of costs, 16s. 6d., but the Bench remarked that no conviction would be recorded. Daniel James Kennedy, 336, Thelwall-lane, Latchford, was charged with causing a boy under the age of fourteen to be on licensed premises. The defendant, who said be had no knowledge that the lad was under fourteen years of age. was ordered to pay the costs, 10s. 6d.
Enormous catches of herrings, estimated at over 10,000,000 fish, were landed at Yarmouth on Saturday, the luckiest boat, with 260,000 herrings, realising over. X. 300 for her night's work.

div.head: RURAL ENGLAND.
div.p: RURAL ENGLAND.
"THE EXAMINER" EDITION OF THE LAND INQUIRY REPORT.

This week "The Land," the authoritative record of the report of the Land Enquiry Com- mittee (vol. 1 (Doling with the fural aspect of the question) has been published .by Messrs. Hodder and Stoughton. _

-- - , We have been appointed agents for the book, with exclusive rights for the Warrington dis- trict, and we shall be happy to supply copies either direct or through agents, who will be supplied by us at wholesale rates. -

Tue hook deals with rural England. It is published in paper covers at the popular, price of one shilling net, and in cloth at two shillings net. The following are some of the chapter headings: The Scope and Method of the Rural Enquiry; The Agricultural Labourer and His Wage; Rural Housing; The Tied Cottage and the Labourer's Liberty; The Agricultural Labourer and Access to the Land; The Garden ano the Allotment; Small Holdings; The Cul- tiv'ation of the Soil; Game; Security of Tenure; State-aided Purchase; The Land Court; Rural Rating; Co-operation; Credit; Transit; Educa- tion.

div.head: BETTER CONDITIONS.
div.p: BETTER CONDITIONS.

'Mr. Lloyd George, says the "Westminster Gazette," was unjustly blamed by people who knew nothing of hard work done behind the scenes, for having rushed his Insurance scheme without proper preparation. That charge, at all events, cannot even plausibly be made about the coming land schemes. The foundations have been well and truly laid by a serious effort to assemble all the facts in which men expert in social research. like Mr. Seebohm Rowntree and Mr. Cross, have co-operated with land- owners, farmers, agents, labourers, clergymen, and other people who have a lifelong know- ledge of rural conditions.

The picture which comes to our mind is :that of some authority armed with sufficient power to make schemes for rural areas, as the En- closure Commissioners made them a hundred years ago,, and adjusting the various interests to the new and better conditions.

div.head: HANGED IN POLICE BUILDINGS.
div.p: HANGED IN POLICE BUILDINGS.
Warrington Man Chooses Strange
Death.

A sensation was occasioned in the Liverpool Police Buildings on :Monday by the discovery of a man's body suspended by a muffler from the lower banister of the staircase in the magis- trates' entrance. Sergeant Fleetwood cut the body down, but life was extinct, and the body was removed to the mortuary. On examination a deep gash was found in the man's throat. The dead man was not known by the officials or the police. It is conjectured that he secreted himself in the building on Saturday before- it closed at 2.30 p.m. Later the body was identi- fied as that of Elijah Birkenhead, a flatman, of 337, Wellfield-street, Warrington. At the inquest on Tuesday, Robert Birken- head, Wellfield-street,.Warrington, said deceased was his brother. He was a healthy man, but was given to drinking. He knew of no reason why ,he should hang himself. James Stanley, master of the fiat Wesley, on which deceased was employed, said that deceased drank to excess. . On Saturday he seemed to be suffering from the "rats," as he acted peculiarly.
A verdict Of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane" was returned.
Apparently carol) of a vessel wrecked. on the Goodwins, eight large hogshead of wine in good condition have been found floating in the 'sea by Deal, Walmer, and Kingsdown boatmen.

div.head: "LOYAL OLIVE BRAIIGH."
div.p: "LOYAL OLIVE BRAIIGH."
The Oddfellows Make an Interesting Presentation.
BROTHER BROWN HONOURED.

A meeting of a very interesting character in connection with the "Loyal Olive Branch" Lodge of Independent Oddfellows took place on Saturday at the Roebuck Hotel. A Past Officer's Certificate, splendidly framed, - was presented to John Brown by District grand Master George Higham for the valuable services he had rendered during his term of office. In making the presentation, the Grand Master said that Bro. Brown had always been a very ardent worker in the cause of Oddfellow- ship, and he was .pleased the Lodge was recog- nising his services, and he was also pleased to see he (Bro. Brown) had now regained his health after the serious accident he met with a short time ago. He hoped that presentation would remind him of the pleasant times he had spent in connection with the Order, and that he would live long and die a good Oddfellow. In response, P.G. Brown thanked the officers and brethren of his Lodge for the beautiful emblem they had given him. He had tried many times earlier on in life to obtain a Past Grand's certificate, but, owing .to circumstances over which he had no control, he had not been suc- cessful. However, he felt very pleased that at last lie had succeeded .in gaining the emblem for which he was sincerely thankful, and lie could assure them it would be treasured as long as he lived.

div.head: Past Grand's Jewel.
div.p: Past Grand's Jewel.

Another pleasing presentation was made by I.P.P.G.M. Herbert Whitelegg, of Lymm, to Past Grand Albert Butterworth, i.e., that of a Past Grand Jewel. Bro. Whitelegg spoke very highly of the .work done by P.G. Butterworth during the time he had been associated with'the. Lodge, and hoped he would still continue to serve the Lodge as faithfully as he had done in the past: He (Bro. Whitelegg) had noticed On several occasions the interest Bro. Butterworth had taken in his Lodge, and it was, certainly essential that every brother should do so if the Lodge was to attain the Success they all desired. He hoped the recipient would live long to wear the jewel, and he felt sure Bro. Bntter Worth was proud that the Lodge had recognised his services.

P.G. Butterworth thanked all the officers and members of the Lodge for the kindness they had bestowed .upon him in presenting him with such a beautiful jewel, which he assured them he was very proud to become the recipient of. It was a pleasure to go through the various offices, and he would in the future, as he had done in the past, endeavour to promote the in- terests of the "Olive Branch" Lodge.

div.head: Another Presentation.
div.p: Another Presentation.

The most interesting event of the evening was a presentatiOn in the form of a smoker's cabinet to P.P.G.M. Alban Boyle, secretary of the Lodge. This was presented by Past Grand George Brown on behalf of the officers and brethren of the Lodge, as a token of their high esteem and ap- preciation of the valuable services he had ren- dered to the Lodge during the eighteen years he had held the position of secretary. P.G. Brown spoke at length in a most pleasant and complimentary manner of the ser- vices and sacrifices P.P.G.M. Boyle had made in connection with his duties as secretary, and hoped that as the smoke curled upwards from his 'pipe of peace it would remind him of his old associations with his Lodge, and always bring back pleasant memories of the happy times he had spent amongst them. Several supplementary speeches with regard to the -Work done by P.P.G.M. Boyle were made by p.p.G3.1. Ellis Clare, P.G., William Hough- ton, P.G. Thomas Seed, P.G. Arthur Cotterill, and the District Secretary, P.P.G.M. Frank Webster.

Came as a Surprise. After several minutes of hearty cheering, and the singing of "lie's a jolly good` fellow," P.P.G.M. Boyle responded in a very able man- ner, and in the course of his remarks said he could hardly find words sufficiently adequate to express his gratitude for the very kindly words which had been said by the various brethren, and also for the handsome cabinet the members of his Lodge had given him. It had certainly come as a very great surprise to him, and he complimented the committee for guarding their secret so well. He felt sure he had always tried to do his duty, and that he considered was all that was expected of him. When he was Appointed secretary about eighteen years ago, the Lodge at that time was going through a very critical period, but after a strenuous effort, and solid, hard work, he was pleased to say he managed to get things into a satisfactory state of completeness. He Was pleased to think that the services he had rendered were so greatly appreciated, and assured the Members that he also appreciated their great kindness to him. Bro. Boyle reminded them that he was Grand Master of the district at the time he was ap- pointed secretary of his Lodge, which, as many of them knew, entailed a great amount of work, so much so that he accepted the secretaryship with great reluctance. He appealed to the young members to take an interest in the man- agement of the Lodge by attending regularly and exerting themselves to secure members, and went on to say .that if Oddfellowship intended to hold the high position it did amongst friendly societies it would have to command willing helpers. - _

The District Officers present (this being their official visit) were :. G.M. George Higham, D.G.M. Henry Lawrence, I.P.P. Herbert White- legg, and P.P.G.M. F. Webster. The meeting was presided over by N.G. Henry Bentley, and there were several Past Provincial Grand Masters present, including P.P.G.INI. T. Rigby, P.P.G.M. Ellis Clare (Douglas, 1.0. M.), P.P.G.M. William Holbrook, P.P.G.M. Peter Lester, and other prominent members of the district. The musical part of the proceedings was well sustained by songs, S.T., rendered by Mr. Welsby, P.G. Arthur Cotterill, P.P.G.M. Alban Boyle, P.G. Thomas Seed, and P. G. Albert Ayre, while Bro. Peter Lawless proved himself an efficient accompanist. The singing of the National Anthem brought a very pleasant evening to a close.

div.head: NURSE'S SEVERE COUGH.
div.p: NURSE'S SEVERE COUGH.
Quite cured. Would like to see VENUS IN EVERY HOME.

Nurse Bradshaw, of 11, Hill-street, Garnet- hill; Glasgow, is a busy professional nurse, well known and deservedly popular. "In my pro- fessional capacity I have to go out in all weathers," she told a reporter, "and one win- ter night I caught a severe cold. I became hoarse, a nasty cough soon developed, and my bronchial tubes seemed to be getting Choked up with phlegm. I ought to have gone to bed, but I had patients to attend, so I just put on a, mustard leaf and tried the usual remedies. How- ever, these did not help, and I was getting worse when it occurred to me to try Veno's Lightning Cough Cure. The effect was surprising. In a short time the hoarseness was gone, I could breathe freely, and soon I was quite well. Since then I have recommended Veno's Lightning Cough Cure to many people, and in every case it has cured. I should like to 'see it in every home." Venb's Lightning Cough Cure is a per- fect remedy for all diseases of chest, lungs and throat. in children or adults. Price 9id., and 219 of all chenlists.
Veit to be Uncovered.

Under the direction of the Italian Minister of Public Instruction, says "Science Siftings," the ancient city of Veii, near Borne; and the most famous of all buried cities, is to be excavated on a large scale. On various previous occa- sions the site has been tapped, the Work being very limited, but sufficient to arouse curiosity concerning the mysteries of the Etruscans, Veii has been in the minds of people who have known about it for many generations, although doubt as to its existence has been expressed by various authdrs, but Dionysius, in speaking of the third war of Romulus against it, says .that it was the most poweilul of, the twelve cities of the Etruscan league. Already in, the present excavations the extreme southern part has been unearthed; bringing to light the lower pait of an amphitheatre, formed of large relics.

div.head: WHAT THE " MERIORIAL: LICA" CONTIthNEI3.
div.p: WHAT THE " MERIORIAL: LICA" CONTIthNEI3.
Seas Broken En the Fresenoe of an HistoriGari gather j.
Old Warrington Bridge, opened in 1837, is rapidly disappearing, making way for the new ferro-concrete one-span structure which has already partially taken its place.

Last Friday our old friend gave up its key- stone, about which so much interest was aroused in consequence of our reproduction on September 27th of an article which appeared in a Liverpool journal more than seventy years ago, dealing with the laying of the stone.

In that article; which was admirably and graphically written, it was shown that the stone was put in position in 1836, with elab- orate Masonic ceremonial, and that in a cavity was placed a glass "memorial box," containing coins of that and the previous reign. His Worship the Mayor (Dr. Joseph) decided to break the seal over the cavity at the Town Hall on Saturday morning, and the stone, whicti weighed 12 cwt., was taken to the front of the Town Hall for that purpose.

As the Masons of seventy-seven years ago had played so important a part in the laying cere- mony, he invited the Worshipful Masters. of the six Ledges. of the town to take part in Saturday's proceedings.

Over the cavity was a brass plate, on which it was stated that the key-stone was laid by L. G. M. Starkie, Esq., P.G.M., W.D.C.L., Dec. 22, 1836. When this had been removed, the 'Mayor extracted the glass "memorial box," which contained numerous coins, ranging from a sovereign to a farthing. His Worship com- mented on the fact that the Masons took a leading part in the ceremony of 1836, when there was no Town Council, and they had to go to a Liverpool paper for an account of the ceremony.
"No Town CCUilCii and no newspapers—happy times!": said his Worship, amid laughter.
might not have been thought of for many years
How the Stone was Laid.

He 'would-like to call their -attention to a recent article in the Warrington " ExaMiner," in which—very likely most of them, if, not all, had read it—there was an excellent account of the ceremony of laying the old'keystone, which they had found in suth an excellent condition. In that article they read df the, great enthusiasm which -existed on the 22nd December, 1836, which called to their mind that the institutions and customs had completely changed. There was no Town Council, no newspapers-. (Laugh- ter.) Some nfight say ." happy times "; he would not deny it. The fact that the interest- ing account in "The Examiner" was sent by a local correspondent to a Liverpool- journal of that day shbwed that they were quite destitute of .a local Press in 1836. They saw from the account that amongst the bodies and persons taking. part in the ceremony, the Masonic brotherhood, were decidedly prominent. (Ap- plause.) He believed that to be' a worthy dis- tinction to the ,brotherhood of that time, and that explained why he had invited the Masonic representatives of to-day. • The account showed that the ladies of the period were ver promi- nent in the ceremony, and were almost the fore- most in their enthusiasm, and also in showing off to the utmost advantage their gaudy plumes and feathers. (Laughter.)
A Well-made Bridge.

The Old structure was now rapidly approach- ing demolition, and the stone had borne a weight, at a modest computation, of 50,000,000 tons and more, and the stone was as good to- day as when it was laid. (Applause.) The en- thusiasm shown on the day of the ceremony was amply vindicated by the ceremony to-day; they knew they had every reason to be proud of the men who took part in that ceremony, and they honoured their memory. (Applause.) With regard to the work they were now doing .under the auspices of their engineer and con- tractor, Mr. Thorne, whom he was glad to see there, and Mr.. Cobb, and those who, acted with them, he hoped the future generations, when the time came for the new bridge to be demol- ished, would look on their memory in the same way as they did Of ,thosa,who were instrumen- tal in erecting the old Structure, which he was sorry to see demolished. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.)
WORK THAT HAS STOOD THE
TEST OF TIME.

Speaking as a Mason, Bro. Alderman TINNION, P.M., said he would have liked Alder- man Pierpoint to reply on behalf of the Masons of Warrington, ,because Alderman Pierpoint was one Of the oldest, and certainly one of the most distinguished, Masons of the town. The fact that struck him (the sneaker) was that the Mayor had said the work had been well done and had stood• the test of time. That, he thought, was largely owing to the interest the Masons took in the building of the old bridge. ;Hear, hear.) Whatever Masons „undertook to do, the stones were well and truly laid, and the results ' here, as elsewhere, spoke, well for the integrity and righteousness of the Masons. (Applause.) At the time when the old bridge was commenced there was a strong brotherhood in Chester, and it Vas probable that the Masons in connection with the structure, were connected with that Masonic body. WhaleVer they did, and whatever' work they undertook to do, not only of the material kind, but of the moral and religious kind, Would bear the light of day, and all Masons believed that whatever was done was done well. He was pleased ,to know that the Masons of the past took such interest in their work, and especially in thal particular work. He hoped all their • work would bear the test of time, as the bridge had done. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: STONE AND ITS SECRET.
div.p: THE STONE AND ITS SECRET.
The large stone was conveyed to the front of the Town Hall on a lurry, on which were Mr. A. Thorne, Mr. J. P. Thorne, Mr. P. 11. Thorne and Mr. Cobb (the engineer). •

His WORSHIP the M7kvoil then ascended and invited Aldermen Smethurst (chairman of tl}e Bridges ,Committee) and Bennett, and the. Worshipful Masters of the Masonic Lodges, to accompany him. These represeatative Freemasons were : W. Bro. H. Isherwood, " Senior " Lodge 148: W. Bro. F. Rose, "Gilbert Greenall " Lodge; W.' Bro. W. H. Stansfleld, " Charity " Lodge; W. 'Bro. It H. Evans, 1.P.M., " Friendship " Lodge; W. Bro. 1% Stringer, "St. " Lodge; and W.,8r0.' H. F: Greenough, 'Lodge of Rectitude."
Mr. THORNE formally presented the stone to the Mayor, who said he presumed that the brass plate would be removed, and whatever was inside would be taken out.
The plate bore the following inscription : TIIE
KEYSTONE OF THE CENTRE ARCH
OF THIS BRIDGE
WAS LAID BY
L. G. M. STARKIE, Esq., P.G.M., W.D.C.L.,
22nd DECEMBER, 1836.

On the back of the plate, which was removed by Mr. Cobb, was the name "Unsworth, War- rington," presumably that of the maker. The MAYOR then gently lifted out a glass box, which contained a number of coins—and noth- ing else.
HISTORIC SCENE IN THE COUNCIL CHAMBER.

When the Mayor and officials assembled in the Town Hall there were present: Aldermen Smethurst, Pierpoint, Bennett, Tinnion, John Evans, Councillors Peacock, Billies, Wilkinson, Gough, Cunnington, Jenkins, Chrimes and Pemberton, Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr. A. T. Hallaway (deputy town clerk), Mr. Madeley (Librarian), Mr. Martin Nicholls (Chief Constable), and others. . The following Masonic Brethren were also present: Bros. H. E. Travis, T. L. CrOmpton, T. J. Lee and E. Warren, and the six Worshipful Masters. A number of prominent townsmen were also present.

div.head: TIIE * COINS.
div.p: TIIE * COINS.

An adjournment was then made to the Coun- cil Chamber, where The MAyoR said Mr. Spinks would take a list of the .coins, as he. (the Mayor) took them out. They would be handed round for inspection, and he might remind them that the Chief Con- stable was present. (Laughter.) He then lifted the lid of the box, which bore the Masonic emblem, and the first coin to be lifted, out was a half-crown for 1834. The full list of coins was as follows:
Sovereign ... 1833 Half-crown ... 1834 Shilling 1834 Sixpence 1831 Fourpence ... 1836 Fourpence 1836 Penny (George IV.) 182- Penny ... ... 1831 half-penny half-penny 1831 1834
Farthing
Farthing Masonic Medal
THE MAYOR AND FORMER /MS.

The MAYOR remarked that they were very sparing, with coins in those days. Continuing, he said they were met upon What might be termed a unique- occasion. They were prac- tically unfolding a new page in the history of Warrington, and it would greatly appeal to all of them—probably to none of them more than Alderman Bennett, whom he would characterise as Irving more in the past than the present Or the future. He certainly lived equally-in those three epochs of time. In extricating the stone, which might be called the representative of a Very noble structure; in relieving it from its weight of responsibility of 77 years, they lad somewhat mixed feelings. They felt they were getting a step nearer to the completion of the new bridge, to which they Rll looked forward with 'pride. They felt they , were bringing to the surface of their thoughtsmeniorie4 of those who Were gone, and the names of those who

div.head: SACRED TRUST.
div.p: A SACRED TRUST.
Coins Presented to the Museum Committee.

In presenting the box and the coins to Alder- man Bennett, in his capacity of chairman of the Museum Conlmittee, The MAYOR said he had great pleasure in doing so, recognising to the full the solemnity of the occasion. He handed over the coins and box, knowing they would be held in safe cus- tody for the inhabitants of Warrington.

div.head: i‘I,DERMAN BENNETT ON PAST, PRESENT
div.p: i‘I,DERMAN BENNETT ON PAST, PRESENT
AND TURE.
A C;tizen of No :Wan City.

Alderman , BENNErr had great pleasure in accepting the box and coins as a sacred trust. What they had witnessed that morning assured him still more - than ever of a fact he could never forget, that he was a citizen of no mean city. (Applause.) They could go back for cen- turies and the history of Warrington was great and famous. The Manner in which their ances- tors had done theirs in the' past was an object lesson for those intent in doing their duty in the present and in the ,future. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Beamont, the first Mayor of Warrington, whose portrait looked down, upon them from the past, is a book to. teach the present how to improve .the future. He thought that was a most wise and pregnant saying. (Hear, hear.) If he lived in the past he also lived in the future. He was interested in the past because he be- lieved it wtis the foundation upon which the future was to be built, firm and strong. Those who laid the stone had no idea that nearly a hundred years afterwards the stone would be removed in such a wonderful condition. The previous bridge had lasted • ..300 years. We ought to do our work in the 'same spirit as it had been done in the. past, and also enter into our duties, thinking we were the cUstodians of posterity. We had a full and proper respect. for those who had gone before. He hoped that the stone itself would be pre- served in_ some appropriate and prominent place in the town.
The Significance of "G."

Unfortunately he was not a Mason himself, but he had been told that a speciaL significance attached to the letter "G," which had been found on one of the sides of the stone. Coun- cillor Wilkinson had told him that he was in- formed that the builder of the old bridge was named Gannon, and that the initial was his. A Mason informed him that there was a greatly different meaning—that the use of the "G" in accordance with Masonic custom, referred to God, the Great Architect ,of the• Universe. He was glad to think til;.? the motto of the town

was "Deus dat Incrementum"—" God gives the increase." If we alvays bore these things in mind while we worked for the good Of the town. God would give us the increase, and Warring- ton would be even' more noble in the future than in the past. (Applause.)-

div.head: REASON WHY YOU SHOULD DRINK
div.p: REASON WHY YOU SHOULD DRINK
A LINK WITH THE PAST.

In proposing a vote of, thanks to the Mayor, Alderman SMETHURST said that his Worship had been very kind in the manner he had arranged for the opening of' the sacred vault. They also thanked the Mayor for his hospi- tality. (Hear, hear.) He (the Alderman) had watched for the keystone To be lifted, and had wondered- when they would get it out. 'On Thursday a small party assembled to see the work accomplished, but so ,little effect had the tools and the hest labour upon the stone that had to be removed before they could reach their prize that night •overtook them and operations had to be suspended till Friday morning. At seven o'clock on Friday morning the stone was secured—and Alderman Bennett, enfhusiagie aS ever, was there to witness it. (Applause.) The. Alderman had been greatly interested in the work. Mr. Penkelh, who then owned Penketh's foundry,. was prominent in connec- tion with the ,building of the old bridge. He had owned, and his son now owned,- that foundry, and it was a coincidence that he should be there, as chairman of the. Brids Committee, to see the work undone-which had been so wvll and .truly .accomplished by his predecessor in business. ..(Applause.). Councillor WILKINSON, seconding, referred to the remark made by' Alderman Bennett in re-- gard to the letter ".G." Some 26 years ago, when in Congleton, he made the acquaintance of a very old gentleman, over 80 years of age, who said, "You, come from Warrington. My father-in-law built that bridge, and his name is Gannon. Yo il will find on the keystone - tfie letter "G," 6id in it a. glass receptacle, with coins and papers in." He (the Councillor) was disappointed that there were no papers. had mentioned the matter to the Town Cferk. Mr. -Whittle; some time ago; and, they had had many conversations about it. (Applause.)

- PRAISE FOR THE ENGINEERS. . Alderman BENNETT wished to add that the engineers had taken a great interest in the work, and it was owing to them that they re- ceived tbe stone in such a good condition that day. (Hear, hear.) Bro. H. ISHERWOOD- supported the vote of thanks on behalf of the local :Masonic lodges. Alderman SMETHURST wa.S delighted that Alderman Bennett had spoken'the words he had with regard to the engineers. The vote having been carried with acclama- tion, followed by cheers for the Mayoress, 7 • The MAYOR, in reply,- said he was glad of what had been said in regard to the engineers. They had shown a great- interest in the matter. • He had nothing but good to say of the resident engineer and his sons, and he said that in face of any opposition, which he knew would .not come that morning, at all events. (Laughter.) He had invited. the Masonic brethren because he thought it was his duty to, do so. He was only sorry that that occasion could _not com- pete with the older one on its ceremonial side, but there had been some doubt as to when the stone would be excavated. .He had given a show of honour to the 'occasion, and he thought , he was not wanting in the same feelings .as . Alderman Bennett in the veneration of the past and his hopes for the future. (Applause.)

div.p: ERUPIION ON BABY'S LEGS.

div.head: WILL OF ALLAH.
div.p: THE WILL OF ALLAH.

A .friend, who returned some time since from the Sultan's capital, told me a-story which cast a very pleasant light upon the mind of the average Ottoman. He was in a tramcar along with a number of other passengers, When the conductor, a yery typical Turk, came in to col- lect the fares. Everyone paid 'with one solitary exception—an elderly Turk with a beard, who might have stepped directly out of the Arabian- ' Nights. He flat,ly, though with .dignity, refused payment, giving no reason except that he would not. Did the Conductor lose his temlier, call in the police, or otherwise seek to eject the recalcitrant traveller? Not at all. .He loOked round at the rest. of the passengers" shrugged his Shoulders, exclaimed aloud, "Is this the , will .of Allah?" and, •deciding apparently thnt it. was, went his way without more ado.

div.p: MAN'S TWAIN PARTS.
Body and Soul Quite Different and Distinct.

centre, that is the insnment, which takes the position of the Ti-rain in the man, only receives the vibration; it does not comprehend what is spoken from the opposite end of the system. The soul itself, emphatically declared the speaker, is the only part of us, because it is really we who understand.

If tle brain did feel and hear, how were they to explain the condition when the body was dead? The ears, eyes, fingers, tongue and nose were merely the vehicles through and by which man himself was affected. This natural body was not the only possession of man; he was the recipient of powers and faculties. Man had another possession, of Vilich he could not divest himself. Some were more sympathetic than others. They had different tempers, some were more susceptible, others more dense. There were hereditary tendencies in each and every one which they could not escape, because they were transmitted to them at birth, yet if these were their only assets they must become fatalists. The Divine wisdom had seen this, and`given them powers and faculties capable of withstanding and counteracting all influ- ences that might be set in motion for the de- velopment of those inclinations and tendencies. Their last thought brought them to the high- est possession of all. It was a promise made in Holy Writ, and therefore attainable—the joy of eternal life. Man had b. natural body, and had special powers and faculties, and if those were used and exercised in the cause of righte- ousness, the divine purpose of man's creation was in the way of realisation whereby all his hopes may be fulfilled. '
Lawyers and Letters.

Solicitors can boast of a long line of literary names. 'Among the men of letters who have practised as attorneys, the "Law Journal ',' men- tions Lewis Theobald, the famous emendator of Shakespeare; Sir John Hawkins, the biographer of Dr. Johnson; James Smith, part author of "Rejected Addresses " ; Barry Cornwall, poet and dramatist; Shirley Brooks, novelist and editor of " Punch " ; and- Sir Theodore Martin, part-author of the "Bon Gauttier Ballads." Still greater names are to be folind among the authors who have worked in solicitors' offices without being admitted. Warburton, Chatter- ton, Cowper, Borrow, Disraeli, Dickens and Meredith are to be numbered among them.

div.head: INTERESTING WARRINGTON LECTURE.
div.p: INTERESTING WARRINGTON LECTURE.
The second, of a series of three, lectures was given in the Masonic Hall, Bold-street, on Tuesday evening, by the Bev. J. Howarth, of Bolton, to expound the theories of the New Church.

They had seen, he said, that every man was a living soul. The soul was the man, and it might be added in passing that he wa*.s im- mortal, for the souls of men were not of this world of matter, they were not material and natural substances. All material things were subject to natural observation and experiment. They would take love as an illustration. It was not an attribute that belonged to the natural body, as not Subject to heat and cola; power also could not be estimated; yet because of that they did not say or believe that it did not exist as a substantial something in the'ex- perience of the soul. - .

- Since man was a soul, and created to become an angel, they were led to inquire what man had and what he may have in order that the wisp end of the. Creator shall be accomplished and .realised. Let them look at some of ihe gifts of which man was the recipient. He had a material body, fitted and equipped with every requisite for the full and free exercise' of the soul which inhabited it. If they examined it they must readily admit, in the words of the psalmist, that "we are fearfully and wonder- fully made."

Exact Organism. So exact was the organism of man thitt an odour was detected, a sensation comprehended, a touch revealed, an object beheld, and the sweetness or otherwise of a substance made known to them in less time than it took to record the fact. But let them halt a moment and ask themselves what it was in them, what part of the constitution; was it that was miCae. cognisant of those' things. Was it the body, the human frame, with all its unity and har- mony of the particles or atoms that formed the whole? He thought not. The nerves and all their ihterlacing and inter- weaving, even the centre of the brain to which they all lead and from which they all extended, are only channels—roadways. They are but as wires to convey the vibrations that are set in motion in the telephone instrument. The

As they looked around they saw the hosts of evil set in deadly array against them. The -*world was mighty, the flesh was mighty, and the devil was mighty, but three mighties did not make an Almighty. The Lord was with them on the side of righty eousness, against the armies of hell, and those who were on His side were not playing a losing game. In return for all that He had done, man must try not only to' do good, but be good, for only then could he do good. He could try to set a higher standard amongst his fellows than in the past. He could.see to it at any rate that the name of Christian should not be dragged l down into the mire, because of what he was and did. He might often fail, but he could get up and begin again. Christ knew the weaknesses, but in His great strength man could honestly aim at leaving this world a little bit better than he found it, because he had passed .through it. During the day the choir rendered Maunder's "While the earth remainoth," and Stainer's "Honour the Lord," whilst the musical settings were also by Maunder. Mr. E. Wilkes presided efficiently at the organ.

Wycliffe Church. The harvest thanksgiving services at Wycliffe on Sunday, which were of a bright and attrac- tive character, were well attended. Decora- tions, not on too lavish a scale, lent an added charm to the appearance of the church. They had been carried out by a committee of the lady members of the congregation, under the super- intendence of the Misses Porritt.. Appropriate hymns and anthems were sung, " Hearken unto tnis " and "The earth is the Lord's" being rendered by the choir morning and evening, respectively. Miss E. Hewitt.and Mr. W. Booth were the .soloists. Mr. W. 11. Payton was at the organ. The Rev. J. Ross Murray, who occupied the pulpit morning and evening, preached on the latter occasion from "Unto Him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask," He said what was wrong With the churches was that People did not believe in God suffi- ciently. div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Church.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church.

Preaching on Sunday night from the Israelit- ish relapse into idolatry at the foot of Sinai, the Rev. W. Reid remarked on the wonderful re- straining influence of one individual—Moses— whose personality was consecrated, and the an- guish experienced by him as he realised the people were condemning themselves to a cast- away life by flinging the reins on the neck of passion, and instead of building up into &nation for Divine purposes, were retrograding towards disintegration. After pointing out the inevit- ability of penalty, and the demand of the human soul for forgiveness, in order that it might not be crushed out of life, the preacher dwelt upon the atonement of Moses as being defective, in so far as he was imperfect, but resting on the fact of the atonement of a perfect life, Jesus Christ, was instrumental in saving Israel, and such atonements were needed to- day by God in his redemption of the world.

div.head: Emmanuel Reformed Church Festival.
div.p: Emmanuel Reformed Church Festival.

' The .harvest thanksgiving services, held on. Sunday, were well attended, there being a large congregation at the evening service, when the Rev. Williain T. Jaye took for his text part of Galatians vi. 7 : "Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap." The object of the dis- course was to demonstrate that just as in the natural world we are confronted by unbreak- able sequence, so in the spiritual realm there is unfailing kinship between the sower's seed and the reaper's sheaves. If we want a fine harvest we can grow one. The substance of our moral harvest is not determined by chance; it is determined by the nature and quality of the seed we sow.

In the afternoon the choir rendered the sacred service of song "Golden Hill" to an apprecia- tive congregation There were special anthems at both morning and evening services. A beautiful selection of flowers was brought by the Sunday school scholars, which were after- wards distributed among the sick. The offer- tories totalled nearly ea, notwithstanding the fact that the congregation has recently sub- scribed over £BO to the Institute debt reduc- tion fund. The organ was presided over by Mr. J. W. Jowett.

div.head: New Conception of Christ.
div.p: A New Conception of Christ.
" Shrouds Had No Pockets." Remarkable Sermon at St. Paul's Church.

There were large congregations at all the har- vest thanksgiving services at St. Paul's Chnrch, when these were continued on Sunday, and to quote from the Vicar, "they were the best har- vest services ever held at St Paul's." There were celebrations of the Holy Com- munion in the morning, and a meeting of the united Bible-classes in the afternoon, preceded by-a children's service. These 'Were in addition to the morning and evening services. At the afternoon and evening services the special preacher was the Rev. Colonel Adams, V.D., vicar of St. Augustine's, Liverpool. Preaching at the morning service, the Vicar, in answer to the psalmist's question .of "What shall I render to the Lord for all his benefits towards me?' said there were three things. Firstly, there was the service of the lips; sec- ondly, the service of their money; and thirdly, the • service of their lives. Speaking under the second heading, the Vicar said 'Gat it wasin- teresting to remember that the word " money " was. really of religious origin, being derived from " Moneta," the surname of Juno, in whose temple at Rome money was first coined. They were all agreed that in all they did they should be actuated by principles. Had they a prin- ciple with regard to the duty of giving? "Ask yourselves honestly and I Will ask myself," he said, "What do I give to God in the course of a year?" What did they give that nobody knew anything about for the work of the Church at home and abroad? What did they give in the ordinary collecti'ons Sunday by Sunday? Before they answered that question they should think in the silence of their hearts of how much they, spent in pleasure, the prices some of theta paid for a seat in the theatre, the money they de- voted to picture palaces, -whist drives, football matches and the like. He did not think lightly of small gifts. His experience told him that the superabundance of brown pennies did not come' from the genuine poor, who were very often the most liberal givers. What he sought to condemn was the giving of those, who placed what they called their mite into the collecting plate, a mite which cost them absolutely nothing, and who, to hide their meanness, quoted the widow in the Gospel in justification of their petty offering. They at St. Paul's had much cause for thankfulness, the freewill offering scheme being a revelation to him as to the self-denial of some of the congre- gation. That day being harvest thanksgiving Sunday, they had their annual opportunity of rendering the service of their money to Him from whom they derived it, to bring a present worth presenting. He ventured to say that if ere 'they left that church, they were suddenly stricken with blindness, and they were told on going outside that that priceless gift of eye- sight could be restored to them for a sum, say. of £lO, they would soon find the money and gladly pay it. They had that wonderful gift and many others. What would they render to. the Lord in return? Why, more and more of their goods and possessions to His blest service. Let them remember that they could not take back with them one penny when they died. Shrouds had no pockets. They brought nothing into the world and it was certain they could carry nothing out. Any good. therefore, that they could do with their money, let them do it

Terrible disasters have occurred within the past week on the sea and land. An emigrant vessel, the Volturno, took fire in mid-Atlantic, and awful scenes were witnessed. A wireless, message summoned help, but although sixteen liners gathered around the vessel they were powerless to help, owing to the mountainous seas. An oil steamer fortunately hove upon the scene, and through pumping thousands of gallons of paraffin, oil from her tanks the angry seas were stilled, and it was possible for the rescuing vessels to launch boats. Gallant rescues were effected, but 146 lives were lost. - An even more appalling disaster occurred on Tuesday in Wales. An explosion occurred in a colliery near Cardiff. This was followed by an outbreak of fire, which cut off the escape of nearly 450 men and boys. Their position was considered hopeless until early on Wednesday morning, when the rescuers succeeded in isolat- ing the fire and penetrating the workings. There they had found 21 men alive up to two a.m., and hopes that had been abandoned were revived. It was regarded as certain, however, that the loss of life would be extremely heavy, probably surpassing in magnitude that of any previous disaster in this country. The mine is a "fiery" one, and coal dust was shown to be an active agent in the-spreading of an explosion that took place there in 1901, when 80 lives were lost.

" Coal dust as thick as a November fog came with the smoke," he added, "and so dense was it I could hardly see my way about. ' "There was near me a newcomer from Aber, a boy who had started work only this morning, and he began to cry and asked me what was amiss. I told him it'would be all right, and he dried his tears. Then the fireman came up and told us to run- for our lives. As we hurried off to the shaft which was safe we could distinctly hear the sound of fire not so far away. It was awful—timber crackling and falling. about, and , the air stifling, whilst very soon the heat became so intense we could, hardly endure it. We reached the bottom of the pit, where a number of the men gathered, hardly appearing to know what had happened. "The little boy from Aber was still at my side, sometimes in tears. I gave him a drink of water and told him all would be well. It was some time before we were raised to the surface."
Miss Alice Collins.

The modern feminist movement is lessening the pressure on women to marry from economic reasons, and it would certainly seem to be true that the girl who goes to a University College is less likely to marry than the one who has led the ordinary life of a young lady at home, or has gone out to business. There is no doubt that the increasing tendency to marry later in life. is largely due to the better education and wider opportunity now demanded by women. The girl, comfortable and having a fairly good time in business life, shrinks from exchanging it for the drudgery of keeping a home on prob- ably very slender means. If she has had a University education, she is apt to stand aloof from' the less cultured classes of the male sex, and a man as a rule is averse from marrying a Woman of superior intellectual attainments to his own. Not long ago some matrimonial statistics were published relating to the Subse- quent life of the graduates at one of the leading and oldest colleges for women in the United States. They showed that fifty years ago, 75 out of every hundred students were married on reaching a certain age; nowadays only 25 out of every hundred are married at a similar age. It would almost seem from these figures as if there was something like a revolt against mar- riage on the part of the " brainy ". or higher- educated girls, at any rate on conditions and marriage laws which satisfy their working class sisters.

div.head: Class.
div.p: Class.

The members of the Women's Bible Class associated with the Working Men's Mission celebrated, on Sunday, another anniversary. Mrs. John drosfield, of Colwyn Bay, who is President of the class, was • optimistic in her thoughts of the institution when it was launched years ago, and the fact that the membership has reached the number of 144 is sure proof of the great good it is accomplishing. In presiding over the class on Sunday, the leader (3frs. Moore) said that many blessings had accrued to all its members as a result of their weekly gath- erings, and she looked forward with hope to the future. The officers, absentee and sick Visitors were appointed; and during the afternoon solos were 'rendered by Mrs. llipkiss and Mrs. Shep- ley.

div.head: St. Clement's New Aisle.
div.p: St. Clement's New Aisle.

- A new and handsome aisle, which will in- crease the accommodation by over 100 seats, erected at a cost of £750, was dedicated at St. Clement's Mission Church, a daughter church of the Parish Church, located in Bank-street, Warrington, on Monday evening, There was a crowded congregation at the special service, and the dedication was Performed by the Rev. Prebendary' Markham, the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis) conducting the service. The Rev. Prebendary Markham, in the course of a sermon on "The joy of the Lord is your strength," said on such an important occasion as that upon which they had met, they, as Churchmen of St. Clement's, could hardly avoid looking back. There would be many who wished to call to mind, as he did, the day, sixteen years ago, when last they worshipped in the old Mission, and when they laid the foundations of the Mission. Such a day as the present must be a day of joy. Religion would be a miserable thing if there was no joy. There was no true religion without real joy. It was dishonouring God to imagine that His religion was chiefly a thing of sadness. Christianity was the only religion in the world which would bring joy.

Starting from Stockton Heath Swing Bridge we were soon on our way to Delamere, and had some very fine views of the Forest, ere passing onwards. A wonderful panorama of views passed rapidly before us, objects of antiquarian interest, curious signposts, tombstones with quaint epitaphs, old buildings of all kinds, and wonderful designs. Our route was via Swansea to Ilfracombe, and Clovelly, over Dartmoor to Exthouth, and homeward via Wells, Gloucester, and Stratford-on-Avon. "Glorious Devon" well deserves its title, judging from the many beau- tiful places shown, and the architectural beauty e cathedrals added to the many and varied charms of the lecture. The views were most thoroughly enjoyed. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Jr. Wilcockson for his kindness in providing the Guild with such a delightful evening.
