div.head: What Is a Living Wage?
div.p: What Is a Living Wage?

Preaching at the Gollltrlnlee-Rstreetil.Boagpdtiesnt tookCll.ur thech on subject Sunday na evening,living wage for his address basing his remarks upon Luke x. : "The labourer is worthy of his hire." One could hardly imagine, he said, that the successors of these men who were sent out with- out purse or without scrip ever inhabited gilded palaces, or mai.ntained a costly retinue. Surely a comparison in primitive Christianity would. reveal how far the Church had strayed from the ordinary life, and from the ordinary conception of the disciples. They had in them still the survival of a feudalism, when a bishop must live to consort with dukes and the landed gentry. It was a satire upon the Church that at one end of the scale they had a £15,000 prelate and a £7O curate at the other, and the satire loses none of its force when they had Free Church ministers at a salary of £l,OOO a year and country pastors struggling upon £6O to 9 main- tain their families.. The Church ought to prove the brotherhood of believers in a readjustment of these varying .scales, and the Church ought to find the way whereby one minister shall not live in luxury and affluence, and another in abject poverty. ,That was the purpose, and that was the aim,.• of the Baptist Sustentation Fund, and he wished to prove that a minister was entitled to a living wage because every unit of our social life was entitled to the same. It had been proved beyond dispute that the evolution of Free Church life had been respon- sible for the individualism of our present com- mercial life. . Consider the names of the Lan- cashire and Yorkshire manufacturers of 40 or 50 years ago, proceeded Mr. Ogden, and almost without exception they would find that they Wesleyan stewards, Baptist or Congrega- tional deacons, Presbyterian elders, or leaders of the Friends. Their industry, genius and their foresight had built up colossal enterprises. In their-immediate midst the success of firms such as Brunner .Mond's, Crosfield's, and Pear- son and Knowles were evidences of the sharp and acute intelligence of their commercial life. One was not ready to place the blame for their selfish iridividualism at the doors of those pioneers of industry. Puritanism at that time was individual in its outlook, but now it was at the'doors- of Puritanisni to show that it could accomplish collectively what in the past it had accomplished individually. A very cursory study would convince them that the individual, that the Unit of human life, was of more con- cern than wealth and national industry. The Master was more concerned with the life of the rich young ruler than with all his wealth, and when one of the fallen of human society was taken to Christ He sought for no apology; in the commercial system .of his time he rescued and helped and saved the oppressed woman. ' They had an evidence of .how thought had moved, by the utterances of Dr. Newton Mar- shall, at the Manchester meeting of the Baptist Union. Fifty- years ago, if any pioneer of thought had ventured to assert what he aSserted at tlie meeting, he would have been charged .with heresy and expelled from the Church, but when Dr. Marshall declared that the first charge on,a nation's industry was a living wage for the individual, the vast audi- ence cheered as almost one man—an evidence of where the thought of. 1913 had brought them.

div.head: To Settle ' the Question.
div.p: To Settle ' the Question.

To settle what was exactly a living wage was more difficult than to prove that a living wage should be the first charge on a nation's industry. One of their local and respected leaders gave them details on 225. a week, and his category proved that such a wage Meant a life deprived of luxury, almost robbed of recreation and abso- lutely destitute of holidays, with demands on intellect and soul absolutely excluded. If the miner received five per cent. on his wages the community discovered that their coals cost 10 per cent. more. If the signalman received a couple of shillings per week on his fages, the fares to Manchester rose, so it was patent that unless some method of collective life was estab- lished the question of a living wage was a question that varied with various standards. The Baptist minister, whether the same 'Applied to the Roman Catholic cure, or the Anglican incumbent, is a matter they must answer: but the Baptist pastor was not only a minister, but a citizen. Celibacy was a denial of God's laws and an absolute perversion of Christian teaching. Believing that, the Bap- tist minister takes upon his shoulders domestic cares and domestic duties, and, whilst they were anxious that every unit of human life should have a living wage, it was incumbent upon them that their domestic policy be just and right. The Church that preached about a living wage should give a living wage to its ministers, that they may live and act as a citizen, with the comf:.-.rts and the luxuries that are the light' of

The remarks of the Rev: T. T. James at the Wycliffe Memorial Hall on Wednesday night makes one wonder whether we have the real conception of Christ The occasion was the first of a series of mid-week meetings, at which he proposes to deal with the Sermon on the Mount, and for his initial subject took the words, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." They had, he said, to inquire what Christ exactly meant by these words. He was going to begin by explaining the term "kingdom of heaven." It was not a new thing that Christ was telling the people about. It was put in two ways—as a thing that lay in the future, as an ideal state of society that was going to come when God's will was going to be established on earth as in heaven; and then He sometimes spoke of it as a present possession. He was afraid that they had been very often apt to represent Christianity as a weak and colourless thing, without any strength in it. He thought there was danger, sometimes, in representing the 'Chriitian faith too much along those weak lines, and they needed to realise that it had strength and vigour. They had an insipid representation of Christ in the Sunday schools. When a boy reached the age of 13, 14 or 15, Christ to him should not be likened to a lamb, but more like a lion. It was a very great mistake, and it was a wrong representation of Christ to interpret Him in that fashion. Christianity was being criticised because pen:)le said that it taught men to be contented when they ought to be dis- contented and vigorous. H. G. Wells, one of the most thoughtful writers of the day, in what was called "A Confession of Faith," stated: if I am to have that love, that sense of under- standing fellowship, which is, I conceive, the peculiar magic and merit of this idea of a per- sonal Saviour, then I need quite other than this image of virtue, this terrible and incom- parable Galilean, with His crown of thorns, His_ blood-stained hands and feet.

That just stated what a great many people felt about the Christian religion, • that it was so poverty stricken, and that they should always be meek and mild in all things, but if they read the' Gospel they would find that this was the wrong description. Besides his meekness and tenderness, there 'was the vigour and strength and power. When He was face to face with wrong His indignation made men shiver; when He went into the temple He threw the tables over; and it showed that Christianity was po "wishy-washy," empty, colourless thing.

div.head: and Chance of Marriage.
div.p: and Chance of Marriage.
COMPULSORY DOMESTIC TRAINING.
CONSCRIPTION FOR GIRLS.

The German women, who, next to the Danish, are perhaps the most notable housewives of Europe, are seriously _considering the advis- ability of making a course in 'nursing, nursery management and housewifery, compulsory for every girl who has reached the age of twerity. Denmark long ago afforded facilities for the thoroligh training of women in Schools of Domestic Science, and no girl 'would contem- plate the serious step of marriage and the man- agement of a household unless she had attended for a year, At least, courses at one of the many efficient colleges, or gained experllce by man- aging the house of a relative or friend under the supervision of someone skilled in all the domestic arts. The result is that the cooking in Danish households is most efficient, and the table of the middle classes the best in Europe, whilst by no means extravagant or wasteful.

A JAPANESE UNIVERSITY FOR WOMEN. The Japanese women also devote much time and attention to matters of domestic interest. In the new University recently opened, hygiene of the body and housewifery are deemed of the highest importance. The college has already six hundred students, half that number being in the preparatory school. The course is divided into three, the first relating to science, and in- cluding the history of the mental and physical development of woman, the history dl the art movement, literature and medicine. In the second, hygiene and care of the body is taught by doctors of science and University professors who deliver the learned lectures of the various courses. The faculty of housewifery includes a knowledge of all food values, cooking, care of the home, and of children, and all that makes up the varied round of duties- that fall to the lot of the mistress of a house; large or small.
MISS BRADDON AND MISS KATHLEEN
HUGHES.

Miss Braddon, although in her seventy-fifth year, is mentally as vigorous as ever. Few novelists, have - beaten her .record, in output, and she is quite fittingly occupied at present with her seventy-fifth nOvel. She has never lost touch with the times, and her later.works are quite different in style from "Lady Audley's Secret" which took the reading public by storm,- when it came out some fifty years ago. Canada, which is far in advance of the Mother Country in its appreciation of the value of women's work to the State, has appointed a distinguished woman jburnalist, Miss Kathleen Hughes, to be the assistant of _ the Agent- General, Miss Hughes, a reporter in the Cana- dian Parliament, was in 1909 appointed archiv- ist to the Provincial ffarliament. .

THE CHANGING SEASON. The muffin man, one of the survivals of the Victorian era, is still a popular institution in suburban life. lie comes a little before the roast chestnut and ,baked potato, men take up their "pitches" ,t the street corners in our towns and cities, but all alike are unmistakable evidences of the changing season- It has been far from being a sunny year like pn, but we have done something to make up for the lack Of sunshine .by extra ..gayness of attire. The greater display of colours, which has character- ised women's summer dress generally, is a dis- tinct asset in adding to the brightness of the. scene in the park, street, or promenade, and one can only regret the unavoidable change tco more sombre clothing, which is .necessary to brave October rains and November fogs. THE ALL-OVER COATEE.

Many people nowadays take their •holidays in the autumn, either from necessity or choice. For convenience both in paermg and for mak- ing 'a smart 'appearance at the dinner table, no garment is better wprth consideration than this season's all-over coatee. It should be cut low in the neck with deep revers, joining the satin collar, edged with insertion. The basque has cut-away fronts, and the band may be of satin or insertion. This useful and 'pretty garment worn over a dark or black skirt, and blouse of the same colour, transforms the dress in a few moments and would be convenient to Wear ,at home or abroad. div.head: INSURANCE AC T WORKING: FABIAN SOCIETY'S RESEARCH.
div.p: INSURANCE AC T WORKING: FABIAN SOCIETY'S RESEARCH.

Sir,—The Fabian Research Department, in compliance with numerous requests, has started a detailed investi>tion of the various forms of Industrial Insurance, beginning. with the work- ing of the National Health Insurance Act. The investigation will have for its sole purpose to discover what actually is the effect of the Act, and in what way its .operation can be im- proved. Will you permit me to invite insured persons, doctors, -nurses, members of Insurance Committees, workers in any way connected with friendly societies-Lsucti as sick visitors, agents, secretaries, branch secretaries, &c., &c.—to con- tribute facts or other information which they think- would be of service?

_ We should, for example, be very pleased to receive copies of the minutes and regulations of Insurance Committees, particulars of societies' admission 'Or refusal, expulsion or transfer of members, or refusal of permission to transfer, adequacy Ipr inadequacy of medical treatment, success and failure, or the Sanatorium benefit, medical attendance available for persons leav- ing home, or away from home, the working of the maternity benefit. a.nd so on. We want to hear of every example of satisfaction or suc- cess, as well as of .every grievance or failure, and. to explOre all the results that can be yet traced. For this we can rely only on the land co-operation of the Press and the public.
SIDNEY WEBB 37. Norfolk-street, Strand, London, W.C.

div.head: DEMAND FOR NOME RULE: A Local illustration.
div.p: THE DEMAND FOR NOME RULE: A Local illustration.

Sir,—Naturaily I appreciate the generous opinion my friend " Pail Squod " expresses of iuiy Personal qualities, but think it is unfortu- nate he is .not better acquainted with the majority of Irishmen; otherwise he would have a much higher opinion of them, and I am afraid I cannot lay claim to be either better or worse than the majority. Anyhow, I could reciprocate his compliments by' asserting that if all Englishmen, or the majority of them, had been as reasonable and sympathetic in the past as "Phil Squod " is at the present, the Irish chili- culty /night not now 'be in existence. • The evil 'spirits of prejudice and suspicion are very difficult to exorcise. It was with no feelings of indifference that I failed to comment upon Phil Squod:s " alternative scheme. In the first place, I \Vtl more than anxious to lift the question.of Home Rule out of the religious rut to which I was afraid "Phil Squod's 'first letter was consigning it. In the second place, I am not"quite sure that I am not, on the whole, sympathetic with his ideal. Only I don't think it is practicable. And, again, I am of opinion that Home Rule for Ireland is really a means' to the desired end; a subordinate Parliament in Ireland, dealing only with Irish affairs and responsible to the Imperial Parliament. This could be extended to Scotland and 'Wales if desired, also England, with a Federal Parlia- ment, to . which you could invite your IColonies and Dependencies if you wish, thus • relieving the present congestion of reform overdue.

Let me. give an illustration from a speech Of Mr. Harold Smith; M.P. for Warrington. You will remember the pile-driving cerembny in con- nection with the commencement of , the new bridge, and the lunch. Mr. Smith then, after congratulating the Corporation and its officials. upon their efforts and the, difficulties they had to overcome; and the expenses they had in- curred, and the time spent in London getting the Bill through Parliament, said: "What, they really wanted was an extension of local power over these matters, for, as a matter of fact, the Bill had to be forced through an Assembly, who were ignorant .of their- requirements. and Un- sympathetic in approaching it." If I have not quoted the exact words, I think I have the spirit of the speech. Just fancy! If an important Manufacturing Lancashire borough, with the powers and influence of Lancashire and Che- shire \to assist in an effort that was for the ulti- mate benefit of -the two counties, could not command sympathetic and intelligent reception in the Imperial Parliament, what consideration do you think is given to a poverty-stricken Irish constituency? No; the ideal of Phil Squod " is either too late, or too early. Irish Home Rule legislation is Starved, and its necessity is blocking the way of long-delayed British reforms. Ireland. too, is a nation, and her desire and ambition is to remain a nation within the Empire, and, by free and unfettered efforts, to win and retain equality and the respect of Great B"tain. •
PATRICK O'BRIEN. 125, Wilderspool-road.

div.head: SPIRITISM AND ROMAN CATHOLICISM.
div.p: SPIRITISM AND ROMAN CATHOLICISM.

Sir,—lt seems worth while to say a feW words in 'reply to Mr. Chrimes' letter under the above heading in your issue of Saturday last. The fallacy that underlies his letter is that he does not distinguish between •spontaneous and induced spirit-phenomena. Mr. Chrimes is right in saying- "that spiritual manifestations and phenomena have appeared in the Church of Borne from the earliest ages," and we might add we believe that they still occur, and per- haps outside the Church of Home, too; but it is an assumption to conclude, as Mr. Chrimes and most Spiritualists do', that these phenomena are identical in every way with those induced at a Spiritualistic seance. It may be true the ,phenomena are often very similar in forth and character, and appear to obey the same laws, but there is this important distinction between them ; that while. modern Spiritistic phen- omena are 'invoked and induced by the forma, lion of " the circle," and by the development and employment of mediums and sensitives, the phenomena above referred to are spontaneous in their Character, and take place according to laws and conditions which are beyond our con- trol and wholly beyond our knowledge. In the one case the initiative is from this world; in, the other The thing is unsought and begins from "the other side." It nary be, therefore, that their origin and aim is quite distinct: If Scriptural authority is sought for in sup- port of this view, we have it. While there is abundant evidence of spiritual manifestations occurring spontaneously, we find ,invoking the spirits of the dead distinctly prohibited by God, e.g., Deuteronomy xviii., "Neither let there be found among you ijnyone that consulteth sooth- sayers . . neither let there be any wizard, npr charmer, nor anyone that consulteth pythonic spirits . . or that seeketh the truth from the dead. For the Lord abhorreth all these things." From the moral point of view there may surely be all the difference in the world between• the spontaneous phenomena occurring by some act or command of God, and those deliberately invoked and invited by men. The agency directing and producing the former may well be believed - to be a vastly different one, from that directing the, latter, especially as we see the latter is directly forbidden by God. Spon- taneous spirit manifestations in any ease almost alvv:lys ,o,.cur with some definite aim and pur- po,re.: inducel phenomena are brought about to gratify human curiosity. As an example, compare the records of the history of' Joan of Arc with that of any modern "spirit control." It is utter folly surely to assert the identity of

r the two. Yet this is the fallacy of Mr. Chrimes' ! letter. The case he gives of the apparition to the priests of Belfast is-'Obviously one of the. spontaneous type of phenomena. How ,differ- ently reads to those occurring in the-- un- wholesome atmosphere Of a spiritistic seance. • I had not the pleasure .of hearing Mgr. Ben- . san'S lecture, so I do not know whether he made .this very important distinction clear, but if not the omission was no doubt due to the fact that it is well known to Catholics, and for these the lecture was chiefly intended. ' (REV.) P. L. BUGOINS. St. Alban's, Bewsey-street.
READING CIRCLE ON THE LIVING WAGE.

Sir,—May I crave the hospitality of your columns to say that the Guild of Help has just arranged that the Reading Circle, which met last year, shall meet again during the forth- coming winter? The subject will be "The Liv- ing Wage and the Cost of Living," and a list of suitable but inexpensive books has been printed. I shall be pleased to send particu- lars to any applicant, for the Circle is open to all. The reading is done at home, but discus- sions will be held at Winmarleigh Chambers on the third Monday in each month. _Next Monday at 736 the Circle will meet for the first time to settle the details of the programme, and samples of recommended books will be on view. Anyone who contemplates joining will be welcome. The Circle will be linked up with the newly-formed Workers' educational Asso- ciation.
• WILFRID J. ROWLAND. Winmarleigh Chambers.

MR. HAROLD SMITH AND UNCONSTITU- TIONAL METHODS. Si—As one listens to the present Member for Warrington, one cannot help but think that he has a very bad memory, or that he must think the 'people to whom he is speaking are very dull, even short-sighted. Mr. Harold Smith \comes and tells the people of Warrington that because of the unconsti- tutional way the Government are dealing with regard to Home,Rule for Ireland, 'Ulster would resist even if it came to the use of arms - Well, what is there unconstitutional? Mr. Smith says that it ought to be submitted to the people for their verdict; and that the Govern- ment have nothing to lose if the cause is a just one—why should they be afraid? Then he goes on to say that if, the Liberals von there was no reason why it should not be placed upon' the Statute Book at once. What silly talk this is: If that be true, it ought to have been on long ago, but Mr. Smith is not the master of his party, nor does he speak the mind of his party. We have fought three elections, and at each of those elections the Home Rule question has had a prominent place in (Tar programme. Even in the 106 election the leaders of the Tory party told . the people that if Cie Liberal party was returned to power they would pass Home ' Rule for Ireland, and after tile peoPle of this country had listened to/whatlhey had to say they gave their verdict. What was it.? Why, they sent the Liberals to the house of Commons by an overwhelming majority. But I would remind Mr. Smith that those who are his mas- ters have told us, in langilage easy to be under- stood, that they will not have Home Rule under any conditions. Again. Mr. Smith tells the people at Bridge Foot that he vill fight Mr. Crosfield at the next election on Home Rule; that to be the only issue. Let me ask Mr. Smith what. was the issue at the last election? Was it not. the veto of the House of Lords? But what happened? Did Mr. Smith or his party fight on that issue? Not by any means; they pasted the town with posters about Home Rule and John Redmond. and now he talks abont fighting on one issue. The Unionists have lied in the past and asked us to do what they sì y is all nonsense. We will have an issue for the next election for Mr. Smith to fight upon. So. I will not trespass further noon your valuable space, but content myself with asking the Member, at his earliest convenience. to tell his constituents the whole truth about the attitude of the Ulster Unionists, and if it is unconstitutional for a majority JO rule. E. W. J.

We have waited to re if 'anything v.ould conic our way, but our patience is, ex. ia asted. We recognise that lin,ther F.E. is wore striking personality, and may be to ‘keep himself in evidence as ." Gal- ,":!"-'1"." We read, for example, in the "Daily "utTor,", a magnificent description of the Prowess of F.E. : Mr, F. E. Smith, mounted on a charger, was a conspicuous figure, and at one time or another he galloped all over the field. In response to Sir George Richardson's orders, be rushed ,here and there in fine style, as though he were in the hunting, field, and when all was over, and the last man had left the field, Mr. Smith returned to the saluting base and, smartly raising hi 3 right hand to the peak of his billycock hat, gravely ,saluted Sir Edward Carson. This is very fine and inspiring, but for. the Our Member would have had a
ARTIST'S

better eye for effect, and borrowed some sort of military headgear. What we say is, Give the younger grottier a chance. Possibly he cannot aspire to such a distinguished office as his brOther, but we do not like to see him slighted. Surely there are minor offices to Nvhich he has a just title—which he could fill with satisfac- tion to himself..

His claim is emphasised by the noble part the, women of Warrington (w.w.T.n.L.) have taken in engaging to provide 'homes . for . the women and children when the Ulster Unionists begin their Civil War. We would suggest that something in the enter ainnient line . might be useful. How would King's Jester do? gut " King " Carson is such a dour, thrawn deivel, as the Scotch would, say, that not even a Belfast' shipyard riveter could drive a jest into his head, as at present constituted. Better consider the interests of the rank and file and provide them with entertainment. Could not the title Of the individual discharging such duties be known as "Entertainer General "? This sounds as well, or better, than "Galloper." Our Smith would be a General- in his own right, not the servant of a General. A great requisite

in any army is to keep up the spirits of its sol- diers, and we think the units of this army will require everypossible stimulus. Forms of tertainment, properly organised under a capable head, are just the thing. Why Not?

Why should our Member not run a theatrical department? Thisiwould.be an honour to "the good Old town," and nO doubt many of its citizens would join his company. There is no necessity for our, Member, or people, to be brought into danger. They could ikeep far from the firing lines—if there be such a thing. It would be the long evenings in which such entertainments would be required. Think of the rebel sections holding the wilds Of Donegal (which has lately been annexed) against its in- habitants and their King. Fancy being set down in Western Ulster, amongst a peaceable population, with Home Rule politics and Catho- lic religion, with nothing to do, no one to molest the conquerors, whose only duty would be to Prevent the peasants paying their super-sax to the King's officers, and to collect it for the rebel .GOvernment—such work would be tame indeed,

attempting to commit suicide by poison. On Tuesday, October 14th, P.C. Keeting was called to the, prisoner's house and found that he was suffering from the effects- of poison. The con- stable administered an emetic, and Gerrard was removed to the Infirmary.—Clara Gerrard, the prisoner's wife, stated that her husband had been suffering terribly from lumbago and sciatica, and ,on the previous night it took four people to hyld him down. Early the following morning, on going upstairs, she noticed a strong smell of liniment, and She called the constable in. —Gerrard told the magistrates that he was suf- fering severely. At the time of the occmcvence he had had no sleep for days, and there were two bottles side by side, one containing morphia and the other the liniment, and it '-as, he said, an easy thing for a man in his state to make a mistake.—P.C. Keeting remarked that there was only one bottle, when he went into the room. This the prisoner denied, and when questioned at the time said "The pains made me do it."— The Chairman said that as there Was some doubt he would be dismissed. ExcEssivE SPEED.--Edward Brierley, of Roch- dale; James Taylor, Lostobk ; David Eccles, Old- ham; and John Walker, Sandbach, were -each fined 10s. and costs for exceeding the five-mile speed limit for heavy motors. The 'police laid traps in Sankey and Buttermarket-streets, and when in Court three of the defendants stated that it was very difficult to say at what speed they were travelling, as they had no speedometers.—The Chairman said that they were determined to put a stop to this kind of thing, which was highly dangerous in the narrow streets of the town; in fact, two miles an hour was too fast at times.

What a help it would be to these brave rebels' to have our Member to,provide,entertainment ! If it were thought that private theatricals would cumber the commissariat with its furniture, why not let our Member carry from place to place the portable instrument for the creation of village mirth, a Punch and Judy show? "The Provisional Government Punch and Judy ShoW" would take everywhere, and win many adherents to tho sacred cause. It would cer- tainly be ti humble task, but it would be more useful than the high-sounding title and office of "Galloper to the General," held by his distin- guished brother,

The W.W.T.R.L. would surely provide the funds to purchase the show. Their warm womanly ,hearts are to welegme the women and children to their homes. It would be a fitting compliment to this generous intention to pro- vide the ffinds for • the entertainment of the brave men, who, lonely, weary and sad, cut off from their homes and their dear opes far oer the sea, were boldly marching up the stony hills of Donegal, and as boldly marching down again. Wi have referred the matter to our artist for a suggestive illustration.

TUESDAY.

Before Councillor H. Roberts (in the chair), and Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes and W. Richardson. Fraious John Lake, a taxi driver, was chaiged with driving a taxi-cab in' Sankey-street at a speed dangerous to the public on September 29th. He pleaded. Detective-Sergeant Clough said near Cairo-street end of Sankey-street a taxi rushed past at A. furious rate and dangerous to anything coming out of the adjoining streets. He could not shout to the driver, but took the 'number. There were a number of people in the street, and they stood and looked at the car as if they were amazed. He later %aw the defendant, whb ad- mitted that he would be going at least 15 miles an hour, and said that he had been engaged to take a fare from Crosfield's, and he was hurry- ing there.—Mr. Guy Williams, for defendant, said Lake had been engaged to go to Messrs. Crosfield's offices, and competition , was very keen. He did not think -that defendant was driving to the danger of the public, and accord- ing to the police, there was not much traffic. Defendant had been driving for, nearly •three years, and had five cars, 'which covered 12,000 miles a year each, and that was the first time he had been in trouble.—The Chairman said it was an extremely dangerous thing to drive, as defendant had done, and he would be fined 20s. and costs, and his licence would be endorsed. PERSISTENT CRUELTY.-3-01M William Risley was summoned by his wife, Miriam, for persistent cruelty, and applied for a separation order.— The applicant said that a week on Monday night the trouble started after the landlord had called. She owed him three weeks' rent, and her husband said that he did not know about it, although he was telling a lie. He further said that he gave her rel a week, whereas he only gave her as a rule 18s., and he was not con- tent with. wing his hands upon her, but also his feet. He said that if it was not for the children he would have thrown her through the window. He said that he hated the " mortal sight of her."-7lnspector Wainwright Said that the defendant had freivently assaulted his wife. —The Bench- made an order that the defendant should pay 10s., the wife to have custody of the children.

div.head: ACID STOMACHS ARE DANGEROUS.
div.p: ACID STOMACHS ARE DANGEROUS.
NINE-TENTHS OF ALL STOMACH TROUBLE SAID TO BE HUE TO ACIDITY
A PHYSICIAN'S ADVICE ON CAUSE AND CURE.

A famous physician , whose successful re- searches into the cause and cure of stomach and intestinal diseases have earned for him an international reputation, said in the course of a recent lecture that nearly all intestinal troubles, as well as many diseases of the vital organs, were directly traceable to a deranged condition of the stomach, which in turn i:iras due nine times out of ten to excessive acidity, which not only irritated and inflamed the deli- cate lining of the stomach, but also set up gas- tritis and stomach ulcers. It is interesting to note that he 'condemns the use of patent medi- cines as well as of medical treatment for the stomach, stating that he and his colleagues have secured remarkable results by the use of ordin- ary bisurated magnesia, which, by neutralising the acidity of the food, removes the source of the trouble. He contends that it is as foolish to treat the stomach itself as it would be for a man who stepped on a tack to rub liniment on the foot without first removing the tack. Re- move the tack and the foot will heal itself— neutralise the acid and stomach troubles will disappear. Irritating medicines and medical treatments are useless, so long as the contents of the stomach remain acid; remove the acidity and there will be no need for medicine—the in- flamed lining of the stomach will then heal itself. Sufferers from acidity should get a small bottle of bisurated magnesia from their chemist, and take half a teaspoonful in a quar- ter of a glass of hot or cold water after meals, repeating in fifteen minutes, if necessary, this being the dose which the doctor has found most efficacious in all eases.

A man hunt which had a rather ludicrous termination took place on Monday on Douglas Head. The police were informed that a man in semi-nude condition was behaving strangely on the Head, and a section of the 'Force were detailed to effect his capture, acting on the sup- positioq that he was a lunatic. For several hours they searched, diligently investigating the cop- pices, and undergrowth, but their quest was fruitless. It transpired subsequently, that a well-known Manx gentleman, after bathing at Port William, had indulged in running and other physical exercises, with a view to restor- ing circulation, afterwards returning home.

div.head: MANDATE FOR HOME RULE.
div.p: THE MANDATE FOR HOME RULE.

your leading article in last Satur- day week's issue of your valuable .paper you did a great service to Liberalism in pointing out to Mr. Harold Smith that it Is hardly con- sistent for one wdio boasts of sincerity to tell a heckler that Mr. Croslield never mentioned
lonie Rule in his election address, when he had

previously told a Warrington audience that Mr. Croslield had mentioned it in his address, and boasted that he, won the election on that issue. Mr. Smith has the misfortune to forget in_one_speqch what he says in another.

But that attitude is only consistent with the whole of the Tory party, from Mr. Bonar Law downward. Mr. Bonar Law, speaking a few weeks after he was ,chosen leader of the Tory party, said that not a single Liberal Minister
lad 7mentioned Home Bulein their election ad-

dresses at the last election, but the truth is that Nlr. Churchill, Mr. Burns, Mr. Buxton, Mr. llunciman, and several others, referred in ,de- tail to the policy of Horne Rule. Mr. Asquith, in his election address, as far back as the January election of 1910, said : The limitation of the (Peers') veto is the first and most urgent step to be ttiiken ; for_it.is a condition precedent

to the attainment of the great legislative re- forms which our party has at heart, and which I laid before my fellow Liberals in a' recent speech at the Albert Hall." What he said at the Albert Hall on the Home Rule question is as follows "Speaking on behalf of the 'Government in Mara) of last year, a week before my accession to the 'office of Prime Minister, I described Ire- land as the one undeniable failure of British statesmanship. I repeat here to-night what' I said then, speaking on behalf of my Colleagues, and, I believe, of my p4rty, that the solution of the problem can be found only in one way—by a policy which, while explicity safeguarding the supreme and indefeasible authority of the Imperial Parliament, will set up in Ireland a system of self-government in regard to purely Irish affairs. There is not,. and there cannot be, any question of separation. There is not, aril there cannot be, any 'question of rival or competing suprefnacies. But, subject to thee conditions, that is the Liberal Policy."

Two elections haVe-Ceen won-1;3:-'lhe Liberal party since that statement was made by the Prime Minister, and yet we see once again the Tory party clamouring for another General Election on the Home Rule question. The Tory leaders at the last election recognised that Mr.

Nsquith had -made Home Rule a dominant issue. Mr. Bonar Law, speaking in Manches- ter during the election, said, "That if this pre- cious Veto Bill passes, Home Rule Will become law." Sir Edward Carson, at Macclesfield, December 9, 1910, said: "The dominant factor in the present. election is the vile body of Ire- land." That is an expression that is typical of the self-styled loyalists and patriOts in Ulster, who arm and drill tO fight the 'law, so that they can show their love for their native land. , With such-evidence before us, one is led to ask if a certain policy has been laid down ,as the issue at an election, and both parties accept the ,Conditions, why does one party, after being defeated, demand another election upon the same issue? The answer is a very simple one. The Tory party in the past has been able, with the help of the House of Lords, and by their opposition to Home Rule,- to block the path of progress, and preserve for the people they reiresent, those privileges which they, as a party, would deny to the whole community. 'What is the reform they wish, through the medium ok a prolonged Home Rule controversy, to stave off? Land Reform is, I Believe, the
policy they, fear most. Lord Salisbury once said "that the Tory party was the landlords' party," and I believe they fear that a thorptigh land policy that kog to the heart of the ques- ._ _ _ _ _
ion mean-the end of the order of thing, or which they stand. If it were possible ' . _ _ _

give Home Rule to Ireland, and preserve fo) the privileged few the power to govern' Ulf country, "whether in power or out of power, as Mr. Balfour.has put it, I believe Home Rule would be granted to-morrow. To argue whether Ulster is bluffing is simply beating the wind; it does not affect the position one iota whether they are or not. The lot of the Orange- man who is playing .with treason, is similar to the pawns in a game of chess, he will have to bear the brunt of the battle, protect those be- hind him, the Tory.- party, and then, when. the game advances, he' will be sacrificed without the slightest compunction. Latchford.
G. TOULMIN.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1913
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1913
THE PASSING WEEK.

"Miss HOOK?' The Musical Society have excelled themselves this week at the Royal Court Theatre, and their efforts have been fittingly rewarded by crowded houses each night. For last night the theatre, in its reserved portions, was fully booked early in the week, and those who have not secured their seats for to-night will be lucky to get accommodation. A patient wait will be neces-

sary to secure an unreserved seat. Mr. F. Booth, as on former occasions, has written some topical verses with which to freshen up the songs. For instance, Miss Mullins tells us of a Flying Dutchman who came over, and there was no wonder he flew after sampling our air, with its additions from the smoke, San- key Brook and Longford, which had their effect, and made his face turn blue.
COMPULSORY DOMESTIC TRAINING.

A fortnight ago we drew attention to the in- human cries, barn of sheer ignorance, that went up froth a, few spectators at a football match cries which demanded the instant removal of a player with a broken leg in order that the game might at once proceed. Such an incident Points strongly to the need there is for all classes to be made familiar with the elenientary rules of first-aid to the injured. Much suffering would be saved if everyone had the knowledge, which can be had almost for the asking, which would enable him to act in the best way in an emergency until the arrival of a doctor. We suppose compulsory training in first-aid is out of the question; but there would be no harm in advocating such a thing. The advocates of compulsory military training—that is, to ensure that we shall know how best to kill our foes if we should ever fancy ourselves called upon to do them that disservice—make a brave show. Why should we not do as well in advocating that all men should learn how to save their friends and countrymen from all unnecessary pain and suffering? We are glad to note that German romen are seriously considering the advisability of making compulsory training in nursing and other domestic subjects. In Den- mark it is a moral, if not a legal, obligation Upon a would-be bride to have had this train- ing. Or lady readers, who are interested in the question, will find it treated in our Women's Column, where our contributor gives it the thorough-going title of "Conscription for girls."

div.head: MORAL.
div.p: THE MORAL.

We cannot all fly, as the Dutchman did, so we shall have to hope that the Town Council will take note of the reminder that there are certain things that are .pressing for. attention. Smoke Abatement League has been formed tor Warrington this week, as a practical out- come of the Stand "The Examiner" has taken on the smoke question; therefore one reason for the Dutchman's flight may be removed by the time he next pays us- a visit. 'lt may urge the Council to do something when they see the weight of opinion that is now behind the de- rband for a purer atmosphere in which to live. Education on the subject is all that is required, and we shall spare.no efforts to give the neces- sary instruction. The idea that We have to be suffocated in order that we may live is the very essence of ignorance. If. reducing smoke meant reducing work, we would say to the
town, Bear with the smoke. But as we can have more work with less smoke, we strongly urge the people to see that smoke is brought to its proper dimensions.

div.head: BUTTERMARKET.
div.p: BUTTERMARKET.

We never knew until Miss Hook paid us this flying visit how it was the improvement in Buttermarket had hung fire for so many weary years. Now it appears it was all due to the work; having been put into the hands of Dutch loafers, who called themselves unemployed, and went to sleep on the slightest provocation. This is how the Lazy Loafers, according to their own account, did the work—or rather did not do the work :
SLINKS.
When the busy Corporation
Of this very busy town Had made up their busy minds to pull
Old Buttermarket down, They entrusted us to dO the job, As men of like renown. As men of like renown. SLINKS.
Well, we started in October,

And we shifted half a brick. Then we knocked off till November, 'Cause the dust we raised was thick! Then to our sui'prise they stopped us— We were getting on too quick.. • MEN. We were getting on too quick.
RF,FRAIN
We're a lot of laiy loafers,
That's a fact we can't deny. But we might have got to Market Gate,
If we hadn't been so spry; And, however, you may look at it, One fact you can't avoid, There were premises unoccupied, Which might have been employed.

MR. AND MRS. CROSFIELD. Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Crosfield will be in War- rington next week, and will be as much occu- pied as they usually at when in town. On Wednesday Mr. Crosileld'will take the chair at le Swift Mac Neill meeting in Parr Hall, and will have the advantage of speaking about, the policy of a party that is advancing resistlessly all along the line. The following evening (Thursday) he and Mrs. Crosfield will attend the Women Liberal's fancy dress ball, to which' Mrs. Crosfield will introduce her father, mother Ind sister. On Saturday Mr. Crosfield stseaks at Widnes.
Mn. HAROLD SMITH AND THn ORANGE
LODGINGS.

We, are much relieved. It must be months now Since Mr. Harold Smith • MR for War- rington, announced that the Warrington Women's Unionist and Tariff Reform League had determined upon finding free lodgings for the Ulster women and children, whose hus- bands and fathers were looking for the last ditch in their unhappy province. The scheme was expected to spread, but the boom came not. No other body, except our Own, so far A we could ever gather, moved in the matter,. and we have not been able io discover signs of very, much movement even in the ranks of the War- rington Women Tariff lieformers.
\‘ e, however, learn Irom our Sankey-street conteniporary unit

:tatty .alosr.)n, ot Mostyn Hall, presided at an Executive tAmnaittee meeting of the t'lint- suire branch of the /North aies NI omen's L monist and Tann 'Reform Association, at Unester, on Saturday, when the Irish question was considered. it was decided to call a general meeting at an early date " to take into consideration the best means of assisting the women and children of Ulster, in case ox civil war." Mr. Harold Smith, ALP., is expected
to attend a meeting of delegates and address

_ taem on the subject. As we said, we feel relieved. , Tlie Orange lodg- ing scheme Ail! be the greatest asset to the Liberal party at the next General Election— especially if Tariff Reform has been altogether abandoned.

div.head: STEWART ROYSTON.
div.p: STEWART ROYSTON.

In next•month's Quiver"" NN:111-begill'a series of "real lives of real people." One of these will ue by, Mr. W. Stewart Itoyston. This real life story, says the Editor, • is pathetic, but brave in the extreme. A young man of considerable literary and artis- tic promise, Mr. Royston at an early age met with an accident ivhich entailed on him years of suffering and a permanent legacy of bodily helplessness. Yet the record of works be has done is remarkable. Few men have been called upon to bear more suffering than he; few have borne it more bravely, and readers will _agree that by cheerful courage, dogged determina- tion, and daily daring, he has won his right to stand among the ranks of the heroes. _

Locally, it is well known ,how bravely Mr. 'Royston has worked for the general good, though so grievously handicapped. His grace- ful pen and thoughtful utterances have given an infinite amount of pleasure, to his .fellows upon whom he looks from hi retirement with boundless sympathy and unfailing discern- ment.

div.p: From Everywhere.
Flirtation might be defined as attention with- out iiitention.
To flatter a woman tell her she is beautiful, and to flatter a man tell him he is working too hard.
Every married man should join some good society—preferably the society of his wife and children.
• The greatest accomplishment a man can have is an ability to mind his own business.
No woman is ever really happy unless she feels that some other woman envies het'.
A man can love a girl and show it without knowing it, and a girl can love a mini and know it without showing it.
We hope for ,the best andahen, when we get it, we hope for something better.

• A minister at a. Warrington meeting said he never heard a proper begging sermon preached. Our office humorist says he never has gone to a church without hearing a begging remark. Even at a wedding he has heard the minister say: "Who gives this woman away?"
An Obedient Doll.
A little girl was 'overheard talking to her doll, whose arm had come off, exposing the sawdust stuffing.
"You .dear, goo, obedient dolly! I knew I had told you to chew your food fine. but I didn't think you would chew it so fine as that."
Gave Another.

"'Dangerous' means full of danger, 'hazard- ous' means full of hazard. These are adjec- tives made from nouns," said the local school- master to his class. "Can any of you give me another example?" The class was silent for a moment; then came a small voice from the back bench: "'Pious,' full of pie, sir !,,
A Resemblance.

--The young lady of Warrington was visiting a farm near Lymm. She admired some young pigs, when the sow came along. "That's the mother," quoth the farmer. "Oh," ejaculated the young lady, "I could have told that, the piggies are,all so like her in the face." An Artist.

In a • Warrington school the' pupils were told to draw any subject of which they thought. mary produced a weird drawing, and the schoolma'm asked what it represented. "Please, mon," faltered Mary, "1 started to draw you, but 'Can't finish, so I've put a tail on and made it a dog." The teacher's answer is not recorded.

Not In Their Class. Sapleigh : "would you—er—advise me tn— er—marry a beautiful girl or a sensible girl?" Flamley : "I'm afraid you'll never marry either, old man." Sapleigh : "Why not?" • Hainley : "Well, a beautiful girl could do better, and a sensible girl iwuld.know better."'
Just In Time.

A German shoemaker left the gas turned on in his shop one night, and on arriving in the morning struck a match tci light it. There was a terrific explosion, and the shoemaker was blpwn out through the, door, almost to the middle of the street.
A passer-by rushed/to his assistance, and after helping him to rise, inquired if he was injured
The little German gazed at his place of busi- ness, which was now burning quite briskly, and said:
"No ; I ain't hurt. But I got out shust in time-, eh?"

Not Related, But, Oh, So Alike She came towards me rather dubiously, as though not sure of her reception.' "Who are you?" I asked. " Truth," she said. - I apologised for not having realised it. "Never , mind," she said, wearily, "hardly anyone knows me. I'm 'always having to ex- plain who I am, and lots. of people don't under- stand then." •A little later I met her again. " I shan't make any mistakes this time," I said: "How are you, Miss Truth?" "You are misinformed," 'she replied, coldly; "my name is Slander." " But you're exactly like Truth," I exclaimed —" exactly !" "Hush !" she said.
HIS NAME. She ransacked every novel, And the dictionary, too. But nothing ever printed •
For her baby's name would do; She hunted appellations From the present and the past, And this is what she named him When they christened him at last :

Julian Harold Egbert Ulysses Victor Paul Algernon Marcus Cecil Syhesier George McFall, But after all the trouble She'd taken for his sake, His father called him Fatty, And his schoolmates called him Jake.
FROM HOME RULE TO LAND
REFORM. The land question and Ireland may be said,
with little or no exaggeration, to absorb an the attention Oren by the public to politics at the

present moment. There has been a tendency in the Tory Press to represent the land cam- paign inaugurated by Mr. LLOYD GEORGE at .Bed- ford, last Saturday, as a mere tactical inanceuvre to divert the British elector from the Irish problem. It would be a sufficient reply in itself to such an insinuation to point to the

elaborate report on the Land Inquiry which was published on Wednesday. This remark- able document, which has been eagerly awaited by all who are interested in social conditions, sums up the results of a long and laborious investigation, and advances. proposals' which would constitute a Complete, scheme of rural
regeneration and an‘organic reconstruction of
our land system. No party has ever yet under- taken, for the sake of tactics, the examination Asocial evils and the preparation of a curative
scheme on this comprehensive scale or in this careful and unscnsational manner.,

It is a ridiculous suggestion that the Liberal Government, after studying the land problem with an exhaustiveness that has taxed the patience of those suffering most from the evils of the present system,. has launched this cam- paign at the present juncture in order to " blanket " the efforts of Sir EDWARD, CARSON and Mr. F. E. SMITH to freeze the blood of the British elector with the phantom of a civil war. If the Tory party really feel these apprehensions they should have seized the opportunities which were afforded at by-ftection after by-election to make the case of Ulster the critical issue. Since they chose to exploit instead the electioneering possibilities of the National 'lnsurance Act's transient unpopularity, it is hard to.believe that they* are terribly in earnest in their concern for Ulster. The democracY of this country would be glad to see, not only any potential grievance, but any reasonable apprehension. of the Ulster "Unionists" safe-guarded by checks devised by mutual .agreement. But the democpacy of this country feels strongly that., after all the time spent in fulfilling the conditions of the -Parlia- ment Act, to which it has submitted in order to give the Tory party ample scope for ventilating the grievances of Ulster Unionists, the road to a long overdue land •reform ought not to be blocked by unnecessary procrastination over a Home Rule Bill which has behind it an unmis- takable mandate from the majority of British electors.. In the report of the Land Inquiry there is' a wealth of material for th(lse who wish to see exactly how the existing land system hampers the proper use of the soil .and produces the deterioration, as well as the expatriation or migration to the towns, of those .who have been employed, upon the soil-. • -Here it must suffice to glance at sonic of the " machinery " sug- gested in the report. The scheme embodied in it contemplates the establishment of Wages Boards, which will fix a wage adequate for the maintenance of an average family' and suffi- cient to cover the economic rent of a cottage. The provision of cottages under such a scheme would be carried out by • .(1.) public utility societies, empowered to obtain loans up to 80 per cent. repayable on. the value of cottages and land,- repayable in sixty years; (2) the Crown Lands authority; (3) the Rural District , Council,- which would be the housing authority. , Persuasion would be applied to the Rural Dis- trict Council through the County Council, which • would receive a relief of rating in proportion to the progress made with sinall holdings and housing. Compulsion would be applied to recalcitrant District Councils by the Local Gov- ernment Board. The former would be com- pensated for the burden of a minimum wage by security of tenure and a fair rent, fixed and revised ,by a. Land Court, and freedom to deal with ground game.

div.head: RICH AND POOR.
div.p: RICH AND POOR.
A Contrast Between. Their, Earnings During the Present Century.

div.head: DIFFERENCE MORE PRONOIMCED.
div.p: DIFFERENCE MORE PRONOIMCED.
35 per cent. Increase for the Better Class; 16 per cent. for Wage-Earners.
BY C. E. PARKER.

It would be interesting if we could determine what class of the community have made the Most relative progress since this century began. Unfortunately the data for forming a strictly accurate estimate is not available, and any -cal- culation must to sonic extent be based on guesses- There are, however, certain, known facts which enable us to form a fairly accurate estimate as to what this progress is. Income Tax Payers.

We have as a beginning the Income-tax assessments, which exceed 1,000,000. Unfortu- nately these assessments do not coincide with the number of people paying laconic-tat. On the one hand, an Income-tax payer may make more than one return, being assessed in differ-

cut localities; on the other hand, a number of assessments are on limited companies and Private concerns, which 'contain a number of individuals who are not assessed separately. After we have made deduction for those who get free under nptseal, the number above the Income-tax level, who are -paid for in groups under one assessment, must be very consider- able. It is unfortunate there is no way of gel- ling at the exact number of Income-tax payefs. If we take it that the number of Income-tax Payers who are grouped, and the number who make more than one return equalize each other, it brings us back to the original number of 1,000,000. 'Taking, then, this figure as approxi- mately accurate, we have data for calculating the increase in. the individual incomes brought under assessment up to last year.

• Wage Earners. We -turn now to the weekly wage earner. From various calculations available the earn- ings of the wage earners stood in 1900 at about £650,000,000. What, then, is the increase dur- ing the last twelve years? What is the worker's share of the increased wealth of the country? Here we are faced with another diffi- culty, and can only form an approximation. There is no doubt that wages have increased more than is shown' by the Board of Trade figures, which are only indicative of the rise and fall of a few specified unions which make re- turns. During recent years the increase has been appreciable in almost all classes of workers, and it has lately been specially noticeable, in low- paid labour. Everyone's local knowledge acquaints him of this, and no figures are re- quired to prove it. What tie average rise may be is difficult to say, but I should think in tak- ing it at 3s. a week we are not far from the mark. The estimate is all the more difficult to make because of' the irregularity in the advances. The other day I heard Miss Mary McArthur, at the Trades Union Congress, tell the delegates that in some of the sweated indus- tries, through the operation of the Trades Board Act, the increase had been 100 per cent.. and generally she seemed to think that the ad- vances had been on the average about 4s. Working out the general increase at 3s. per week on the 13,000,000 (the number of persons brought under the Insurance Act), we have an annual increase of £101,400,000, or £7 16s. to I he Proportionate Increases.
Broadly speaking and ignoring the increase in number of both classes, winch, if propor- tionate, will not alter the main conclusion, we have fotnal that in
Individual increase for In- come-tax payers, £278; per cent. increase, 35 .278,000,000
Individual increas,N for wage earners, 165.; per cent. increase, 16

It will therefore be seen that the wealthier classes have got the advantage in every way. During the twelve years the higher forms of labour, and especially the earnings of capital, have increased proportionately much more than those of the class known as wage earners; the percentage is more than double. Further, In consequence of the increase, especially in food, the advance of the wage earner is discounted more than that of the man with the larger in- come, because his speildings ca footl are ,(pro- portionately to his incbme) greater. On the other hand, there is no doubt that the amount of 3s. does not represent the full increase that has .come to the wage earner as a result of `recent national prosfrrity. Full time and over time, the granting of walking time, and the like, have undoubtedly brought more inOome to the wage earner than is represented by the 3s. There is the. further- benefit of reduction in hours worked, but this ,does not. directly, effect the earnings. Some have made larger ad- vances, hut there are others whose wages have remained almost stationary. nut the difference between the increase of the two classes is so great that no adjustment from these minor causes would alter the general conclusion already come to. namely, that the wage-earner has not benefited nearly to the same extent cis the 'capitalist and income paying class. • •

Great Difference Made Greater. . My readers will note that in the above I have confined myself entirely to the advances since 1900. I have not entered into the larger economic and ethical question, as to whether the basis of 1900 was anything like a fair one. What I have tried to make clear is that the great difference which existed at the beginning of the century between the \ vorking classes and the classes over the theft w-tax minimum, in- stead of becoming less, has become more pro- nounced. This is _a condition which ought, to make every man who looks to the larger human interests, apart frdni his own individual posi- tion, think seriously. The rich are becoming richer; the workers—l mean the wage camas —while their position is improving, are by com- parison, becoming poorer. This is not a healthy tendency, it does , not seem just, and it is not good socially, commercially, or nationally.

div.p: KILLED BY A TRAM. Another Street Fatality Last

A LITTLE CHILD VICTIM.

Another car fatality occurred last night in Liverpool-road, Warrington. The victim was Harry, the two-year-old child of Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Hong'', 234, Liverpool-road. The driver of the 6.20 car from Sankey, when within 20 yards of Barnard-street, saw inum- ber of small children Congregated in the street. As the car approached one darted in front of the car, and was knocked down. The emer- gency brake Was applied, but, it was found that the child had been jammed under the car be- tw'een the lifeguard and the wheels. It was speedily extricated, but was dead. In the course of an interview -with the motorman, our representative 'learned that some time ago he received a connioniCation from the Corpora- tio'i regarding his smartrwss th averting an acc,ident,.

The new motor fire engine • arrived at War- lington late on Thursday, night, and Yesterday demonstrations were made in front 'of the Town Hall, when many , members of the Conn- Q - including the Mayor, were present. div.head: Life sand Death.
div.p: Life sand Death.

The community of Warrington was increased last week by the arrival of 46 babies (22 male and 24 female). Death claimed 28 persons, of whom 15 were male and 13 female. 1 The birth- rate was 33.0 and the death-rate 19.6. One death occurred from scarlet fever, and nine ne* cases have been notified.

div.head: Mr. Swift Mac Neill, M.P.
div.p: Mr. Swift Mac Neill, M.P.

The visit of Mr. Swift Mac Neill, M.P. for South Donegal, tO Warrington, on Wednesday, is being eagerly anticipated, and a large audience is expected to attend at the Parr Hall. An im- portant pronouncement on the Home Rule ques- tion and the attitude of Ulster is anticipated. The other speaker will be Mr. P. M. Oliver, and Mr. A. H. Crosfield will preside.

Girl Knocked Down by Motor. Yesterday afternoon an accident, happily not attended with serious, injury, befell a nine-year- old girl in Knutsford-road. Gladys Simmonds, who resides in Barry-street, was running from behind a tramcar, when a motor car caught her and knocked her down. The driver, in his attempt to avoid her, ran on to the footpath.. He conveyed the girl to the Infirmary, wliere it was found that she was not seriously hurt, and, after receiving _attention, was discharged.

div.head: Success at Blackpool Festival.
div.p: Success at Blackpool Festival.

Miss Marie Hawley, , daughter of Mr. Felix Hawley, of 77, Knutsford-road, Warrington, has won the first prize in the pianoforte playing competition for ,competitors between 14 and 16 years of age at the Blackpool Musical Festival. There were 31 competitors. Mr. IL J. Forbes, in adjudicating, described the test pieee, Scar- latti's "Capriccio," as being altogether too diffi- cult for most of the competitors. Miss ,Hawley received 87 marks. Both she and her teacher, Mr. William Cooke, organist of Lymm Parish Church, are to be congratul4ed.

div.head: Bold-street Men's Bible Class.
div.p: Bold-street Men's Bible Class.

The speaker on-Sunday was Alderman James Evans, who took for his subject "The Bible," or "The Book." He gave what he called an old-fashioned talk on what .he termed "the book of books." The Bible, he said, was the Word of God, and to fully realise the treasures it contained, it was necessary to remember its divine authorship, as well as to have a real faith in its Author. The Alderman gave instances from his own experience, which prove that even to-day the promises are as effectual as ever they were, and that men who trust and wait are not disappointed.

Captain E. J. Smith Memorial. - A committee has been formed for the pur- pose of arranging for the erection of a suitable memorial to the late Commander Edward John Smith, R.N.R., R.D., the captain of the Titanic, who had many friends in and near Warring- ton. It is proposed that it should take the two- fold form of a monument, with inset meilallion, at Lichfield, in the county in which he • was born, and of a stained-glass window and tablet in the new Cathedral at Liverpool. H.M. Queen Alexandra has been • graciously pleased to .express her sympathy with, and interest in, this. movement. Contributions may be sent to the 'Manager, National Provincial Bank of Eng- land, Lichfield, cheques -and postal orders being crossed ." National Provincial Bank of England. Lichfield, a/c Captain E. J. Smith Memorial Fund." Unless specially ear-marked for the Liverpool part of the memorial fund, contribu- tions will be applied, in accordance with the committee's discretion, either to Lichfield or to Liverpool. •

div.head: AVorking Men's Infirmary Colici..rt :
div.p: AVorking Men's Infirmary Colici..rt :

Over £4O Raised. • ' Again the ' Working Men's Infirmary Com- mittee have been able to raise a goodly sum for the funds of the institution, whose welfare they have So much at heart. At their annual concert which took place in the Parr Hall last.Saturdas night, there was a large audience, and it is expected' that the net proceeds will be over £4O. There was a very fine programme, the ar- tistes including Miss Emily Taylor (soprano), Mr. Harry Worthington (tenor), ,Mr. Ernest Walker (baritone), and the Lyric Quartet Party, 'consisting. of Miss Carrie Hastings, Mrs. E. A. Sanders, Mr. J. Willett and Mr. E. Walker. All did extremely well, and encores were frequent. Mr Payton accompanied on the piano. Mr. J. P. Stafford, who gave several humorous selection's, was a host in himself, and created endless laughter by his new jokes and old jokes, told in his sown attractive manner.. Mr. Down's .orchestra gave six items, which were much enjoyed; and, during the interval Mr. George Walker, speaking in the absence of Alderman Burton, who missed attending the concert for the first time, called upon the Mayor to thank Mr. Down on behalf of the committee for having rendered the committee invaluable service for the last.. 25 years. ' This the Mayor did, stating how much the town, and especially the poor of the town, owed Mr. Down for his sympathy and assistance. Mr. Down, who was loudly cheered, expressed his itpprecia- tion of the acknowledgment, and stated that it had been a nleasure to him and the orchestra to do what they had done..

div.p: Baker's Assistant Injured.

Walter Littlefair (14, 109, fongford-street, whilst delivering bread in Manchester-road yes- terday afternoon, slipped from the step of the van, and the wheel passed over his leg. He was detained in the Infirmary, suffering from a broken thigh.
Warrington "Bank Quay" Bow iino Club.

The club's final main was commenced on Saturday on the "Bank Quay" green, in wretched weather. The handicap could not be finished and there is still the final ,to be played this afternoon. The finalists are John Weave (owes 1) and John Stewart (4): It is expected that a very close and interesting game will be played.

Ladies' Infirmary Ball Committee. A meeting of the Ladies' Infirmary Ball Com- mittee was held on Thursday afternoon in the Board Room at the Infirmary, when Mrs. F. Aylmer Frost presided. Mr. Blackburne read the statement of accounts, from which it ap- peared that the total receipts amounted to £175 2s. 2d., including the balance brought ;forward of 15s. 4d. and the sale of tickets for the last ball £139 7s. 6d. After meeting the liabilities they were able to hand £9O over to the Infir- mary, which amount constituted a record. It was proposed to hold the next ball in January.

The Corporation Accounts. ' The abstract of the Corporation accounts for the year ending March 31st has• just been pub- lished, and from it we gather that the Corpora- tion's trading undertakings profits are: Gas, £14,449; water, £2,155; electricity, £2,944; and tramways, £2,981. The total amount borrowed by the Corporation equals £1,786,790, of which £509,297 had been repaid, leaving the outstand- ing debt at £1,277,493. The assessable value of the borough- rate is £272,133, and the total rate is Bs. in the .2, making the average for the last seven years 7s. 7d. The amount expended on Warrington Bridge during the year was equal to £6,569, and on the Howley footbri-.lge £1,503. The improvements in Butterroarket-tqreet and the adjoining streets necessitated an expendi- ture of £27,168, and the educational outlay was, for elementary education, including £642 for medical inspection of children, £47,068; for higher education £8,804. A new item is that the Warrington Insurance Committee paid £348 for the maintenance of patients in the 'Sankey Sanatorium, whilst the treatment at this insti- tution of tuberculosis cost the borough £1,195. The receipts from the bowling green at Vict3ria Park were £56, against the £74 that was ex- pended. Streets apportioned under the Private Street Works Act amounted to £2,968, and the money received from property owners was £8,527. The reserve funds for the various trading undertakings is given as follows: Gas, £10,000; water,: £8,077; electricity, £9,358; tram- ways, £lO,OOO. A sum of £69 12s. 6d. was paid in pensions out of the Transvaal Relief Fund to the widows and orphans, and the balance in hand on this account is £929. Some interest- ing figures are given in connection. with the Tramways Department, and they include: ,Pas- sengers carried, 6,064,139; car mileage, 449,205.

div.head: IRON WORKERS' WAGES.
div.p: IRON WORKERS' WAGES.
Labourers are Seeking an Advance in the Pay Rates.

div.head: EMPLOYERS CONSIDERING.
div.p: EMPLOYERS CONSIDERING.
By A WORKER.

_lmportant negotiations are in progress, I learn, in connection wita the wage question of the unskilled workers employed in the iron trade of Warrington, who number several thousands. The men are out for a minimum of 235. per week, not a very large ,demand, and, already, their request has been made known to the employers. They have listened, at a conference, to what the men's representa- tives had to say in support of the claim, but, as yet, the masters have given no indication as to what they will do. The negotiations are, however, still in progress as I write, and it is to be hoped the employers will be able to meet the employes' reasonable request.

Miserable Pay. The unskilled and semi-skilled workers in the great iron industry of Warrington are but miserably paid. The. average works out about 20s. per week, and with the employing firms showing large dividends, it is but natural the workers should seek some advance. It is the economic condition of the homes, about which Mr. A. H. Crosfield made a brilliant speech a fortnig... ago, which has brought the present request so -acutely to the front. It is almost an impos:sibility for the men to rear a family on a pittance of 205., and, even if granted the 235. minimum, they will not be able to live a life of luxury. It would be in the interests of the em- ployers to make the concession, for the better fed and more contented their employes are, the greater will be the output. Napoleon said he won his battles through the stomachs of his sol- diers, and . the local Napoleons of industry should seek to realise the truth of his remark. No Strike Yet.

There are some who aver we are on the verge of a strike about this matter. Such talk is not only premature, but irijurieus to the cause. A strike has not yet been even officially men- tioned, but all the same it would be unwise for the employers to stretch the patience of the men to breaking point. I notice that the Chairman of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Sir J. Har- mood Banner, was inclined to hold out the olive branch, and he thus set an example which might well be copied by Other employers. The men are only asking for what Seems their just right--a small wage that will permit ttiem to subsist on the verge of a livelihood. Even if the 23. per week was instantly conceded, the Warrington men would not be so well situated as many of their fellows in kindred industries elsewhere. If concessions have been made in other districts, they can be made in Warring- ton, where 8 per cent, dividends have been recorded. Steel Trade Federation. • The new Federation of the Iron and Steel Trades has not been long before getting to work. Born at the Trades Congress in Sep- tember, the new body has already held an im- portant meeting, and discussed a national policy, which embraces shorter hours, safe- guards of minimum wages, and local autonomy foilidealing,with local affairs. This is a policy tolt'thich any worker in the local iron trades can heartily subscribe. The evident desire is to end the 12 hours' shifts in favour of eight hours in the continuous industries. We have thus two bodies working in the same direction,' the new Federation and an international body of Labour representatives, of which Mr. John Hodge, M.P., the secretary of the Steel Smelters' Union, is a typical example, and of employers. Mr. A. H. Crostield is also deeply concerned in the matter. Surely it is possible for two such powerful organisations to bring the issue to a successful climax. Twelve hours at the furnace or forge is four hours too long, and the sooner this type of slavery in the iron works is end the better. The tin plate trade .of Wales has had the eight hours for some time. Dividends have not decreased, and the men are- happier and more healthy.
The Postal Trouble.

The local postal employes, in conjuncticin with their brethren all over the country, are getting impatient at the delay in bringing their grievances under the Holt Report and other grievances to a climax. The mills of the Post, Office grind slowly, but the exemplary patience of the men has almost reached breaking point. They want something definite done, and pos- sibly when Parliament meets it will be asked to do that something definite very quick. The wage conditions are deploratle. Men in the postal department hold very responsible posi- tions—just imagine the millions of money in cheques, money and postal orders, registered letters,. &c., that pass through their hands an- nually—yet they have to undertake that respon- sible work at wages not comparable with labourers in quite unresponsible positions. It is scarcelY conceivable such could, exist, but unfortunately it does. I note some papers are announcing a strike of postal employes at Christmas: As I have said before, this is the wildest of speculation, but it has an object, and it is to blacken the men's cause as much as poSsible.

Minimum for Parsons. • As a trade unionist, I have been much inter- ested in the agitation which is going on in the Baptist Church and other'churches on the ques- tion of a, minimum wage, or rather a subsist- ence wage for pastors and parsons. I thought I was at a /trade union meeting on Monday night, when I heard the principles of a living wage enunciated with so much fervour at a Baptist meeting. I do -hot think the ,time will •oitie when we will have a pastors' trade ,union, but things are shaping in that direction, and as a trade unionist, I welcome this unrest amongst the pastors and parsons.. It will help to bring forward the cause of every worker more vividly to the front, And will thus press on the ques- tion of working and living to a final issue. In the Church there are most outrageously sweated curates. Imagine a man having to keep a family on 21s. per Week, while a certain bishop in the same religious Body says he cannot live on £lO,OOO a year. Truly, our boasted civilisa- tion and brotherhood has become topsy-turvy.
