Musical Socsety Triumph in Face of Difficulties.
A CONSPICUOUS SUCCESS.
Photograph by Parkinson. 77777,4-=6 MISS ELSIE WILKINSON, • Who, at a few hours' notice, stepped from, the chorus to the position ,of chief lady in the Opera, and achieved a great success.

During the present week the members of the Operatic Section of the Musical Society tia‘e had possession of the boards at the Boyal Court Theatre, and it may safely be said taut never in the history of the society has higher success been achieved. It may be true mat "Miss Hook of Holland" has not the capabili- ties of the more ambitious works that the society entered upon in some previous years, but that, we venture to assert, only tends to make their latest success the more emphatic. Lacking the opportunities that such master- pieces as "The Yeomen. of the Guard," "The l‘pkado," " Merrie'England," and "join Jones" give, the -utmost has been extracted from this musical comedy by Rubens and Hurgon, and proof has been afforded that Warrington ama- teurs can hold delighted audiences in present- ing the plpts and the lightest of light music. just as they have done when they have. been dealing with more substantial things. More- over, they have done all this in face of unpre- cedented . troubles. Never before,, we believe, has an artiste cast and traihed for a particular part, been unable to appear, and the company at all events have' not been faced with the diffi- cult WU of. filling up gaps in the ranks of the principals.. This year, however, Miss Nellie Anderton, who had been selected • to fill the title role, was suddenly 'attacked during last week-end with laryngytis, and on Monday her medical adviser forbade her to appear, at any rate, that night. Fortunately, an admirable substitute was found in Miss Anderton's under- study, Miss Elsie Wilkinson (niece of Council- lor Peter Peacock, the Mayor-elect), who played the part to 'perfection' on Monday night, and by Tuesday night Miss Anderton was ready to pro- ceed. On Wednesday and Thursday Miss Nellie Mullins 'Was ~suffering from throat trouble, and she was assisted in the singinA of her songs by Miss Blackburne. It is .highly .satisfactory to know that 'the .local society are so strong in reserves and so ready in resource, that when ill-luck hits them hardest., they can pull through so serenely as they have done this week.

this quaint play. Her acting, dress and singing were quite in keeping with her part, and she fully maintained the reputation She has been building over a course of years as an amateur actor. " he •Flying Dutchman" and WA- Little Pink Petty from Peter" have been nightly en- joyed and repeatedly encored. Mr. Babbitt, us Van Vuyt, showed us how readily he can adapt himself to circumstances. Altogether different have been the parts in yhich we have been accustomed to see him, but, thanks to his wonderful versatility, he made a perfectly self-possessed and triumphant bandmaster. The Violoncello," a song in which he imitated that most seductive of musical instruments in splendid fashion, was undoubtedly his most meritorious performance', though it had a rival in quite another style in his singing of "Is there any other man. so envied in the land?" with its Tra-la-la refrain. Both were every evening loudly and deservedly encored.

Mr. Fred Fieldhouse, as the wealthy liqueur distiller, Mr. Hook, in the course of a long ex- perience, which covers the whole range of the operas performed by the !:lusical Society's opera section, never had a finer opportunity of giving full scope to his abilities, and he brought out all his own good points and those of Mr. Hook with complete satisfaction to nimself and his audience. He bubilled over with humour, and it is saying nothing derotatory to' the lead- ing comedians of the work to state that Mr. Fieldhouse was‘second to none of them at their own .game----that of laughter-making. schnapps and Slinks had charge of the comic element. Mr. Partridge (Schnapps) was a dapper distil- lery manager, and sustained the part ex- ceedingly well. Mr. Davis (Slinks), as The chief of the loafers at Arndyk, whom he dignified by the name of the unem- ployed, came to the society with a considerable reputation gained as a member of Messrs. Cros- field's Operatic Society, and he did full fugtice to that reputation. A splendid auxiliary was found in Mr. J. E. Hannan, the unemployed Van Eck-, who has a failing for going to sleep standing. Mr. J. W. Bibby made an admirable Capt. Paap, and was well suited in his song "Soldiers of the Netherlands." A little stiff in his stage ,presence and manner in the early part of the week, he greatly improved with later stage practice, and from this point onwards Capt. Paap's‘ acting in the love episodes with Freda added greatly to the interest of the second act. Miss Mamie Bfackburne, as Freda Voos, was the best of the minor characters. So well did she sing the song "The Cigar he brought her," that the committee's decision to include it in their Miss Hook music was at once seen to be a sound. one; as was attested by the nightly call upon Miss Blackburne for a repetition of the last verse.

Miss Rhoda D. Bond, Miss Lena Duckworth, Mr. R. F. Anderton, Mr. S. Baxter and Mrs. E. W. Clarke had sinall parts, in which they T•quitted themselves in a manher that made the company a perfect whole.

div.head: PRINCIPALS:, AN UNDERSTUDY'S
div.p: THE PRINCIPALS:, AN UNDERSTUDY'S
SUCCESS.

A subdued murmur of disappointment rippled through the house—which was well filled in every part—when, on Moriday night, Ali.. Cross- ley announced, just as the curtain was to ascend, that Miss Anderton could not appear. In the circumstances he bespoke the considera- tion of the audience for Miss Wilkinson, but when the new Miss Hook made her entrance, it became immediately apparent that she would need no allowance for any gliortcomings, due to unpreparedness At once she, took posses- sion of the stage and house, and played the leading part in leading .style, and sang the de- lightful songs that fell to her lot with the confi- dence and finish of the true artiste. It would indeed be difficult to conceive a more 'satisfac- tory Miss HoOk than that of Miss Wilkinson, and the loud recalls with which she was favoured showed how completel the house had been captured by her clever accohiplish- ments. Fortunate., indeed, is the society that can at. such short notice produce a soprano of Nliss ‘VilkinSon's calibre to fill so serious a breach.' That she had prepared herself with Such con- spicuous success for a contingency which seemed hopelessly remote, entitles her to grati- tude from more quarters than one. Her solos,

" Fly. away, Kite,"," Miss Wooden Shoes," and the broadly melodious "Cream of the Sky" were given with rare grace. She was no less ,successful in her duets with Mr. .1. Babbitt, our gredtest local tenor. "The Sleepy Canal" and "Love is a Carnival " are delightful numbers, from which .Miss Wilkinson and Mr.- Babbitt extracted the very best results. Miss Nellie Anderton, who assumed her place .as Miss Hook on Tuesday night, and continued to play the part for the rest of the week, sang the music associated with the titular part with dultured grace. It was a venturesome step to put a contralto vocalist hithe position of prin- cipal lady in a work of this kind., but the tri- umphant. end here fully justified anything un- usual in the means. Miss Anderton's assump- tion of the part of Miss Hook was a wonderful revelation of that lady's adaptability to diffi- cult circumstances. The recasting of the keys of some of the songs and the making of sonic quite justifiable modifications of the' score, have made Its aware that Miss Anderton's range. is rather that of the mezzo-soprano. • Thus .it is that the mellowness and richness of the upper notes of her voice and the keen sense of the dramatic, which she undoubtedly possesses, have been demonstrated to be a splendid equip- ment in portraying the part allotted to her. As the week wore on, and Miss Anderton became accustomed to the exigencies' of the theatre" stage, one saw and. listened to a presentment of "Miss Hook." as novel a.S.it was unquestion- ably admirable and adequate, the choice of the opera company's management being thus, inci- dentally, entirely justified. Numerous encores 'of Misg Anderton's songs, and both the duets in which she is as 'haled with Mr. Babbitt as Van Vtlyt, have marked the steady flow of her successes during the week. Miss Nellie Mullins, as the maid Mimi, was the most Dutch of all the Dutch who figured In

div.head: CHORUS AND ORCHESTRA.
div.p: CHORUS AND ORCHESTRA.

The work of the chorus has throughout been of the most praiseworthy, kind. Alike in the freshness of their singing, in the mazy gyrations of the Sabot Dance, and the busy animation of their stage action,' they have backed up the tasks of the various principals in a whole-hearted way, and in doing this they have not oily gained the high appreciation of the audience, but ,have reflected infinite credit upon their joint instructors and trainers, Mr. F. 11. Crossley and Mr. B. W. Lomax. The members of the orchestra and the stage band ,also did exceedingly wett—the first-named in giving support, to principals without unduly obtruding themselves, and the latter in lending to the finale of Act 1 a charming an realistic feature, and in touching off the refrain to Van Vuyt's song in crisp military fashion. It should. be mentioned that the stage bandsmen were recruited from the 'band of the 4th Battalion I'AV.V.) South Lancashire Regiment, by the kind permission of Lieut.-Colonel Fairclough "and other officers. The larger and more exact- ing choruses, suCh as occur near the encOlf-the first act. were splendidly sung. In "The Sleepy Canal," if would, indeed, be difficrilt to say how much of the credit of the recurring encore was due to the singing of Van Vuyt and Sally, and how much of it must be allotted to the excel- , lent choral singing "in the wings." The un- accompanied madrigal, "Bottles," never failed in its nightly appeal to the audience, its four- part harmony 15eing splendidly vocalised by eight singers from the male chorus. div.head: VIARRINGTONIANS TRAIN SMASH.
div.p: VIARRINGTONIANS TRAIN SMASH.
Some Undesirable Experiences but, No Fatalities.

" EXAMINER " INTERVIEWS. A serious collision occurred on the Che Shire Lines on Wednesday, a mile out of the Liver- pool Central Station. The 2.30 p.m. train .W Warrington and Manchester was run into :and wrecked by the 2.35 bound .to Warrink,ston, Sheffield, &c. .For some reason the first express was stopped, and the second ploughed its way through the tear coaches. ,Six persons were killed and many injured. Warrington pas- sengers had narrow escapes.
At the Board of Trade inquiry yesterday, W. Thompson, the signalman, said: "A mistake was made on my part." The telephone boy had worked the block instruments.
"Are you in the habit," asked the Inspector, "of allowing the booking boy to work the 111,ck instrumentsV
"Yes," was the reply, "burl consider myself responsible for his actions, which were by my instructions."
Ygu know the rules by which no telegraph or train boy is allowed to interfere with the block instruments or levers?—Yes.

And on your own responsibility you let this booking boy work the block instrument?—Yes, and it has been done for twenty years, simply because ,we could not work the box alone. LOCAL 'PASSENGERS' STORIES.

The train which was dashed into is largely used by Warringtonians, and there were many local ladies and, gentlemen returning by it. Fortunately for them the front portion is allo- cated to the local traffic, and' the back portion donsists of carriages that are detached at Man- chester for through traffic with the East Coast. As the train was run into from the back, it was the, rear portion that suffered, all those in the front escaping with a good shaking.

div.head: MRS. MORLEY STEVENSON.
div.p: MRS. MORLEY STEVENSON.

Mrs. Stevenson, wife of Canon Morley Stev- enson, Principal of the Training College, and Mrs. Hendy Cock, wife of the Rev. W. Hendy Cock, Vice-Principal of the College, were in the train. They. received a severe shaking, and when they saw what had happened they re- turned to the Canon, who was attending the Diocesan Conference in Liverpool, and came home later, via Lime-street Station.
COUNCILLOR LINDLEY AND THE WORK OF
DR. MEGAN.

Councillor Firth Lindley was in the front part of the first train and detailed his experiences to Our representative. He said: "When we stopped the rear. of our train was in the tunnel. I heard afterwards that the train was stopped because someone pulled the communication cord. The first ',part of the train- was, I understand, examined, and as nothing was found amiss the train was being moved on in order that the rear portion could be inspected. We were just on the move when the other train dashed into' us. "I jumped out and ran back to the tunnel. The wreckage was appalling. The last two carriages of our train had shut, up like a con- certina. You can imagine what it was like mien I tell you twit one man nad been Lifted right up into the air and jammed between the scat and the roof of the carriage. I did what I could to get the injured out. I Should very much like to pay a tribute to Dr. Megan, now of Liverpool and formerly medical ()Meer at Warrington Workhouse, who was in the train ,and was -one of the first to attend to the injured. He took off his jacket
and N\,orked in a way that was really, splendid.

"He improvised splints from the wreckage and made bandages for' the Jiving from the clothing of the dead. I cannot speak too highly of his coolness, his quickness, and his resource.'' Councillor Lindley assisted at the work of rescue and assisted to remove several of the injured. He also went along the line to ascertain whether it had been blocked to other trains, and was satisfied when he hear4l the sound of fog signals.

MR. MOSSE AND A PATHETIC APPEAL. Mr. T. A. Mosse, a manager of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, said :-- "My part of. the train had just got through the tunnel when we stopped. I was looking out of the window to see what Was the matter .when the collision occurred, and I was flung 'Violently across the carriage. I, got out as soon as I could, and ran back along the line. The last carriages of Our train were telescoped, and the engine of the other train was lying on its side, with the wheels whizzing round in the air. "The tunnel was full of smoke and steam, and cries and groans were coming from the wreckage. I saw one young lady pinned underneath a great heap of debris. She was conscious and said to me. Please get me out.'" He was, however, helpless, as a great weight had to be lifted before she could be reached.
When seen on Wednesday night, Mr. Mosse was suffering from bruises down the left sid.

Another Shield.—Messrs. Hayes Bros., bakers, have won a silver shield at a bakers' exhibition at Bolton. Recently they won championship honours at the International Exhibition in London. Their latest trophy is known as the " Sanitas " silver shield, presented by Messrs. Fairclough and Sons, Warrington, for bakers of white bread. The Bolton Show, where Messrs. Hayes have proved so successful, is the largest held outside of London.

" Under the Palms."—The *harvest festival of the Independent Methodist Church, Stockton Heath, on Sunday, was marked with an excellent rendition of the popular sacred cantata "Under the Palms." This was given to a large congre- gation in the afternoon, Mrs., Henry Roberts presiding. The music was enchanting, both principals and choir seemed to feel its influence with the result that the cantata was rendered' admirably. The principal parts were: Soprano, Miss Gwen Roberts; contralto, Miss Wardle; tenors, Messrs. J. Clayton and R. Ellison;• bass, Mr. J. McArthur. The preacher was Mr. Wil- liam Mort, Lymm. The church was :tastefully decorated.

Hill Cliffe Baptist Church.—Harvest thanks- giving services .were held on Sunday. The church 'was beautifully decorated by the 'ladies and friends. The Rev. George Curtis preached appropriate sermons morning and evening. Mrs. Kenworthy sweetly sang the .solo, "What shall the harvest be?" The evening solo was beau- tifully sung by Miss Tanner, "Nearer, my God, to Thee." The choir,. under the leadership of Mrs. Kenworthy, sang with ;fine taste ,the an- thems "The Lord is loving" and "Great and marvellous." Miss Grounds and Mr. H., Moore took the'solo parts. Mr. Brocklehurst and Mrs. Roughsedge were the organists. In the after- noon a young people's service was held and this was presided over by Ir. W. H. Bradford. An address was given by Mr. S. Albinson;.superin- tendent_.of Latchfcerd Baptist School. This was highly appreciated. Miss Bates gave two solos, ",The gift" and "Then Shall the eyes of the, blind be opened." - These were .sung most sweetly and 'were much enjoyed. The Boys' Brigade, 'under Captain Tom Moss, paraded to afternoon service. , There were good congre- gations all day.

div.head: STOCKTOIA: Ii EATII
div.p: STOCKTOIA: Ii EATII
1 O TITTLE-TATTLE.

And everything in the meMing was lively. The parishioners made of it a glorious night. Truly the Heathens "..are eloquent speakers:T Councillor J. Whitley was a tactful Chairman. He kept everybody in the best of humour, And he did not stay the torrents of eloquence. "We live, work and die in Stockton Heath, "And wi3 can't get books to' road," said a "Heathea."
He was making a plea for a free library. It is interesting to know that when we do die We shall require books to read—it is.
What. books shall we want then?
"The Dead Man's Tales," or "Old Mortality"? Gaskell-street is to be tar-sprayed. Should the name not be changed to "Gas-tar Streat " ?
_ The lively Parish Meeting lived pp to repu- tation. .
The liveliness, however, was accompanied with humour.
The parishioners say they thoroughly enjoyed themselves.

Some Councillors were conspicuous by their absence. Were they at home, sitting on their dignity? Their absence gave an erroneous impression. It was that they could not face the "parish- ioners' music." The sanitary arrangements were reported. "deplorable." "Fifty years behind the times," . said one speaker. Yet " Heathens " pride themselves On being up-to-date. "Chuck 'em out l" and Turn 'em out !"

These were comments made anent the coun- cillors. I Perhaps giat is why some didn't turn out to tile meeting. Some "Heathens" think Warring.,,,lon should take them over. And give them "the blessings of civilisation." Then there will be a big jump up in the rates. Perhaps the "blessings" will prove far too, costly. The, Chairman said his position "was not a bed of roses," • He sticks gallantly to his post and works while others talk.- .
The. next meeting is already being anticipatee with interest.
One speaßer said the PresS only gave two lines to Parish Council- meetings.
tie must be one of those few folk who dd no read the "Examiner."
Stor,ktori 1-lehth rates nre to be still lower.
Perhaps that will satisfy the ratepayers who grumbled at the meeting. A..man is easier converted through his pocket than his brain. • _
The 'lentil, under Warrington rule, would not have a ss. 8d: rate: -
It 'would be nearly doubt that—possibly 9s. Gd in the <-£. .
Thus, after all. 'Us good to be alive and to reside in the Heath.
THE RATES REDUCED. A Decrease oi 3. in the Z.
We are able to announce to the residents of Stockton Heath that there will be a reduction in the rates during the ensuing year, equal to 3d. in the X.

Mr. J. Whitley, the Overseer, reported to the Parochial Committee on Monday evening, at the close of the ordinary business, ,that the new rate tor the next six monthg would be, for all purposes, 2s. 10d. in the X, a reduction of one penny in the half-year. The, rate tor the year will work out at ss. Bd. in the £, compared with ss. ltd, during the past year. Despite this the Parish Council and Parochial Committee have carried through several schemes calculated to benefit the town- ship. Whatever complaints the parishioners may, have they -are not likely to consider the reduction in the rates/a cause for complaint.

The Street Paving.—At a meeting of the Parbehial Committee on Tuesday it was re- ported that the Runcorn District Council had appointed a committee to inspeelt the roads made by the Northern Granite Company before the contract eApires. •

Premature.—The Buildings Committee recom- mended to the Parochial Committee on Tuesday that 'permission be granted to an applicant to erect a wooden stiucture in Walton-lane. Coun- cillor Whitley: I have seen the "place and the building is already there. (Laughter.) • A Mem- ber: It's premature.

Public Convenience.—A letter was.read at the Parochial Committee on Tuesday night, enclos- ing the resolution passed at the Parish Meeting re the provision of a public cOnyenience.— Councillor 'Mclntyre: I move that it be referred to the Sanitary Committee.—Councillor Bottom- ley: T.; hope the matter will he dealt with quick. The resolution was 'adopted.

Lumb Brook Lighting.—Councillor Whitley asked at a meeting of the Parochial Committee on Tuesday it they had any communication from the Warrington Gas Committee about the light- ing of the ..dangerousi s”ot at Lamb Brook.— Councillor J. Hallows: Shall we • have these lamps by stflnmer time?-r-The Chairman (Coun- cillor G. Pilling) : You shall ,have them as soon as the Corporation start—perhaps next week. ,

_The Fire Brigade.—Councillor )tcDermid re- ported to the Stockton • Heath Parochial Com- mittee meeting on Tuesday evening. that .a bri- gade practice had taken place) The hydrants' were tested and showed a good pressure. The hose was also tested and several lengths gave way under the pressure. The conduct and work of the firemen was most satisfactory.—Councillor Hallows: The men did their work extremely well. -(Hear, hear.)

A Consumption Question.—The question of disinfecting houses where consumptive residents had lived was raised at the meeting of the Paro- chial Committee on Tuesday. Councillor Mcln- tyre asked if it was customary to disinfect such houses.—Mr. Ashton (the clerk): Consumption is now a notifiable disease and disinfecting- has to be done.—Councillor Bottomley stated that a the Parish Meeting it was said it was not done. The Clerk: The Act compelling it only. recently came into operation.

Illness of Mr. 1-1. J. Westbrook.—Mr. H. J. Westbrook, solicitor, and. a 'member of the Stockton -Heath Parish Council, 'has undergone a severe operation at his residence in Whitfield- road, and is now well on the way to convales- cence.—The matter was refeyred to at the meet- ing of tip Parochial.. Cordraittee ,on Tuesday, *then Councillor J. Whitley Said it would. be .within the knowledge of that Council that one of their colleagues, Councillor Westbrook, had just passed tbrough a very severe illness and an operat,ion. He moved: "That the deepest and sincerest symPathy of this committee be' sent to Mi.. Westbrook in his severe and protracted illness, and trasN he may min be fully restored to, health and strength." div.head: TAR SPRAYING OF ROADS
div.p: TAR SPRAYING OF ROADS

The question of tar-spraying certain roads was discussed at the Stockton Heath Parochial Com- mittee ow Tuesday. Mr. Ashton, the Clerk, said he had', according to instruction, ascertained the cost. The cost ~would be about lid. to lid. ppr yard. The first coat of tar would last nine months, the second 12 months, and the third 11,months, or an average of 12 months. Councillor Melntyre : Can we get the County Council to do the work?
Mr. Wright (the surveyor) : Warrington might do it. , Councillor J. Hallows: Is it really necessary to,do it?

-Councillor 'Clr. Pilling (the chairman).: The. Cheshire Surveyor recommends it to be done. - Councillor Mclntyre: It would make the roads more sapitary. Councillor Whitley: The managers of the Church School would like to have the, school- yard done at the same time. It was agreed, on the motion of Mr. Whitley, that. the Runcorn District Council be asked to carry out the work.
WHENCE COME THE ODOURS? Parochial Committee Take Action.

At a meeting of. the Stockton Heath Parochial, Committee on Tuesday a -letter was read, in which it was stated the Parish Meeting .com- plained of a nuisance at the Lumb Brook end of qrappenhall-road, and asked the committee to take steps to have it -abated.
Councillor Pilling (the chairman): It sounds like the brook.

Councillor MeDermid said that at the Parish Meeting held on the previous evening Mr. 'John Taylor drew 'attention to the bad smells from the place named, and they were attributed to various causes, ,including the manure deposits. on the land. The deposits were, brought by boats on. the canal.

The Chairman: The best thing would be for the Inspector to investigate. The smell that comes from th 6 foreign manure at the wharf is something terrible. Councillor J. Hallows: Yes; when a big steam- boat comes in the smell is dreadful,

Councillor Bottomley said part of the smell came from the, manure and part from the place where the refuse of the district was tipped by the committee's contractor. The smell was abominable. In a district like this with a big population the matter 'was one which called for Urgent attention. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman: It is an important matter. Councillor McDermid : This matter is continu- ally coming as a complaint to us, and we had a surfeit of it at. the Parish Meeting. The only real remedy is to take up the matter at the point we left off and convert the whole pail sys- tem into the water-carriage system. It will be a burden on the ratepayers, hut not a heavy one. I move that the matter be referred to the Sani- tary Committee. Councillor Mclntyre: It is a serious matter, which requires consideration, and action should be taken. The 'motion was carried unanimously.
-Councillor Whitley: I think it might assist us if a letter was sent to. the Appleton Parish Council, calling attention to Pe nuisance which arises in their parish from the _boats._
The Chairman: We, had best leave that to the committee.
The subject then dropped.

div.head: LIVELY PARISH MEETING.
div.p: A LIVELY PARISH MEETING.
Mr. Pemberton Wants the 'Oilmen "Chucked Out."
PLETHORA OF TOPICS.

There was a plethora of topicliscussed at the Stockton Heath Parish Meeting on Monday evening. For two hours the proceedings were of a racy and lively character, and Councillor ;Tames Whitley,•the chairman; had a hard task in keeping the voluble parishioners to the point. The ghairinan, referring to the suggested amalgamation with Warrington, as discussed at the Parish Meeting six months' ago, said : War- rington positively refused to receive a deputa- tion from us, and thus it seems the matter has conic to an end. • We have learned, and I have reason to believe that our information is cor- rect, that Warrington is intending to bring forward the matter in the future in the form of a much larger ,scheme, which includes some parts .of Sankey and some pBrtions of Penketh, Padgate,, Latchford. Without, Lower Walton flnd Stockton Heath. The matter is, however, not ripe yet. Mr. Crossley: Has' the Parish Council sub- mitted any proposals to WarringtOn? •
The Chairman: We had no authority to do so, and it would have been unwise to do so with- out the authority of the parishioners.
Mr. Thomas Miller: I takelt that it is useless to go into anything connected with the parish until the amalgamation question is settled one wkty or another?
The Chairman: Not necessarily. Other ques- tions can be discussed.
Schemes of Kr. C. Mikes.

Mr. C. Dukes thought the Stockton Heath Parish Council had set their backs •against the amalgamation scheme. The parishioners were wishful'. that the Council should prepare a scheme, but the councillors I),ad taken up a negative Policy, which prevented progress. They had had the provision of a recreation ground talked about for 112 years—(Mr. Pember- ton: Twenty years)—and he- remembered Mr. Pemberton talking about it when he (Mr. Dukes) was a boy. Unless the -parishioners would waken things up in that direction the Council would still go on talking,about it. (Laughter.) iThere was land suitable for a recreatiOn ground

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1913.

around the new school, which should not be closed in with buildings, and Make it unhealthy. , They had no public convenience in Stockton Heikt • (Jr. -Pembertan-: "Shame!') They'had been so dependent upon other people to provide things for them that they had not provided such a convenience. They also wanted allot- ment gardens, and their housing scheme was to cram the most houses on the least possible spaeo. They wanted a recreation ground, on which the children'could play, so that the police need not hound them off the streets as if they were there for criminal purposes. -

were, and it was said the garish Meetings wore only held for the purpose of letting off gas. I think we should have more meetings of this kind, instead of a less number. I assert these are the most useful meetings held in the village. The Chairman: The resolution was passed that we should meet half-yearly. It is for you and not for the Parish Council to say. whether these; meetings be continued. We must meet, according to the law, at least once a year.
Mr. Dukes: Then without a resolution we shall continue the meetings as usual? The Chairman: Yes; that is. AO. The Meeting then terminated with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

chaff "._and ".The nature of God's 'harvest in humanity." In :the, evening the choir- gave a spirited .rendering of .Maunder's "Praise the Lord, 0 Jerusalem," the, solo being capitally sung by Miss- Appleton.—Following a long estab- lished custom, the choir gave a service of song on Monday evenin,g. The music, which was above the average for. this class of, work, was excellently rendered. I Solos were contributed by Miss Appleton, Messrs. A. Appleton, G. Ap- pleton and H. Clare, and a duet by the Misses D. and B. Cross. The descriptive text was dis- tinctly read by Mr. G. L. Welford. The sale of fruit, &c., which followed in'the schoolroom, was productive of much mirth and high prices, Mr. Cross being the salesman. The festival throughout was a great. success, and the congre- gation larger than on any .previous occasion of this nature.

div.head: "Chuck Them Out."
div.p: "Chuck Them Out."

The Chairman said they would have to keep the meeting to definite subjects, else they would be there until twelve at night. Mr. Pemberton : If we are here until twelve o'clock we will be in the interests of the parish. The Council has been here for nineteen years and have done nothing. I. defy you to show me one thing they have done in those 19 years. I say "chuck them out." I would turn the whol gang out and would not have one of them in. Get somebody in who will do the work. There is no one to blame for the position you are in at Stockton Heath ex- cept you, the ratepayers. If you want to see things done throw out the Parish douncil and get someone .else in. (Laughter.) You take it all like lambs; all you do is to grumble and pay. (Laughter.) The inaptitude of the Council is so great that it exceeds anything I have heard or read about. If they were active we would have had a recrea- tion ground long ago. They have not lighted the place. All they do is to put in lamps re- quired by the by-laws and light them inade- quately. in Alexandra-road they have put up only one lamp. The Chairman: Two lamps.

div.head: "Get a New Council."
div.p: "Get a New Council."

Mr. Pemberton: That property pays ,R,50 in rates, and the Council has done nothing for the road. The ..C.50 a year is clear profit to them. Thei have made 'a noise _about paving the streets, but that has been done at the explmse of the property owners. The Council have not paid a farthing to it. It seems to me if you want to get anything done here you. first want to get a new Council. The present Council is absolutely the limit. (Laughter.) Mr. Al eDermid expressed surprise at the out- burst of Mr. Pemberton. Ile was once a mem- ber of the Parish Council that had done noth- ing in 19 years. Surely Mr. Pemberton might have accomplished something when he was on the Council, but as he did not the ratepayers turned Mr. P!)mberton out. (leaud laughter.)

div.head: "Personal Grievances."
div.p: "Personal Grievances."

Mr. Pemberton's .grievances, continued Mr. Mcljermid, are to a certain extent personal. We have not provided a lamp in a street in which he is particularly interested. If we were to provide lamps,,for all the parishioners who made application we should have a big job on hand. I am convinced that there is no suburb in the United Kingdom better lighted than Stockton Heath. (Hear, hear.) The public recreation ground is a matter for the ratepayers. Some years ago we had the offer of suitable ground at reasonable terms; but the mattef-fell flat.- There was no enthusiasm shown by the ratepayers. Applications were also invited for allotments and we had not a single application. On the question of amalga- mation we cannot force .the situation. War- rington contemplates a comprehensive scheme, and I consider we must allow that matter to develop. I consider the Parish Council and the Paro.Wlial Committee .have done well for Stock- ton Heath. - - -

div.head: An Emphatic Denial
div.p: An Emphatic Denial

Mr. T. Miller: Unfortunately we have elected a Parish Council that blocks everything re- quired by the ratepayers. The Chairman: I emphatically deny that assertion. They have 'abr.-ars made it their duty to carry out any suggestion presented to them by the ratepayers. Even at the time Mr. Pem- berton was with us we were making improve- ments, and we are still- doing so. In. Alexandra. road there ,are 4amps as far as the buildings have gone. You don't expect us to pay for costly gas lamps to light fields? Mr. Pemberton: Your assertion about Alex- andra-road is wrong. --The lamps don't go as far as the houses. . .
_ Mr. C. Dukes moved that it be an instruction to the Parish Council to inquire as to the pos- sibilities of acquiring the land adjacent to the new school for a recreation ground and allot- ments. -

Mr. Joseph Moss said that they should „get small plots in different places, where the chil- dren could play. Mr. Dukes amended his resolution to include the suggestion, and the resolution was carried unanimously. It was also agreed that the Clerk write to the Clerk of the Peace at Chester for permission to hold open-air meetings in the vil- lage. The Council were instructed to consider the erection of a public convenience.

div.head: Parish Council Work.
div.p: Parish Council Work.

Mr. Bottomley said the Parish Council met four times a, year, and there was no business except that of a routine character to transact. They had not a single sub-committee, and most of the Council's work was done by the Parochial Committee. The Parish Council had • full powers to deal with the Fire Brigade, but that was left.to the Parochial Committee, who were subservient .to the Runcorn Rural District Council. He did not think the Paris‘h Council was on amicable terms with its neighbours, and there was a great amount of antagonism that should not exist. Was it a case that the Parochial Com- mittee had arranged with the Brewery Brigade before the offer from Warrington was received? He thought it .would .have been better to have entered into an agreement with a body like Warrington, than with a voluntary concern that had no locus standi. He moved that all the powers the Parish Council have be exercised by the Parish Council alone, and not relegated to the Parochial Com- mittee.

On Amicable Terms; Mr. McDermid said there was absolutely no antagonism between them and Warrington. They were on the most amicable of terms., They now had an admirably equipped Fire Brigade at their dispAal, as well as their own equipment. To confine themselves solely to the powers con- ferred upon them as a Parish Council would be ridiculous in the extreme. There were many questions the Parochial Committee could deal with better than the Parish Council. The Chairman: The Parochial Committee are in advance of the Parish Council.
Mr. Bottomley's motion was carried unani- mously.
On the motion of Mr. Miller, it was agreed that the Council should consider the provision of a free library and news room for Stockton Heath.
Wall Paper and Consumption. 0 An important question was raised by Mr. Dukes, who asked: What powers have we as a Council to compel property owners to periodi- cally renovate their property?

Mr. Pemberton: It is a -shame if property owners do not do it. All the most responsible property owners keep their property in order, and the only way to get at those who do not is to get at them through, the Public Health Act. Mr. Dukes: Is it not a fact that if it is proved to be detrimental to health you can compel them to strip.off old wallpaper? I know of a house where a man died of consumption and the paper was never stripped off the walls.
The Chaipman. : .It must have been neglected in that case.
The subject then dropped.
A _Sanitary Complaint.

. _ Discussing the sanitation of the district, Mr. John Taylor asked how the night-soil was dis- posed of. Mr. Pearson, chairman of the Sanitary Com- mittee, replied that the contractor undertook the disposal. He understood it was disposed of at the old quarry at Cobbs.
The Chairman : We are now going in largely for the water carriage system.

Mr. Taylor: The offensive smells in Grappen- hall-road are something abominable. The Chairman: There are other sources from which the nuisance emanates. The cattle boats which come ,from America deposit the filth at the wharf for the farmers to cart away. On the motion of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Dukes, it was resolved that the Clerk (Mr. Brad- shaw) should write to the Parochial Committee and ask them to consider the complaint.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.
LINES FROM LYMM.

It's an ill-wind that blows nobody any good. The fly pest has helped the bazaar funds. A local lady has made "fly 'caps." They met with a very ready sale. The bazaar in consequencq, benefited. After all flies have some use on earth. The harvest festival- crop has ended. Arid the largest marrow has not yet appeared. A tidy. sum of money has, however, been raised.
Language has different values at the Petty Sessions.
One man, for indulging in his "vanity," had to pay ss. Another found himself rated on a higher basis-10s.
The Congregationalists have had a very pretty bazaar. How the deft fingers of the ladies must have worked.
They turned out some very fine articles, that they did.
The stalls simply groaned under their bur- dens of wares. _
As the Chairaan on the opening day said, the Congregationalists are waking up. There is, plenty of work for them , to do in Lynim.

Petty Sessions Magistrates.—At the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday, the presiding magistrates were Colonel Legh (in the chair), Colonel GroVes, Messrs. W. P. Rylands, A. Cal- lender and T. J. Ridgway.

Horses Without Reins.—At the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday, William Sanders, High. Legh, Lymm, was fined 2s. 6d. for having been in charge of two horses and lurry and riding on the same without —reins on the 2nd October. Sergt. Washington proved the case.

St. Mary's Festival.—The harvest festival ser- vice of the St. Mary's Newfield Mission was held on Sunday night. The room was prettily decorated with an abundant supply of season- abke gifts, and a large congregation was in attendance to hear the. Rev. Horace Gray, the preacher.

Language.—For having used obscene language Walter ,Wright, Rush Green, Lymm, and Walter Mair, Thelwall, were fined 10s. and ss. respectively, at the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday. For having been drunk and dis- orderly in Booths Hill, Lymm, James Lennon, Warrington, was fined 10s., including costs.

H ary est Festivals End.—Sunday and Monday marked the termination of the harvest festival season, as far as Lymm, is concernvd. For several weeks past large congregations have been singing hymns of thankfulness; pred.chers have been drawing valuable spiritual lessons fcom the products of the field and garden; and incidentally, much money has been collected for deserving funds, and will, 1T46 43 St, yield some sixty, and some one hundred fold in the interests of the good causes benefited.

A Serious Charge.—A case which lasted several hours was heard at Lyrtim. Sessions on Wednesday. John Gibbon, commercial ,travel- ler, Manor House, Higher-lane, Lymm, was charged with a serious assault on a girl aged 13 years and ten months, named Emma Davies, who, had acted as domestic servant at defend- ant's house.' The charge of assault was dis- missed, and the defendant was committed to the next Chester Assizes ' on a charge' of at- tempted .assault. Bail was granted, defendant in A:200 and sureties for A:150.

Death of Mrs. Norris.--There passed away, at her residence, Brookfield, on Wednesday after- noon, one of the best known ladies in the local- ity, in the person of Mrs. Norris, widow of the late Mr. !Thomas Potter Norris, millowner. The deceased, who had been a resident in Lymm for over 40 years, was at one time hon. treasurer of the local Habitation of the Primrose League, and, until her recent illhealth compelled her to relinquish her office, was the hon. treasurer of the Lymm and District Nurses' 'Fund. She leaves four sons and four daughters.

Temperance Women.—The members of the Lymm Branch of the National British Women's Temperance Association opened their winter session with a public tea and meeting in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom on Tuesday night. Mrs. Willan presided. Mrs. Paw, of Altrincham, was the speaker, and gave a strik- ing address on the evils of intemperance, as it. affects women. She expressed her disapproval of the use of medicated' wines, and said that she even did not believe •in trading with the grocer who held an "off licence." A vote of thanks to the speaker was proposed by Mrs. W. Mort, seconded by Mrs. F. Wright, and carried. A duet by Mrs. Margetts and Miss. Winstanley contributed to thc 'n.ening's enjoyment.

Pretty Baptist Church.—No efforts were spared to make the Baptist Church as pretty -as possible for the harvest thanksgiving last Sunday, and the result must have been very gratifying to those responsible. At the morning service the Rev. E. E. Lovell gave an interesting and help- ful address to the children on the word "Wheat," and by the use of acrostics taught the lessons of Wisdom, Humility, Energy, Assurance and Truth, impressing upon the minds of his hearers the importance of possessing these vir- tues. He afterwards preached from the words: "They joy before Thee, according to the joy in harvest." Miss Jenks gave an able rendering of ,the solo, "Nearer, my God, to Thee." There was a large congregation at the evening service to hear the Pastor deliver another appropriate sermon. Miss Ball's solo, "Abide with me," was much appreciated. A Charming Decoration.—The interior of the Primitive Methodist Church kesented a charm- ing appearance last week-end on the occasion of the harvest festival services. The super- abundance of flowers, for which the present autumn stands out conspicuous, supplied the decorators witli ample material for the exercise of their artistic abilities, and the best possible use had been made of the immense quantities of bloom at their disnosal. Two unusually fine sermons were preached by the already popular young minister, the Rev. W. Daw, on the sub- jects of "The separation of the wheat from the

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL BAZAAR.
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL BAZAAR.
The Ladies' Dainty Work Results in a
Fine Display.
AN INTERESTING FUNCTION.

In aid of the church funds and for the pur- chase of the chief rent in connection with the Lymm Congregational Church, a two days' bazaar was. held in the schoolroom on Wednes- day and Thursday. On the first day the open- ing ceremony was performed by Mrs. 011eren- shaw, of Mere, and on Thursday Mrs. Ridgway opened the bazaar. There were good attend- ances each day and the sales were brisk. The committee responsible for the splendid organ- isation of the sale were the Rev. J. A. Penaliggon (chairman), Mr. J. D. B. Smith (secretary), Mr. J. H. Holt (treasurer), and Mrs. Gotobed (ladies' secretary). The room vfas tastefully decorated and the stalls were artistically laid out. Mr. Armitage presided, and there were also on the ISlatform the Revs. J. A. Penaliggon and Fer- guson, Mrs. 011erenshaw, Mr. J. H. Holt and Mr. J. D. B. Smith.

The Chairman's Address. • The •Chairman said, that they all had a great respect for that church, whose history they knew. They rementhered Lymm in the long ago, when the Rev. Mr. Bedell was pastor and did wonderfur work Then came a quiet time, but they were now waking it up. They had got a good man in Mr. Penaliggon to lead and guide them in their church life. There as going to be new wdrks erected at Lyn, and these would no doubt bring a lot of people, who would need helping in their times of trouble. A great many people would come from other places, who might have got out of touch with the House of God. . People who , cAme away from old sur- roundings had sometimes lost touchipithichurch life and had got cold or indifferent. It was for them as a Church to warm these people up and do their utmost to let the people find a happy, spiritual home in that church. They would, by that, be carrying on the noble history of that church. •If they, did so the church would prosper; they would prosper; and the men and women would have a happier and nobler ending to their lives. They had to set their eyes on the best thing they, knew, and do it. They should keep *their eyes on that church and do the best they could for it, and it would blossom like the rose. (Applause) ,

div.head: Sympathy with the Work.
div.p: Sympathy with the Work.

- Mrs. 011erenshaw said she. had a great sym- pathy with what they were doing at Lymm. Mr. Armitage had given them really wonderful advice when he told them to -work for the best. She would like to see the Young people taking advice from older people. (Hear,. hear.) They had Miss West amongst them there, and she was a wonderful lady, with a great experience. If any of the boys and girls were in difficulties they should go to Miss West, who would advise them, mother . them, and help them to decide in the right. There were many boys and girls who could not ask any woman for advice when they were in difficulties, and the children who went .to that church were placed in a happy position, for they had Miss West with them al- ways. They had also 'Mr. Penaliggon, who- was always willing to help. They should take his advice, for he was a good leader, and they should not forget that old people did know things, be- cause they had been that way. The young people .should love the Bible, because it was such a wonderful book, and such a great help in the journey through life. They Should make it their daily companion. She then declared the bazaar open.

' Thoughts of Each Other. - Mr. J. IL Holt proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. 011erenshaw and the Chairman. He said that Mrs. 011erenshaw had remarked that young people should take advice from older men and No-omen. He had h i eard t said when he was yount,ver—whenthe thought it silly, but as one grew older one realised that it was true—that "young people think old people fools, but old people know young people to be fools." (Laugh- ter.) It was a fine thing to be connected with religious work. They had one of the best ,of ladies opening that bazaar. He had heard much of her generosity and sympathy, that sympathy which was never indiscriminately given, for the object had to be good and, noble before she assisted it. They had a reully good cause there, or they would not have Mrs. 011erenshaw with them.• , They were also indebted to their Chairman, for he represented the Cheshire Congregational County Union, of which he was chairman-elect. They owed the union a great debt, for the inter- est they took in that cause during, thWr days of adversity-. Mr. Armitage also represented the Congregational Church at Bowdon, where he was the deacon. In conclusion, he said they were anxious to purchase the chief rent, which had been such a burden for many years. (Hear, hear, and applauSe.) Mr. Smith seconded, and said he knew that Mrs. 011erenshaw set a fine midi grand example to the womankind of that and every district throughout the country. If they had more ladies like her, who were willing to sacrifice, their time and leisure, their causes would not languish in the .way they did. (Hear, hear.) The Bev. J. A. Penaliggon said they fully annrecia led the sympathy and help whiph Mrs. 011erenshaw gave them. Mrs. 011erenshaw, in rculy, said she hoped she might be .worthy of all that had been said of her.

The Rev. J. A. Penalion sl tliat on behalf of the friends of Bucklow Hill they wanted those in Lymm to feel that they lied behind them the sister ehnrch in symq,thetic touch, and they were doing all they could to help them forward. (Applause.)
THURSDAY'S CEREMONY. The Need of Co-operation in Churches.
The Pastor presided at the opening ceremony on Thursday, and he was supported by Mrs. Ridgway, Mrs. Miller (fOughtrington), the Rev. E. E. Lovell, Mr. J. H. Holt, Mr. Smith, and Mr. G,Villan.

Ile Chairman said it was unnecessary ,for him to introduce Mrs. Ridgway to them, for she and her family were so well-known in' the dis- trict. He was, however, delighted to offer to her, on behalf of that church; a most hearty welcome. Mrs. Ridgway, whO was there to open the bazaar; was a member of a very old family, and a member of the Established Church of England. It was particularly gratifying for one to see that it was possible to co-operate not only amongst the Nonconformist Churches, but amongst their own and the Established Churches. He was sure it betokened a great interest in their movement by members of the Established Church, and he was glad because of that. They were confronted with the indiistrial, economical and theological problems, . and the great problem of civilisation, and ,he was of the opinion that the Churches would have to co- operate more in the future in order to Meet the great tendencies against them. The Estab- lished and Nonconformist Churches would have to understand one 'another better and have to see that the futherance of the spirit of Jesus Christ was the most essential thing. A spirit of co-operation' would enable them to deal with the great problems Of the day. Mrs. Ridgway said she thought bazaars ,excel- lent, because they drew out such unsuspected good and great unselfishness. They promoted a kindly feeling and brotherly attitude, and drew together those with the same object at heart. She had been reading a pamphlet in regard to the history of that church, and one thing stood out strongly in her mind, that the .small band of members with faith and hope had stood time after time shoulder to shoulder during the storms,- encouraging each other with- words of cheer until the rain ceased and the sun shone once more. To-day, in their jubilee year, the sun had emerged from the clouds, and his genial

smile had already warmed and comforted those who had waitect i“s advent. The object of that sale appealed to her, and to all there that after- noon, for they believed that God's House should be free from debt. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Smith said that the proceeds the previous day amounted to A:169. He had to apologise fQr the absence of Mrs. Gotobed, who was unwell, and he was sure they all regretted her illness.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL.
GLEANINt;S FROM GR ‘PPENIIALL.

Have you felt the odours? Rattier pronounced, are they not? Is it Stockton Heath that is to blame? The Heathens deny the soft impeachment. They blame some other folk. Amongst them is the canal cattle boats. Whoever is at fault, it is a nuisance. Grappenhall does not want to be swallowed up.
The eyes of Warrington are, however, bast our way.
A scheme for annexation is simmering in the pot. It may be ready for dishing up in a year. Grappenhall is to be One of the victims.

MOTOR CAR v. BABY_ CARRIAGE. Case Dismissed on Payment of Costs. William James Barker, Abbingdon-street, Northampton, was summoned, at the Petty Sessions held at Stockton Heath on Tuesday, for having driven a motor car in Knutsford-road, Grappenhall, to the danger of the public, on the 6th September. " It appeared from the evidence., that Mrs. Mil- lar, Smith's Cottages, Knutsford-road, Grap- penhall, was wheeling a baby carriage with two children in it, when she saw the motor car about 40 yards .ahead of her. The driver had plenty Of room, but he, turned sharply to the right, then to the left, and then his motor car caught the carriage and knocked Mrs. Millar over. The carriage remained upright. The car -Would be travelling at ten miles per hour. Frank Grimes (13), Knutsford-road, Grappen- hall, said the car was going very slow, but '" zig- zagged" down the road. ;
Thomas Hankey, coal 'merchant, Knutsford- road, Grappenhall, also deposed to witnessing the accident. Defendant had said to him it was the "nearest shave ". he had had.

div.head: " A Brilliant Sunset."
div.p: " A Brilliant Sunset."

Mr. G. IL Ormerod (Manchester), who de- fended, said the charge was one of the most serious that could be brought against a motorist. Mr. Barker was on his way from Northampton to Liscard, and he had an old lady of 70 years and his chauffeur in the car. It was extremely unlikely, having the old lady with him, that he would be in any way negligent. He did not see Mrs. Millar until he was quite close to her, and he (Mr. Ormerod) could only account for that by the fact that there was a brilliant sun- set that evening. The ra vs fell on the wind- screen, and so obscured fl,q view. He shouted out as soon as he saw 11.1!.- Millar and swerved to the left. The carriage must .have been caught by the back mudguao as the carpwerved. Mr. Barker had driven a car for 14 y'ears and had never had a complaint made against him. Mr. Barker 'bore oiAt this statement. in evi- dence.
After a lengthy consideration the-Bench dis- missed the case on payment of costs.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD
JOURNALIST.

Road Hogs. For driving a motor car at a speed estimated .• at from 40 to 50 miles an hour, an offender has . been fined 20s. and costs by the Warrington Borough Bench. I' venture to submit that so Paltry a penalty is calculated neither to deter Others nor to encourage the police. Besides creating an everlasting nuisance, regardless of .the rights of other users of the public highways, , these road hogs constantly take the most awful risks, and it is by sheer good luck that so many of them escape more serious consequences than summons for driving to the common danger , and a fine which affects them no more than a flea-bite. It is beginning to be suspected that Magistrates adjudicating in such cases, being themselves motorists in several instances, are unconsciously biased in favour of their class. I now write generally, for the leniency shown to reckless scorchers by the Great Unpaid is , Vowing scandal; but such cases as occurred here last week' go far to strengthen the argu- nient for a stipendiary magistrate. ' Smoke Fiend. • Prosecutions for smoke nuisance may well be reckoned in the same category. It appears the local authorities are so tenderly solicitous • for the feelings of those of their fellows who are peFsistently guilty of tile really serious offence in question that they do not even blacklist them tor Press pillory. Elsewhere, even though there may be some hesitancy about taking o.ses into Court, full particulars respecting 81noke observations are entered on the corn- Tlittee's minutes and left absolutely to the dis- cretion of the reporters.

"When Knights Were Bold." Boniehow I cannot help expressing especial Pleasure at the keen appreciation of this amus- IN play repeatedly shown by Warringtonians. I think I never felt so humiliated and ashamed aS I did on witnessing it four or five pyears ago 41U Lancashire town of 26,000 inhabitants. It W4S an admirable performance, but patrons Utterly failed to enter into the spirit of the thing ; indeed, many of them frankly confessed that they did not understand what it Was all 'bout !
