div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1913.
A PILGRIMAGE TO BOSCOBEL
Touching and Almost Unequalled Stories of
Devotion to a Fallen king.

div.head: _THE FAMOUS OAK TREE THAT CONCEALED CHARLES 11.
div.p: _THE FAMOUS OAK TREE THAT CONCEALED CHARLES 11.

Neither in the annals of England, nor of any other nation, shall we find anything that quite matches the story of the flight of Charles after the battle of Worcester. As a siory of de- Votion to a king, it is almost unequalled, and its homely features rather help than hinder its attractiOn. Of how King Charles hid in an oak tree, we have all heard, us well as of sundry perils and adventures by the way, but romance has, been plentifully mingled with truth, and some sift- ing and study is needful 'before we can be sure of our ground. This is unfortunate, for nO story ever needed less help from the romantic imagination than does the story of -Charles 11., after the Worcester fight. We propose to take our readers to Boscobel, and, in going over the ground, to go over the story.
house should be unsafe, • the three concealed tneinsel‘ es in the wood.

THE SOJOURN IN THE OAK TREE. It was 'about three o'clock in the morning when they arrived, and was full day when they passed out into the woods to hide.. At whose suggestion the step was taken we do not know, out Lhey decided to take refuge in a tree. A uushy oak was chosen, and by the aid of a ladder Charles and the Colonel were helped to the level Of the branches: Two cushions were handed up, and the King, after his night of wandering, fell asleep with his head on the Colonel's lap. , He awoke hungry, and the Colonel produced some bread, cheese and beer, packed by the thoughtful dame who had bathed Lie Kings feet. The whole day was spent in what must have been a rather comfortless perch, and evening found them back hi Boscobel house, grateful, we may suppose, for .its com- fort.

This is all that can be said of the adventure in Boscobel oak. Sober history tells of nothing that happened there, except of what happened to the bread, cheese and ale. We have heard of lots of things that happened on that famous day, and have Seen them depicted on public- house signs, but these seem to belong to the realm of romance and artistry. The King and Colonel had much to listen to when they entered the house. Richard Pen- derel had been to Wolverhampton ,and Hum- phrey to Shifnal, and they were brimful of ex., citing ,information. Humphrey had been hek: up by a colonel of Cromwell's army and inter- rogated.. He had been told significantly that the penalty for concealing the King was death, and that a thousand pounds was offered to any- one who would discover him. The King re- ceived this information, but it had no appreci- able effect upon his appetite. He slept in one of the hiding places, which must be mentioned by and by. Rising early in the niorning, he spent some time in devotion and in watching through .the gallery window, which gave a view of the road from Tong.. It was Saturday, and the King purposed making flight after nightfall. When ask eil what food he would like for dinner, he expressed a desire for mutton. A sheep was killed, and when cold a leg was brought into the parlour. He asked for a frying-pan and butter, and after cutting off some collops, fried them over the parlour tire.

THE ESCAPE FROM BOSCOBEL.. Meanwhile, John Penderel was travelling to Moseley, where Lord Wilmot was known to be in hiding, to say that the King intended to join him that night. But Lord Wilmot had gone to Bentley, and it was Sunday evening, September 7th, before the. King left Boscobel. He took leave of Colonel Carlesse, who afterwards man- aged to escape to France, and'accompanied by a band of the faithful Penderels and Francis Yates, bestrode Humphrey's mill horse, and rode off in the darkness. It was slow move- ment for the King, who complained that the mill horse was the "dullest jade" he ever rode. The miller had spirit enough to jest in reply, and told_the King that the beast was "only accustomed to carry six striks of corn, but now it had the weight of three kingdoms on its back."

It is to be feared that the Sovereign head of three kingdoms cut a rather sorry figure that night, with toes wrapped up in paper, where the blisters were worst, and with limbs that ached from exposure and strain. But all, went smoothly, and ,MoSeley was reached without hitch or adventure.

div.head: FLIGHT FROM WORCESTER.
div.p: THE FLIGHT FROM WORCESTER.

The date of the decisive day at Worcester was September 3rd, 1651. To .Cromwell, whose gratitude often leaped out in picturesque phrases, it was " the crowning mercy."' Charles might, with equal truth and terseness; have called it "the crowning disaster." The battle over and lost, the chief concern among the King's advisers was for his safety. His father's head had fallen on the scaffold, and Charles 11. had taken the risks of the same struggle, and with the same men ,who signed the death war- rant of Charles I. A consultation was held at Barbourn Bridge, about a mile nofith of Worcester, and the deci- sion was made to fly northward. With the King were the Duke 'of Buckingham, Lord Derby, Lord Wilmot, and others, and the jour- ney began. They rode through Barnhall, Ombersley and Hartlebury, across Lea Castle Park, crossed the Stour at Blakeshall, and arrived at Kinver Edge. Here a halt was made, and a second con- sultation held. Lord Derby had used Boscobel as a hiding place, and suggested it as such for the King. The advice was taken, and the party pressed on in the darkness through Stourbridge to Himley,. and passing through Wrottesley Wood, emerged at daybreak at the monastery of Whiteladies.
This old place dated from the 12th century, but had been shorn. of much of its glory after the Reformation.

DISGUISED IN HASTE. Here in the inner room, Tom and Richard Penderel, who had been summoned. by Lord Derby, began the process of disguising the King as a woodman, while Lord Wilmot hacked off his curls with a dagger., A 'leather doublet, belonging to. Richard, and a green pair of breeches, with an old grey hat, borrowed from the, miller, made a -fairly complete transforma- tion, and a coarse hempen shirt and pair of old shoes were added. The 'final- touch of reality was given when Charles was led out into the wood, and placed in the surroundings for which he now looked quite fitted. _

The rest of the party rode away towards New- port, but were overtaken and made prisoners before they reached the town. The Duke of Buckingham escaped, Earl Cleveland was im- prisoned in the Tower, Earl Derby was be- headed at Bolton, and Francis Yates, who had acted as guide, was hanged. The 'occupants of the house at Whiteladies were not numerous. There was' Dothy, widow of John Giffard, its mistress,:who regaled the King with biscuit and wine whilst the hair cutting was in progress; Charles Giffard, who had acted as guide; George Penderel and his brother John, who were woodmen; tyMiss Anna Andrews, who undertook the risky duty of keeping the King's clothes; and an old priest named Walker. •

In less than an hour after the King had left the house, ,a troop of Cromwell's horse were at the door inquiring if the King or any of hI horse had passed that way. They replied that a party had called three hours before, and after some inquiries the pursuers rode off. The King was meanwhile beginning to follow a day of imuinary duties as an amateur wood- man. But The day was wet, and was an un- happy. one for the King. He sheltered under a tree, wrapped in a blanket brought for him by Margaret Yates, who lived in a cottage near by, and was in the secret. This same sympa- thiser: brought a mixture of milk, eggs and sugar, only part of/which he was able to eat.

Darkness was very welcome, and as soon as it had closed in, the King, with Richard, George and Humphrey Penderel, and Francis Yates, travelled to Richard's house at Hubbal Grange. Here the moharch, in his character of "Will Jones," a wood chopper, sat down to a supper of eggs and bacon, and nursed the 'youngest child. The mother of the Pendercls crept in to see the King and to bless God that her sons were to he, as she prayed, his deliverers. Francis Yates offered the King thirty shillings, of which he took only ten, and then ,began the, effort to escape.

It was the King's idea to escape into-Wales, and helad planned to get to Madeley, and there cross the Severn.. It wfis arranged that Richard Penderef should alone go with him, and 'after supper on September 4th, these two began the adventurous journey.

div.head: NIGHT ADVENTURE.
div.p: NIGHT ADVENTURE.

Passing from Hubbal Grange through Tong; th.dy came safely to Evelith Mill. Here a-stream was to be crossed, and by the side of the wooden bridge was a mill. A gate proteqed the bridge from wandering cattle; and in opening this some noise was made. The fugitives received here their first shock,„ for the miller rushed forth, Cudgel in hand; with the demand "Who goes 'there?" Richzird leaped into the stream, followed by the King, who followed as well as he could, guided only by the rattling of a pair ; pf leather breeches. The alarm of the miller, arose from the fact that the mill contained some of the King's sol- diers, and he feared the newcomers might be Cromwell's men. If he, ever learned that his, cry had driven his beloved king to the bed of the stream his remorse must surely have stirred his enemies to pity. Climbing on the other side of the stream by means of a d.eep ,and dirty road, the King and Penderel reached the village. of Kemberton, and then the house of Mr. Woolfe, at MadeleY. Charles waited under a tree, while Richard went to ask .for .protectiom The old inmate had suffered sufficiently in the Royal cause, but when the whisper was given that it was the King, he gladly,' offered iTelp. It was pointed out that all the hiding holes in the house were known, and that in the event of a visit- from' the enemy, escape would be impoSsible. only cover that offered safety seemed to be the barn, and here the two wanderers rested through the night and the next day.

div.head: TO BOSCOBEL.
div.p: TO BOSCOBEL.

Discouraging news reached them in the barn. The Severn' was being carefully guarded, ferry boats were seized, and watchers eVerywhere. It was decided that they .should retrace their steps, and when night closed on the sth of September', guided by Mr. Woolfe's maid, they made the journey back to Whiteladies, and thence to Boscobel. Here Colonel Carlesse had already taken shelter, and quickly came forth when Richard Penderel appeared at the door. A meal was prepared, and the mistress of the house, touched with pity for the King's plight, removed his stockings, cut and tended tile blisters, and bathed his feet. Afraid lest the

div.head: 'SIX WEEKS IN DISGUISE.
div.p: 'SIX WEEKS IN DISGUISE.

For six weeks King Charles wandered in dis- guise through the land, of which he claimed to be king. Fully forty persons, were in rile secret, but his friends were too loyal to • be tempted by the reward. It is a narrative quite unmatched, and neither romancer nor novelist has ever invented any- thing so striking. Through the western counties, and then through the southern- ones, he wandered in the dress of a serving man, until a coaling vessel took him to France.

_ It lies beyond our purpose to trace the move- ments of King Charles through those weeks of sltess, but our readers may like to know the results of a tour in search of Whiteladies, Madeley and Boscobel.

A VISIT TO WIIITELADIES. Of the monastery, buildings at Whiteladies there is little to' see. It is a ruin, and its walls staid dejected in the 'middle of a large field. It is walled in, and appears still to be used as a graveyard. Cattle graze on the land over which the King galloped, covered with blood and foarn,,and wet to the skin, after his flight from Worcester. Here, within the walls, he sat, while Lord Wilmot hacked off his Cavalier curls with a dagger. A sorry figure he must have 19,oked in yokel's dress, pushed forth into dripping woods at daylight, while -The neavenS (to quote a Royalist tract written later) "wept bitterly at, the calamity that had befallen this inestimable jewel of England."

div.head: MADELEY AND THE DARN.
div.p: MADELEY AND THE DARN.

There is a pleasant surprise for the pilgrim who is able to get to Madeley and seek out the house of Mr. Woolfe. There has been little change as far as we can judge since the King and his "trusty Dick" sought it out in the darkness. The old man Woolfe makes a lather touching figure in .the story. He was seventy years old, a Royalist and a Catholic. His son was in Prison, and he felt Wilt he had suffered enough for the cause. Richard Penderel got a cool reception when he asked for protection for "a gentleman of quality." We can seer in imagination, the old man,standing in the door- way, with dejection written across his face, and a body bowed with age. But Penderel whis- pered "It is the King," and in a flash all was changed. rhe house was unsafe, but there was the barn, and so England's King lay down with one of England's herdmen in the straw. Happily the barn is also standing. It is a fine old place, looking very much like an ancient tithe barn, and big enough to conceal a small regiment. We have not heard of the barn being visited, yet to us it was far more inter- esting than Boscobel oak 'tree. Of course, there is more romance in perching like an ea7g'le in a tree than lying among straw in a_ barn like a rat, and popular fancy has made much of the oak. It- was here in the barn that Mrs. Woolfe came to take a look at the Royalist fugitive. His clothes were good enough (or bad enough) for Purposes of disguise, but .slic considered that his fair face .quite gave him away. Who could pose as a country labourer and carry a lily white face and hands?
It was the period at which walnuts were being gathered, and the clever old lady managed to make a brown dye, which brought -the King's face and hands to the right colour.
_ A PILGRIMAGE TO BOSCOBEL—cont.

div.head: BOSCOREL HOUSE AND OAK.
div.p: BOSCOREL HOUSE AND OAK.

And now to.Boscobel. The old house is hard to find, and the tourist must give himself ample time. Itt is an old hunting lodge, built by the Giffards (who Oill oivn the land around) in a remote part of Brewood Forest. As a hunting lodge, it is spacious 'and good, and its many gables give it a fine flavour of quaintness and beauty. Its name comes from bosc and belle, which means a beautiful wood. Though reared for pleasure, its builder evidently anticipated that other uses might be found for it, for it had

two secret chambers, one of them constructed with the greatest skirl. • About a hundred yards away is Boscobel oak, surrounded by a fence, and bearing a Latin in- scription, which tells the visitor that "This tree, under the blessing of the King of kings, had the honour of sheltering his sacred majesty," Stc. _

This is the only unreal thing about Bdscobel. The oak that sheltered the King ,paSsed quickly into snuff boxes 4rid relics at the Restoration. The best that can be said for its successor is that it probably was a scioli-of the ad tree and that it probably occupies the same site. In the centre of the garden is the mound and arbour in. which Charles spent the Sunday afternoon before his flight. He did not trouble to hide on the Sunday. He knew his enemies, and probably believed that they would give the day to psalm singing. He was unljappy enough, sand one can be sorry for him. Many a time on the road thither he had flung himself upon the -ground and welshed for death, while poor pick Penderel almost' dragged him along in a very sweat of terror.

What would not one have given to see the young King as ,he sat that afternoon, stained brown in face and hands, and enduring the horrors of leather breeches and •blistered feet under the shQes of a country clodhopper!

div.head: TABLE TALKS
div.p: TABLE TALKS
The World's Tribute of Interesting Items of News.
QUAINT AND ArkIUSING.

A new life jacket, invented by M. Allain liedou, of Havre, consists of a strong vest equipped with inflatable rubber crowns or tubes, resting on the shoulders and passing under the arms, and covered with material like the vest. A leather belt keeps the vest in place. When required the tubes are filled by blowing into them, and in a test the ,garment was put an and completely inflated in 87 seconds. A sailor with his legs tied and a 221 b. weight at- tached to hii feet, easily kept above the surface of the water.
New Zealand's Child Death-rate.

I was very much struck by one paragraph in the report of the Otago Plunket Society (New Zealand). It shows that the death-rate among children under one year in Dunedin was 8 per cent. in the seven years from 1900 to 1907. For the last five years 61 per .cent., for the last two years 5 per cent., and for the last year 4 per cent. . . . If only half this reduction is due to the efforts of Dr.-Truby King and the Society, what a good work is being done for the Dominion as a whole.—The Hon. W. Massey (Prime Minister).
Chinamen Deserting Rice.

It is stated in a Colonial report on Hong-Kong tat there, was an increase of 16,620 tons in the quantity of flour imported into the golony, , attri- buted to the fact that The Chinese arc. quickly learning new uses for this commodity, win& in many parts is taking the place of rice. "This increased use of flour," says the report, "is evi- dent in the colony, being noticeable even among the boat population of the harbour, where it is a Common thing to see cakes and 'Flap Jacks' being cooked and eaten instead of the, formerly universal rice."
Phosphorus for Consumptives.

Dr. F. Lemon states that he has employed phosphorus successfully in all classes of cases of lung disease during the past eleven years. He is convinced that this drug has a direct action upon the lung tissue—which perhaps accounts for its rapid effects in acute bronchitis and pneumonia. Not only does the pulmonary condition improve, but the whole bodily condi- tion shows greater vigour. The doctor sug- gests that the tendency to consumption is brought about by a lack of phosphorus in the nervous and other tissues of the patients.
The Japanese and Canada.

The vigilance necessary to keep the yellow races from being smuggled into British Colum- bia and the United States is brought home by the capture recently of ten Japanese labourers who had braved the 'terrors of a 6,000-mile sea voyage in a small fishing junk and were landed twelve miles north of Eureka, in California, on a bleak coast. Only a few days ago Sir Richard Mcßride, Premier of British Columbia, stated in "The Standard " that it was the intention of the authorities to make Canada a white man's country, and the Japanese who have been ar- rested admit. that Canada was their destination.

div.head: KING'S §ECOND HAIR CUT.
div.p: THE KING'S §ECOND HAIR CUT.

We enter the house with deep interest, and are glad to find it quite unspoiled, save that some vandal ha S painted the oak panelling, to gain more brightness. We are shown the room in which Charles sat when he arrived at Bos- cobel. Here some further attention was given to his toilet. 'Lord Wilinot'S daggeof had re- moved his locks, but the job looked very un- workmanlike to the faithful Penderel. If the King must pass as a yokel, he must have a yokel's crop. And so a basin was put over the head that was Supposed to be adorned by a crown, and the hair was clipped round 'ft, good tufts being 'left to protect-the ears from rain. They show us the table at which he ate tthe chicken, and the fireplace where he cooked the mutton collops. That sheep, by -the way, was stolen from a neighbOur. Colonel Carlesse stabbed it with his dagger, and Penderel ,dragged it in by slealth. It has to be remem7 bered that the inmates of the lonely house dare not go out for extra supplies' of food, lest sus- picion should be aroused. Hence the fate of the chicken and of the sheep that belonged to Farmer Staunton.

After all was over, Penderel, like an honest fellow, went and offered to pay for, the sheep, but when StauntOn knew the facts he refused the money. In the room where the mutton was cooked, there is a quaint old picture which represeniS the 'departure of the Kin from Boscobel on the Sunday night.. The five Brothers Penderel are there armed with pikels anrCKubs, evidently resolved to sell their lives dearly. • Most interesting of all is the hiding-place, where the King slept. It is high up in the house, under the cheese-room. The entrance is by a trap door, and this, if hidden by a few cheeses, would be hard to discover. Here also from the cheese-room the King peered forth on the watch for enemies. -

div.head: REFLECTION.
div.p: A REFLECTION.

We can always form the best mental picture when we have :the true background, and here at Boscobel is the place to realise the simple and altogether admirable devotion of these simple folks to the King. Charles is remembered as one of The . most despicable figures in history, the most loath- some ruler that ever filled the throne. He was saved from his enemies to become a moral leper in the high places of England, to corrupt the nobility and leave a legacy of debt and dis- grace.
What contrast, as we picture his deliverers.

aey are men from the mill and the soil, and they cheerfully risk their lives for a man 'whom they had never seen, and whose tharacter, had they known it, they would have despised. We think of Richard Penderel dragging the King to the safety of Boscobel through that dark night; the dandy of Whitehall lying upon the ground wailing for death because his labourer's boots had blistered his feet, and honeist Dick, at the risk of his own life, refusing to leave him.
King Charles owed his life and his throne to that bit of old religious teaching which the clergy had managed to instil into the peasantry —"Fear God o.nd honour the King,"

div.head: WORLD OF LETTERS.
div.p: THE WORLD OF LETTERS.

of the ward and held him by both arms, while Leschoff and two other warders struck him on the face and head with their fists. Volkoff kicked.Borissoff twice in the stomach, and then began to belabour his victim on the head and shoulders with the handle of his glittering, heavy weapon. " Borissoff crouched under the blows, groan- ing feebly. The beating went on in silence. Only the sounds of the blows and the sup- pressed groans of 'Borissolf were to be heard. Volkoff, however, shrieked now and again with rage and excitement, while Archipoff, who was holding the prisoner, kept .on whispering the admonishment: Won't you stand still? Stand straight, I tell you; don't wriggle about.' The prisoner was then thrown on the - floor and kicked. At last Volkoff gave the order: 'That will do. Carry the, beast to the punishment- cell. There he will get a rest.'"

div.head: Literary Gleanings.
div.p: Literary Gleanings.
lIAS THE ORIGM OF LIFE BEEN FOUND ?

The most remarkable discovery announced at the International Medical Congress was un- doubtedly that made by Dr. Charlton Bastian, consulting physician to the University College hospital. He gave a striking demonstration of bodies said to be living organisms, and to have been spontaneously generated in the course of sonic of his experiments. He told the members of the conference that he had performed certain experiments with fluids, which at the beginning were absolutely free from living forms of any, kind, and that during his investigations living beings—minute, indeed, but nevertheless alive— came into being. _

The plain meaning of this is that Dr. Bastian claims to have witnessed the origin of life itself. .He started with chemical) solutions from which all living things—even the tiniest microbes— were, as far as possible, rigorously excluded. He continued, by sealing ,his solutions in tubes to which there could be no entry of life from without. He then exposed them to great heat on three successive days; exposed them to heat that must certainly have destroyed all- living things, such as microbes, animalculte or lowly plants of any kind. Yet a few months after- wards he is able to show in his sealed tubes forms of matter which even to experts have the very closest resemblance to elementary forms of vegetable life.

Dr. -Bastian showed bodies that to all intents and purposes are organisms resealing yeasts and other moulds, and also further demon- strated similar specimens taken from other of his previously sealed tubes, which had been placed for. several days under favourable con- ditions for stimulating their growth and which appear to have multiplied very considerably. Dr. Bastian considers that his experiments conclusively show the origin of livinq organ- isms which not only grow themselves but can reproduce their species. The solutions used by Dr. Bastian in his experiments consist- of such, simple substances as pernitrate of iron. sodium silicate and phos- phoric acid, mixed in certain, proportions and dissolved M distilled water. After the mixing of a solution it is sterilised and then simply exposed to the action of diffused sunlight for some weeks or months. Dr. Bastian himself 'believes that. it is that light that is the chief agent in the production of life in his sealed and sterilised tubes.

div.head: Bt. RBAGES.
div.p: THE Bt. RBAGES.

Who was the first builder of a theatre. in England? It was James Burbage, the father of the more celebrated Richard Burbage, who acted in so many of Shakespeare's tragedies. James, the father, in many ways a very 'remarkable man, and a joiner by trade, conceived the bril- liant idea in 1576 of providing a. permanent house for the. Earl of Leicester's Players, to whom he belonged. Leicester's men had ob- tained a patent in 1574 authorising them to act in every part of the kingdom, and in the very next year they figured in the festivities at Kenil- worth on the occasion of the Queen's visit. But it was an obvious advantage for them to have a fixed home, and Burbage:s idea was destined to have very , significant consequences. In Shoreditch, close to the Finsbury Fields, arose during the summer of 1577 The' Theatre," so- called, a building of wood and timber. erected after the model of those courtyards of inns, which probably often .served as a place of entertainment. Burbage at once received the compliment of imitation, for close by his theatre was built another playhouse, called " The Curtain." They had stormy times. The Puritan preachers exhausted their very exten- sive vocabulary in denouncing the wickedness of dramatic exhibitions. The Corporation of London made a habitual practice of petitioning the Privy Council to suppress the Theatre and the Curtain, mainly on the ground that they were the haunts of vicious characters. Above all, the Constant outbreaks of the plague fre- quently led to sudden closure, for, of course, the assembling of crowds would help to spread the infection. James Burbage himself was over and over again involved in a network of law- suits, which made large holes in the profits of his undertaking. levertheless he prospered, and in 1596 we find him starting another theatre at Blackfriars. Difficulties with regard to the Shoreditch site eventually led, in December, 1598, to the removal of "The Theatre" to the Bankside, where it was rechristened "The Globe." By that time, however, James Burbage was dead. His spirited enterprise had led to the erection of three principal playhouses of Queen Elizabeth's reign. Of all this and much besides Mrs. -Carmichael Stones tells us in her very interesting book on the Burbages.
RUSSIAN PRISON ATROCITIES. 7

The " Busskoe Bogatstvb " is publishing the recollections of M. Voytinsky, a former student, who was sentenced to four years' penal servi- tude Tor being a member of the Social Demo- cratic party, and who, after having served his sentence, was sent intO perpetual exile. . M. Voytinsky grimly describes the "amuse- ments" of the inferior authorities of the convict prison to which he 'MIS consigned. "With trampling feet, noisy exclamations, and coarse laughter," he writes, "a gang of warders came up the stairs, after Which every-- thing became inaudible behind the thick walls. Then they turned into a. side corridor, and en- tered one of the cells. Now one could distln• .guish shouts, resounding blows, sobs, and the clatter of chains, whicli soon grew louder and came nearer. Something heavy was rolling down the stairs, accompanied\ by the clanking of chains. The whole prison resounded with the loud despairing cry: 'Oh! they are killing me!' . "The hollow sound of blows is heard from below, to which a. voice Seems to keep time, saying: !Shout away! Go on shouting, you carrion!' Somebody cries out: ' Kill at once, executioners, but dot not torture.' To which the chief warder Volkoff's voice is heatd to shriek in reply: Quiet! I will make dog's meat of all of you." At. that time M: Voytinsky only heard the thrashings, as he was then confined to the infir- mary; but later on he both witnessed and ex- perienced them • himself. He describes the cruelties practised on a consumptive workman named Borissoff, who occupied the bed next to him in the infirmary ' "The door was 'opened, and the gang of warders rushed into the ward, headed by Volkoff, who seemed to be quite drunk. He held himself firmly upright., however, expand- ing his Chest in military fashion, while some of the warders were reeling about. Among their red, perspiring faces one Could distinguish a few that were quite pale, with frightened, puzzled eyes. "'Beat him!' commanded the chief warder, pointing at Borissoff. The latter was then standing close to his bed, tall and as thin as a skeleton, and his face turned white. He. stood motionless, and resembled more a .corpse than a living being. while even the characteristic flush of the consumptive had disappeared from his pointed cheekbones. He was approached by two warders—the tall, stout, and heavy Archipoff, and the lean, black-moustached Cossack Leschoff. Archipoff seized Borissoff by the shoulder and drat,fged his body towards him, while Leschoff struck a blow on the patient's face with his fist, and with his whole might. Borissoff staggered. and his face was covered with blood. He neither cried out nor groaned, ,and made no attemnt whatever to defend him- self. He merely asked in a low voice What for?'
" Quiet, you rascal! Don't talk! Beat awn v.'

REVOLUTIONISED CHINA.

Some good stories about modern Cfiina is published by Mr. J. Stuart Thomson, a jour- nalist with a wide knowledge of the Celestials. Here, for example. is an amusing story of a stern mandarin, who had inherited the nick- name of the "old devil."

"One day, ahead of his escort, he reached his inn, where quarters had been engaged for him. On attempting to walk into the best room the innkeeper, ,who did not ,know him, strenu- ously objected, explaining that the room was reserved for 'the Old Devil himself,' and woe betide them all if the engagement ,was not re- spected. When his escort came tip the man- darin had the innkeeper flogged for daring to speak disrespectfully of a judge who was a .dignified 'father and mother' of the •people, and, at. the same time, hapded the man a hand- ful of coins' as a reward for keeping faith with the said mandarin." •

And here is a characteristic story of an Eastern medico, whose habits are proverbially strange to Europeans: "It is well known that Chinese doctors are only rewarded for cures and for keeping patients well. A physician was called in to see a sick tax-collector (yamen runner). 'You'll have to call in another doctor,' said the physi- cian. 'Am Iso bad that you must have a con- sultation?' inquired the alarmed patient. No. You will remember, however, if you have as good a memory as I, that last week you searched high and low, and, taxed me the last cash on the limit of my property and maximum income. I have too much conscience to kill you, but I'm honest enough to say that I want as little as possible to do with curing you, so good-bye.'" These sketches; by the way, give a good idea of the national standards of China, which are often, it must be confessed, of a somewhat low order of morality. There seems fQr example, to be little difficulty in raising " cooked " evi- dence upon any point of law, or of getting it through the authorities with imp Unity. "The method of ` planting ' fcirged evidence (says Mr. Thomson) is met with in China, where a powerful enemy wishes to ruin some victim. The Yuen Fung Yuen Bank, of Bonham Strand, is one of the largest native banks in Hong Kong, in which colony it is illegal to import opinion except through the Farm, .which pays the Government a large royalty. This valu= able drug passes almost at bullion, value. Anonymous infbrmation was sent to the Farm contractor that at eight o'clock p.m. the bank would receive illicit opium. Detectives were put in ambuscade. At the hour mentioned a coolie bearing a basket rapped at the bank's door and shouted 'A letter for you.' Then he ran, but was caught. An examination re- vealed a tin of opium at the bottom of a basket of eggs. Investigation disclosed the whole thing as a ` plant ' prepared by an old enemy of the Yuen Fung Bank. In the same way bodies of the dead and murdered are often secretly placed at the doors of innocent victims, and as much motive as possible is prepared, so as to get them in trouble with law and popular indig- nation."

Marriage in China is dealt with by Mr. Thom. son in some animated pages, and the position of woman seems to be gradually \ improving. Nevertheless, the parasitic attitude of the son- in-law takes some time to disturb, and it con- tinues to be necessary to choose your daughter's husband with discretion. "The ' mother-in:law ' joke does not obtain in China. Its place is taken by the son-ip-law joke."

Meanwhile, it is not surprising that Chinese womankind should be striking for independ- ence, nor that the Suffragette movement should have 'gained adherents in the Kingdom of the Dragon. Says Mr. Thomson:

"Perhaps the most significant sign of China's reform is the new status of women. Never before have Chinese women travelled with their merchant husbands. In a few i-olatectinstances Chinese Ministers. have taken their , wives abroad; but there have never been • mixed parties of men and women until the reyolution In November, 1911, a touring party of pro fninent members of Chinese. trading guilds of several provinces met at Shanhai for a busiehriS tour of Japan, ,They were accompanied by their wives. The New China has its Mrs. Pan;:- hurst in Miss Yik-Yung-Ying, of Canton, whi is foreign trained, and has admission to the Nanking Assembly, as representing the women of her province of Kwantung. She has ob- tained from the Nanking Assembly a promise of equal suffrage .on equal property and educa- tional Conditions. Some' of her suffragettes attacked the assembly police and broke win- dows in true Pankhurst style. the. patient, Chinese wits only remarking, 'This froth will blow, off the glass and leave the clear liquid! ' "

A Clever Pussy Cat. Maternal instinct led a big black cat to ignore names and smoke in an effort to shield her six little kittens in the six-storey loft building at No. 114, West Seventeenth-street, New York, until the firemen had to carry her out of the place to save her life. She was limp and almost suffocated when the firemen piclied her up, but was still making a valiant fight for her. offspring. All six of the little fluffy felines were dead, but the mother was struggling toward the front windows with two of them in her mouth in a hopeless .effort to get them into the fresh air. The fire started in the underwear shop of Fisher and Co., on the sixth floor of the building. When Lieutenant- Comiskey reached the place with his fire company he •noticed the cat walking feebly toward the front of the loft. She had in her mouth two little kittens,-but the fire had attained such headway that the Lieutenant's attention was diverted from the mother cat for a few minutes. When the fire was under control he again saw the cat standing over a box. He went up and found that there were four more kittens. All of them had been smothered by the smoke, as were the two the mother had been carrying. The Lieu- tenant carried the mother to tho.:, street, and Acting Chief Ross decided to adopt her. The cat will .spend the rest of her life in luxury at . the Fire'Station.

Catching a Bear. " Why ! What's that?" said 'Norman, as be came out of school one day., and he ran up to the sign-board which was on the .schoolyard:l fence. On it was this notice, in big letters Live Bear Wanted. One hundred dollars will be paid to anyone who can give us an uninjured- live bear." The notice was signed by the man"' ager of a well-known circus. ,

. , As the other boys gathered round him, Nor- man said, "11l bet you I can catch one, and I'm going to try, at any rate." "How will you do it?" said Charley. "Oh, you wait till I've caught him, and then you'll see,"

As Norinan Went home, he devised this plan. In the woods not far from his house. there was a regular bear-track, where a trapper had caught two bears that season. In the middle of this • track he would dig a hole big enough to hold a bear,..and so deep that if he got in he could not climb out; and he would cover the hole with sticks and dry leaves, so that when the bear . came along he would not know it was a h01e.4 As soon as he got borne he took an old shovel from the barn and went off into the woods to, look for a good place•for his trap. Soon after he struck the track he found a soft place near a brook, where the ,bears evidently came to drink. He began to work right away, and got quite a hole dug, when the sbund of a bugle 'Warned him that he ought to be at home, heijj- ing his father in the night duties. That was the way his father and mother had of calling Nor- Man when he was off in the woods. -So, drop- ping his shovel, he ran back to the house as fast as he could go, for he was a good boy, and always wanted to help his father'all he could.

Foi.•the next week he used all his spare time digging the hole, and the boys could not get him to play' with them when school was out, nor would he tell them what he was doing. It • was a hard job, and We need not take tirne'to tell, how he did it and how, he made a little • ladder out,of the trunk of a tree when the hole was so deep he had to lug the dirt out. But at . last he finished it, and covered it over nicely with branches and fallen leaves. If you had gone along there you would never have, dreamed. there was a hole in the track. .

Every day, sometimes heave- breakfast, some- times in the afternoon, he went to the hole to Sct if he had caught a bear. He went so many, times without finding anything that one Satur- day afternoon he made up his Mind, that be would give it up after one more try. So off he went, taking a pail with him to get ;some -straw- ; berries which hellad found in an 'open place in the woods-near his hole. "Don't be gone long, . Norman'," said his father, " for it's nearly work- • , time.", • ,4,)!` "No, I won't," Said the boy. And lie was • not, for soon he came running back, shouting, • •, as he came out of the -woods, "Oh, father, I have caught a bear!" And, coming up, he told him about the hole that he had dug. and that 4 when he went to it he saw. the sticks were broken, and heard the whining of the bear, that .was trying his best to get out - " Bun, Norman," said his \father, "and ask , 4 some of the neighbours to some and help us pull him out, and I will find some rope to make a noose." Soon the proud boy came back with ,several • men and boys he bad picked up. "What are , • you going to do with your money, Norm?" • said Charley Smith. "Oh, I'm going to buy a horse with part of it, and perhaps one of tho§e singing machines." As they came up to the hole, loud whines . showed that the bear had. not got away. The men began, to fix the rope and to 111 TM-we what each should do in order to gel the priie safely out of the hole. Then they ,went to the edge and pulled away the sticks and looked in. "For the land's sake!" exclaimed Toni Kirby. "That is no bear! That'si Damon's big black pig that got out of the sty 'a Week ago r And • sure enough so it wins, and you may • believe that Norman did not, hear the last of his: bear for quite a while. "Bought your horse 'yet?" or "Got your talking machine. Norm?" were - common questions from the boys when he mat them at school.

Song.—" Stars of Love." By Percy Elliott. is. 6d. net. This is really a good song, and no singer ought to be without it. It is not difficult to play and contains some fine harmonies. It is written in two keys, No. 1 in F and No. 2 in G. •

Waltz.—" Wedding Bells." By Frank Brad- sell. Price Is. 6d.. net. No orchestra ought to be without this. really fine waltz. We hope to hear it played often in the ballroom this season. We predict an unbounded success.

Poorer Livings.

It is a noble effort that the Ratatist commu- nity has set itself to accomplish,, and judging from the remarks of the various speakers in Warrington on Monday afternoon and evening, it is a step which is being taken none too soon. The scheme is the raising of the sum of a quar- ter of a million pounds for what is termed the Baptist Sustentation. Fund. • The women members of the Baptist Churches in the town assembled at the Golborne-street Church on Monday afternoon, under the presi- dency of Mrs. Chodburn. Miss Marsden, a Blackburn lady, gave the address.

Following upon the ,opening remarks from the chair, Miss MARSDEN outlined the scheme, • which, she Said, was very dear to her heart. She did not belong to any minister's family, nor was she connected with any, but she knew that many ministers were not receiving what they ought. The Baptist Union wanted to raise £50,000. It sounded, and really was, a large sum, but she was sure it was not too much for the Baptist denomination to raise. The minis- ters themselves had started excellently, and had raised £B,OOO, and much of that came,from the poorer ministers themselves,- at a very great sacrifice. Atter the ministers had done some- thing, they, the congregations, did not want to be behind. They had a large number of minis- ters in their denomination who got .150 yearly, some 160, some £7O, dao, and SO on, and the idea of this sustentation fund was to raise these small stipends to not , lcss than .1:100 to ci:l2o for unmarried men, and A:120 to ,2150 for mar- ried ministers.. She had heard it said that some of those small •churches which could not afford to pay their ministers must not have One. The Gospel must be preached, and preached everywhere. The Gospel flag must he kept flying, and they wanted to make it possible for the Gospel to be preached by raising the stipends not to a point Of luxury; the minister's did ,not ask for that; but they wanted to make it possible for him and his wife to do far more faithful service. Some of these men, with . their wives and families, had to struggle bard upon their stipends, yet under all ircumstances they expected their minister and his wife to go to their houses with a, smiling face. "They cannot do. it any more than we can, under such depressing circumstances,"- re- marked Miss Marsden.

100- Those little churches had a great claim upon their sympathy and support, and they wanted to help to roll away the burden. .(Cheers.)

div.head: No Luxury Wanted
div.p: No Luxury Wanted

Villago churches could not increase the min- isters' Stipends. lie cannot enlarge his congre- gation, for; as the children-of the families in the villages grow up, they are attracted, and off they go, to the big towns. Then they wanted their minister to be capable of representing them, and to stand side by side with the clergy- man of the village. ,The wife they wanted to stand side by side with the clergyman's .wife; she could not do it on .€5O a year. She liked to have a new dress and a new hat from time to time, just as they did, but she wanted no luxury. They must have them capable and able to repre- sent them to their credit. A minister must have his books and papers and' magazines just as a joiner or engineer must have his tools. A third point was that they wanted to be able to give temporary help to those ministers who were without a church. The audience knew as well as she did how absolutely necessary that was. Again and again ministers were str,anded with- out a church, through no fault of their own, and as they had never jearned a trade, they wanted to give them relief *until they got a church. She had felt it Very strongly that they did not make it possible for their young edu- cated men; to enter their Baptist ministry. There were plenty of young men at *Oxford and Cambridge, who would really in their ._hearts like to preach the Gospel, but there were no attractions, and they wanted to Jake it tempt- ing for these young men, who also did not seek after luxury. They could not afford to have an uneducated ministry, and to prevent this they would have to offer more attractions than in the past. They did not ask them to pay the minister for his preaching, they wanted to make it pos- sible to preach the Gospel. She wondered if they had ever thought of the minister's influ- ence and how much they owed to him. In the 20th century they could not for a moment imagine what it would be like without the min- isters. Let them look at. the influence upon the children and young people. ,This kind of thing went on so quietly that they were hardly aware of it.. What a hard lot it was for some of the poor country ministers. yet they must have their poor, churches, and they must be supported by the stronger ones. The scheme allowed them three years in which to pay their , contribution, and the women wanted to raise .€50,000, and the secretary. speaking of the scheme, practically said that if the women would raise .€50,000, they would be assured of the success of the scheme. She was quite aware that most women were dependent upon their husbands, but there were many means of raising money, and the women were determined to give something. They wanted to see the effect of the scheme in their lifetime. and she hoped the women of Warrington would respond heartily. (Cheers.)

A Most Critical Moment. The -Rev. F. G. BENSKIN, of Bristol, expressed • the pleasure it gave him to see so many ,Baptist ' women of. Warrington. They in the, denomina- tion had come to/ the parting of the ways, and were face to face, perhaps, with one of the

most critical movements that they had ever been / called to undertake in the history of the Bap- tist Church. They had had their si?are in years gone by in enterprises for the strengthening of the Baptist Church, but he did not think there was any piece of work equal to that before them. They all understood that • they were now em- barked, Ntithout any chance of looking back, upon an effort to raise a quarter of a million pounds. By that scheme they were asking for the support of all their weaker churches. At the outset ha said he recognised, with very great thankfulness and very great pleasure and gladness, the immense debt they owed to the women in their churches. In the Bible there were numerous accounts of the help women had given, and right down through the centuries in the history of their Churches, women had been splendid in their service, and, speaking a's a minister, he knew something of the debt they owed to their wives. If it had not been for the help of his wife he did not think it would have been, possible to have got through his work. Now they were appealing once again to the women, and' he was sure that he was not pleading in vain. The women had promised -.1-'50„000, and they wduld raise it. (Hear, hear.) There ;was no doubt about it that they were taking their part every- where, right through the country. The Baptist 'Union was asking for their sympathy for the minister's :wife and children. Some of the women could contribute out of their own private resources, but there were all sorts "of methods of raising money. They had 'a large number of poor churches. One Church in every seven had membership of less than 50. and one church in every three had a membership of less than

div.head: Stirring and Pointed Addresses.
div.p: Stirring and Pointed Addresses.

In .the evening a public meeting was held, when there were speeches from a deputation, composed of the Revs. F. G. Benskin, of Bristol; William Owen, of Manchester, and .Mr. .1. W. Scholefield, of Liverpool. • Mr. JAMES KIINWORTIIY, who presided, said that the main object of the meeting was to interest them in what Was called the Baptist Sustenta- tion Fund. According to the report of the Secretary of the Baptist Union at a Manchester meeting a' few weeks ago, £12,000 had already been raised. thid it was expected that by the end of April the whole of the £230,000 would be raised, which, if invested at 4 per cent., would bring in £lO,OOO a. year. They had in that neighbourhood no rich churches; neither had they any who would benefit from this scheme. But there were churches that could not afford to pay the amount of the minister's stipend., fixed by the Sustentation Fund Committee, and it was worth while to remember that the eye of the Master was upon them. Mr. J. W. SCHOLEMELD said that he dared say they had some idea of the extent of which everyone of them had been forced to believe that' the conditions of things in their Baptist ministry had become intolerable. Intolerable was a very strong word to use, but it was not too strong for the condition of things that had been cast upon them, when men could tell them and they could not contradict, that their minis- ters were the poorest paid in. all the Free Churches. That surely should have been intol- erable. He was the district treasurer of the Western District of the County Association, and he could, perhaps, say that nearly one-half of the amount promised had already been paid in. That meant another very good thing, that not only had the response been prompt, but it meant that the people recognised the need. They had had meetings in the large • towns, and those meetings, although they had mat done as much as some of them had hoped, they had done nobly. By the aid of the capital that was just being raised, it was to be made possible to level every minister's stipend to such a point that the country minister shall have his £lOO and the town minister his £l2O, fpr unmarried men. The scheme quite necessarily demanded that the men who were to share in this sustentation shall be duly qualified miqisters. They should not think that the spiritual condition of the Churches was bound to suffer if such a scheme was carried. They must help their poorer churches. He wondered how many of their members realised that they were members of one body. They were not only members of one Church, but inheritors to a long and glorious history.

div.head: Great Inheritance.
div.p: A Great Inheritance.

He had just been reading with great care a history of the Baptists of the North-West coun- try, and he had been impressed as he had trav- elled from the source to the end, with all the different streams that converged at last to make their county associations. They had to, thank the men who had gone before them for the in- heritance they had received, and let them say to themselves by act, as well as by speech, "We will not hand over ,our inheritance to those to come not only no poorer, but all the more richer and vigorous." (Applau§e.)

The -Bev. WILLIAMi OWEN said that he did not wish to stand between Mr. Benskin and the people, because he (the speaker) had been there before. The poor they always had with them. (Laughter.) He wanted to speak to them that night on the grace of giving. He had heard hundreds of sermons in his time, but had never yet, so far as he could recognise, heard one on the grace of giving. It was a delicate question for a minister to handle, especially when he depended upon the congregation for his stipend, and undoubtedly that ,was one Of the reasons why it was not spoken about. There were tremendous miscon- ceptions on this subject. The collection ghould be an attraction as much as the sermon was. They should give according to their means. There were scores and scores of Churches work- ing practically under the sweating, system, unable to maintain their ministers worthily, to whom they paid an inadequate wage. The greatest institute in the world to-day was the Church. If they supported the Church in War- rington they would be supporting the work in China. "Freely ye shall receive if freely ye shall give." If they did not give •freely, did they really exPect to receive freely? He won- dered if they had ever thought of self-denial in relation to this gift. How many of them denied themselves to the point of self-sacrifice?

div.head: Vote of Two.
div.p: The Vote of Two.

He illustrated self-sacrifice by a story of a couple who had saved £lO- for their annual holiday. At that time the Church was badly in need of money. A conference was held, and the two only were present. The husband proposed that instead of the going away they should give the money to the Church. The wife seconded that; carried unanimously. (Cheers.) "All those," he said, "who applauded, go and do likewise." (Loud laughter.) One of their min- isters had contributed A:75 to the fund out of a salary of £5OO. All praise to him. Another had given „t 3 out of £lOO. There was more merit in the latter gift. The one had £425 left, and the other £97. He wondered if the Lord judged by what we had left, and whether He praised the same people as they _did._ (Cheers.)

_ The Rev. F. G. BESSEIN said that it had been keyed again and again that the Baptist people could respond to their- various calls upon them, and now was the opportunity of proving it once more. Undoubtedly, as Mr. Owen had said, the Church was the greatest institute in the .world. They .were passing through some very critical changes. Every :time of change was necessarily a time of crisis, but every season of crisis was also a time of opportunity. What measured the strength of the Church? The power of an Church was to be measured by the power of her ministry. They must have a strong ministry, and the Church wolild necessarily be strong also. No Church could rise above the level of its officers. A weak ministry meant a feeble Church, and an impoverished ministry an in- efficient Church'. They had adequate resources now to .meet the task. but the problem was that they wanted in their midst a ministry that would show, guide and teach the Church that she will be able to use her resources for the dis- charge of the, task in front of her.

div.head: Not a New Problem.
div.p: Not a New Problem.

That problem was not by far a new one. It had been with them for long, long years, and how had they dealt with it They had treated it in the way they had treated many other i pro- blems. It was first mentioned at a meeting early in the seventeenth century, and at inter- vals sin::c, but it was not until April, 1:312, that they started to collect coatributions. div.head: THRIFT AND HORSERACING.
div.p: THRIFT AND HORSERACING.

Devotion to horscracing would not by some people be considered a good advertisement for a young nation. Australians are very fond of horseflesli of all descriptions, and they patronise the racecourse to a greater extent than the resi- dents of any other country. It is remarkable that the various racing Clubs of Australia pay away £622,000 .annually in, prize money. This exceeds by £13,060 the total amount paid out by the race clubs of Great Britain and Ireland, including £30,000 given for races under National Hunt Butes. • 'Racing in Australia is attended by very -little vice. The betting is not excessive, and the great amounts paid in prize money serve chiefly to demonstrate the extraordinary prosperity which is enjoyed by all classes of the inhabi- tants. Horseracing, too, is a reat stimulant to the horsebreeding industry, which is one of the Commonwealth's big rural assets. Those who think that a strong disposition to horse- racing does not go with thrift, should turn to the statistics which show the records of Aus- tralia's Savings Banks; where they will discover that the average Australian spends by no means all his money upon horseracing, or indeed any other sport or recreation.

Grappenhall St. Wilfred's v. Widnes Juniors.

At Widnes. Grappenhall started and at once became aggressive. Smart combination on the part of the juniors' forwards resulted in Dever- all going through on his own account, beating Shakeshaft with a low shot. At this reverse Grappenhall attacked., and from a pass from the left Woodcock equalised. Splendid football was witnessed, and Pickering was prominent with a clever centre, for tiollins to score a, second for Widnes. Richards got. the Grappen- hall left wing going, and from a good centre Wocdcock again scored, the interval arriving with the score 2-2.

On the resumption the visitors attacked .strongly, and the home defence was severely tested. The " Saints " keeping up the pres- sure again scored, Richards being the contribu- tor. The Widnes forwards pressed and forced a corner, and, to the delight of their supporters, Deverall, after a scramble in front of goal, scored. At this point, play was of a give-and- take nature, and Widnes forced. another corner, from which Deverall headed through in grand style, time arriving with the score 4-3, in ,favour of Widnes. Evans, H. Parr and Richards were the pick of the Grappenhall team.

ENCOURAGING LATE SEASON.

The fine weather last week-end was respon- sible for drawing more members out than usually go out at this time of the year. We have known many anglers to put up their rods until the next opening season about this time, but up to the present we have not heard of one giving the sport up. Whether it is the list of specials, or the poor sport we have had near home, it is difficult to say. After the rain we have had lately the fish. in our canals and rivers will be all the better, both' in condition and sport, and if members who anticipated putting up their rods for the season will only continue a little longer we are sure they will be repaid for their efforts. It will not take a great catch at Norton to win the first three specials for roach, and these are valued at otl.

The Gowy had a fair share of visitors last week-end, but again they returned without up- setting calculations. Several runs were gut with pike by a member, but his tackle was not good enough for the occasion and he retirned disappointed. However, he brought home a great catch of flowers to remind him of his day at the Gowy. HARTFORD,

The Coopers' Arms fished their third match of the season here with a fair amount of success. An enjoyable journey by 'bus was followed by favourable fishing conditions, especially for con- tests. The Secretary, Mr. R. Bradshaw, soon had his men to their pegs and the contest was started without delay. The winner was found in J. Bradbury. It is the second contest this year that Bradbury has won from this house, his weight being 11b. 70z.; 2, IL Owen, 11b..50z. 12dr. ; 3, B. Bradbury, 11b. ;oz. Bdr.; 4, W. Owen, llb. 3oz. 2dr.; 5, J. div.head: N.A.A. EMERGENCY COMMITTEE.
div.p: N.A.A. EMERGENCY COMMITTEE.
The committee visited Warrington on Satur- day last to hold their meeting at the Bay Horse. After about two hours' discussion on the grand

match they had tea, provided by Mr. Tom Roberts. This is the first meeting of N.A. offi- cials in Warrington for several years, and, ac- cording to the impression on the working of the Warrington clubs left with them, it will be no distant date when we shall have them again. They were delighted by the returns on the set board from the Gowy, and several have arranged to have a day with one or two of our members to inform their members on the fishing of it. Mr. 17! W. Redford is quite in favour with a scheme our delegate, Mr. 'Pottgr, is prepared to put forward. If this is brought about War- rington will have no need to subscribe to the Upkeep of the Gowy or any other water, that any centre may require. . A. S.

At half- time the home team led by 2-0. In the second half the play was more evenly distributed, and Winnington scored twice and Latchford once (througn .3finards). A keen, pleasant. game ended, in a victory for Latchford by 3 goals to two. On the home side, Bruhl played finely in •goal and kicked with judgment and power. Billington played very well at full-back, and Knight was the best of a good half-back line, while the forwards all round gave their •best display of the season. The second eleven at Winnington Park came off victorious by two goals to one. It was an enjoyable, fast and open game, and the •Latch- ford second eleven showed that the first team have some good reserves to call up when neces- sary. The defence especially was very good, Bradshaw and, Banks at back holding the, op- posing' forwards well in hand. Furness and, Holt found the net for Latchford, while Fletcher had hard lines in not adding another twd goals to tbe score.

_ The Warrington half-backs were good. In eyery department they Were superior to W. Farnsworth and the much-praised Anlezark. Nicholas got the ball away quickly from the scrums. Ruddick opened up many useful runs. The little half-back was.there all the time, and made so many so many circles round Anlezark that the • latter did not quite know where he was.

All through the Warrington "threes" played splendidly, but with the exception of Renwick, they had not the speed to cope with the Oldham quartette once they got away with an open field, as happened for them every time they scored. RENWICK :TO THE FRONT.

Renwick was . the most conspicuous man amongst the Warrington foursome. His tack- ling was good, and he brought off several fine runs, which, but for downright ill-luck and nothing else, should have produced at least a couple of tries.' Howard Davis was more con- spicuous for his defensive' than hi aggressive work. Some of his tackles were as timely as they were clever. Dickenson was a useful man, if somewhat on the Slow side, when put in comparison With the opposing threequarterS-. His conscientious game was fittingly capped' by the remarkably dropped goal he scored.. Waywell justified his selection. He Played a sterling game all the way. In a few runs he showed a welcome turn of speed, and he has a considerable knowledge of the swerving art. It was in defending that lie was most successful, and some of his tackles were as smint as they were effective.

div.head: JOLLEY MADE SOME SLIPS.
div.p: JOLLEY MADE SOME SLIPS.

Jolley was not cinite up to his usual game. Ile. did not gather the ball with his accustomed sureness, and one bad mistake let the Oldham- ites,score their last try. His game was not that which We witnessed at Wilderspool the\p'revious Saturday. It was rather 'a repetition of that given at Swinton. Jolley was very fitful, and at times brought off some brilliant saves; at others he mulled, and from one of those he allowed Oldham to rush him and score, when they should not have done so. It was undoubt- edly an "off" day with our little back. A slippery ground and a greasy ball is not suitable for Jolley, as was proved at Swinton, and again at Oldham. In addition to this, which undoubtedly upset his game, he was rigorously watched by the Oldhamites, who used more force than was necessary. The .way they attacked Jolley indicated that their game was to knock him out, and once or twice this intentional rough work was so palpable that it . . was surprising should have escaped the notice of the referee.

div.head: CUP TIE AT WILDERSPOOL. Warrington Should Beat Barrow.
div.p: CUP TIE AT WILDERSPOOL. Warrington Should Beat Barrow.

Warrington v)-day meet Barrow in the first round of the Lancashire Cup at Wilderspool, and if they play up to the form displayed at Oldham on Saturday, victory should rest with them. Barrow must not be under-rated. They have now shaken down, and as the seapor't men are notorious cup .fighters, they will put in all they know. The visitors already hold a stronger position in the League table than Warrington, but they have played one match less, and thus on the League games the two teams seem well balanced. _ _ .

It must be remembered that while Warring. ton have met some of the strongest teams in the League, Barrow on the other hand have Met teams of a lesser character; and therefore it is scarcely a fair, criterion to base judgment upon the League performances. Barrow have met at home and defeated Bram- ley, Leigh, Swinton, while they have been heavily defeated at Rochdale and Salford, but won at Bradford. Warrington, on the other hand, have defeated at home Leigh, Broughton Rangers and St. Helens, and Batley away, while they have been unsuccessful at -Huddersfield, Swinton and Oldham.

On'the points scored in the competition, Bar- row have an advantage over Warrington, but it must be remembered they have not played the standard of matches that Warrington has, and these figures convey very little information as, to the prospects of the two sides.

div.head: MUST GO THE PACE.
div.p: MUST GO THE PACE.

Warrington all the same will have to go the pace if they are to win, but they have an ad- vantage in being drawn at home. If we have an improvement on the standard shown at Old- ham I have no fear, but that they will win; perhaps by about five points, if not more. Dob- kin and Mitchell are the. two Barrovians they will have to watch most closely. The committee on Wednesday night made drastic changes in at least one department of the team, namely at half-back. Ruddick has been substituted by Renwick, who, it will be remem- bered, played in this position last season. Re will be "stand off" to Nicholas. Captain Bra - shaw is able to resume, and will be in his old position at wing threequarter. Skelhorne has not qualified in time to participate in the cup tie, and will be an absentee. Blundell, who has been playing so well with the reserves, will fill his place in the pack. . The Warrington team will take the field as follow:

div.head: HONORARY MEMBERS TO PAY.
div.p: HONORARY MEMBERS TO PAY.

The gate behind the honorary members' stand will not be open to-morrow, and honorary mem- bers will have to pass through the members' entrance. Honorary members have to pay ad- mission to ground and stand for the cup-tie.

div.head: WARRINGTON CLUB MEMS.
div.p: WARRINGTON CLUB MEMS.

It should be remembered that the cup tie at Wilderspool starts to-day at 3 o'clock. Councillor Peacock, the Mayor-elect, is to attend the match. He has become an honorary member of the club; and we shall see our future Mayor at many of the match& His patronage is much appreciated by the committee. Green, who was sent off in the "A" match at Wildorspool for fighting with an Oldham "A" man, was suspended for two matches by the N.U. Committee on Tuesday.

div.head: WARRINGTON "A" DEFEAT OLDHAM "A." Had Brarnhall a " Nerves" Attack?
div.p: WARRINGTON "A" DEFEAT OLDHAM "A." Had Brarnhall a " Nerves" Attack?

Warrington "A," two goals two tries (ten Points); Oldham "A," nil. Such was the read- ing•of the score board at the close of hostilities at Wilderspool. Oldham brought a strong side, and undoubtedly meant business, but had to return home without having even penetrated the " Wirepullers' " defence. Considering the "class" players Oldham have on , their reserve list, Warrington did much more thaii their supporters anticipated in win- ning so handsomely, and it is reasonable to sup- pose, from the way they played in the second half, that, had the ground not been so slippery, the score might have been much larger. The heavy downpour of rain about noon did not have much effect on the attendance, a good number of spectators lining the arena when Warrington commenced operations. The first half mostly went in favour of Old- ham, and once, or twice they were almost through, but the keen tackling of Daintith, A. Browiik and Douglas prevented a score. The only tangible point recorded in the initial half was a fine goal kicked by Critchley from near the touch4ine. It was a really fine effort, and well iiierited the applause he received. In the second moiety Warrington did most of the pressing, and Oldham were kept hard on the. defence. They did make one or two raids on the railway goal, but failed to put on the finishing touches. A. Brown scored a beautiful try for Warrington, from which CritchleY landed another fine goal. Douglas also put on the finishing touch to .ft really fine movement, hut this time Critchley was unsuccessful with the kick.

div.head: A. Brown's Mastcrly Game.
div.p: A. Brown's Mastcrly Game.

On the Warrington side, A. Brown, at half- back, played a masterly-game, and his try was really a beauty. Douglas, too, was very little inferior to his clubmate, and he and Brown are developing a splendid understanding; and, judg- ing them on Saturday's play, both are worth a trial with the seniors. The threequarters were best represented by Daintith and Baker, the former especially doing good work. Time after time he got going., and was almost a certain scorer, but his final transfer was generally spoiled by Davies, who either overran the ball, or could not stick to it. There was some excuse for this, however, as the sphere was somewhat slippery.
C. Brown, at centre, shaped very well, and will do still better with a little more practice. The forwards all played a good game, and none were more prominent than Naylor, Harmer and Critchley.

div.head: / Bramhall Disappoints.
div.p: / Bramhall Disappoints.

A. Bramhall, the latest " capture " from Rylands' Recreation, occupied the full-back position. I cannot say that he played a very convincing game. The Bramhall of Rylands', and the Bramhall on Saturday were two differ- ent beings, but, perhaps, he was suffering from an attack of "nerves." Once or ,twice he brought off one or two good tackles, but his kicking was very poor indeed and lacked judgment. An- other great fault of his on Saturday was that he stood too far behind his "three," and will do well to rectify this error in future. I have seen him play some extraordinary good games with the " Wiremen," his kicking being, one of the great features of his '1)14, but on Saturday I was greatly, disappointed with his exhibition. I hope, however,', he will do better when he has got settled down to his new surroundings. On the Oldham side, Cook played a great game at full-back, and had it not been for him the score must have been greater. Young showed a fine turn of speed, and at times the three- quarters gave a good exhibition of passing. The half-backs were smart, but could not make much headway against the Warrington -pair. • The forwards packed well, but in the loose could not

div.head: MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAD' E.
div.p: MANCHESTER AND DISTRICT LEAD' E.
First Division. Rylands' Recs.' Fine Win.

Wardley were the visitors at Gorsey-lane. Wardley were at full strength, Rylands' being short of three of 'their regular hacks, Carter, Griffiths and Bramhall, the last of whom had signed a form for Warrington. Rylands' com- menced toward the pavilion end. Floyd dropped a goal in the first five, minutes. After this re- verse Wardley, by good forward work, com- menced to attack, but could' not break through the defence. Rylands' next had a chance, but the backs being disorganised, they failed to take the advantage. At this point Morris was carried off injured. Half-time arrived with the score: Rylands', one goal (two points); Wardley, nil. RYlands' commenced, the second half a man short, and Wardley were not slow to take the advantage. After attacking for a short spell Mooney, the ex-Leigh half-back, scored, Cooper failing at goal.' After this reverse Warren went half-back, Floyd going centte. This seemed to improve the game, and Warren, being ob- structed, was awarded a penalty, from which he landed a goal, putting Rylands' one point ahead. Wardley were next awarded a penalty in front of the posts, but Mooney failed miserably. The game ended in favour of the home team by two goals (four points) to Wardley-, one try (three points).

div.head: Rylmids' Recs.' " A " v. Dillon Recs.
div.p: Rylmids' Recs.' " A " v. Dillon Recs.

The above match in the St. Helens and Dis- trict League was played at Ditton under wretched conditions. The first half Was evenly contested, and half-time arrived with, the score sheet blank. On resuming, Ditton forced mat- ters, with a result that three tries were scored, one being converted. In the latter stages of the game the " Wiremen" pressed hard, but the Ditton defence held out: Final: Ditton.Rees., 11 points; Rylands' Recs. "A," nil. Riley and Adamson were the pick of the Rylands' team, whilst 01Garra and Hankin played well for Ditton. •
